repository.issues_template:
## Summary

Please summarise the issue or bug. What (exact version of the code did it happen with? Was that a vanilla or modified version?

If this refers to a more general issue or feature, is it important to fix right now, and would you have time to help?

## Exact steps to reproduce

How one can reproduce the issue - this is important; remember to attach all relevant files, in particular the original files so we can regenerate the TPR when necessary.

## For developers: Why is this important?

As a user you can let the developers discuss this, but for those of you who are developers:

1. Is this an actual issue (file it), something that will have major positive impact in the project (file it), or something you are working on (file it)? If it's merely a possibility of making code a bit nicer, or general good-to-have thing, consider that we can likely come up with 10,000 such ideas - most of those work better as concrete merge requests that address the matter rather than first keeping issues open for months or years.

2. If this is a follow-up issue from a previous code review, is this something the author & reviewers agreed to do as a follow-up in the short term (then assign it to them). Avoid using issues as a general way of scratching down code improvements that might be nice to do some rainy day, although neither you nor the original author have any intention of actually looking at it any time in the foreseeable future :-)

3. Again if you are a developer, are you fixing/closing roughly one old issue for every new one you open (in particular this one), or are we creating new minor issues that somebody else will have to go through and close in 3-6 months?

4. Finally, as a seasoned developer we typically expect that you also contribute to making sure the issue has both a person and milestone assigned, not necessary immediately when you create it, but if the original submitter doesn't contribute to finding somebody to handle it, don't expect that some other developer will do it for you, and expect the issue to instead be closed when it remains unassigned for extended periods.


## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

## Relevant input files, logs and/or screenshots

Please attach at least the top of the GROMACS log file (it provides important information about the hardware and software versions), and likely a TPR file together with the raw GRO/MDP files required to regenerate it.

## Possible fixes

If you have any suggestion, or even finished fix or merge request, that's awesome!

closed_issues.title: Runtime error with certain NNP models
closed_issues.description:
When using e.g. the [Nutmeg](https://github.com/openmm/nutmeg) NNP models, running inference on the GPU produces a
```
RuntimeError: Global alloc not supported yet
```
This seems to be due to an [issue](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/144965) with automatic graph optimizations in TorchScript.

Turning them off will solve the problem, with little impact on performance.

closed_issues.title: Stream priorities reversed with AdaptiveCpp < 25.10
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Since !5468, we are using `cudaDeviceGetStreamPriorityRange` to query the priority range when running on CUDA or HIP backends of ACpp. However, the arguments are reversed: `cudaDeviceGetStreamPriorityRange(&highPrioValue, &lowPrioValue);` while the signature is `__host__ ​cudaError_t cudaDeviceGetStreamPriorityRange ( int* leastPriority, int* greatestPriority )`.

Since AdaptiveCpp 25.10, there is an extension to query priority range (3fa495d936b0ebef7f447ed68d88cb58ccdc39d0), so it should work okay.

## For developers: Why is this important?

On Dardel with ROCm 6.3 and AdaptiveCpp 25.02, it does not seem to have a major effect on performance, but having the priorities off is hardly helping.

## Possible fixes

Call the API correctly.

closed_issues.title: MPI parallel free energy calculations process were not killed
closed_issues.description:
Dear GROMACS developer.

Thank you for your fast and useful GROMACS MD engine. With the recent popularity of Free Energy calculations, I use GROMACS to execute FEP.

In my environment, I use the -multidir run option of the GPU/MPI compiled version in a container (apptainer) to calculate FEP in 4λ increments.

When a job is canceled, the execution of the container itself is killed, but the GROMACS calculation running with mpirun is not killed and continues to remain on the server.　Additionally, this behavior only occurs when calling free energy routines like FEP (following exection), not when just computing conventional MD with -multidir (same execution but -dhdl dhdl option and related option in MDP file were removed).

```
mpirun -np 4 gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm prod -multidir lambda_0 lambda_1 lambda_2 lambda_3 -dhdl dhdl -ntomp 2 -pin off -quiet -nobackup -nb gpu -pme gpu -bonded gpu -gpu_id 0
```

I use GROMACS 2025.4 to execute those runs. If anyone knows how to deal with this, please let me know.

Best regards.

closed_issues.title: gmx mdrun performance issue on multicore cpu
closed_issues.description:
Since GROMACS 2026, the performance of a trivial benchmark can be much lower compared to previous series:

for example, running the `benchMEM` benchmark with zero iteration and 48 `tMPI` tasks on `2025.3`:

```
$ mdrun -s benchMEM.tpr -nt 48 -nsteps 0

               Core t (s)   Wall t (s)        (%)
       Time:        1.376        0.031     4484.2
                 (ns/day)    (hour/ns)
Performance:        5.630        4.263
```

but the same command on `2026`

```
$ mdrun -s benchMEM.tpr -nt 48 -nsteps 0

               Core t (s)   Wall t (s)        (%)
       Time:      633.048       14.224     4450.6
                 (ns/day)    (hour/ns)    (ms/step)  (Matom*steps/s)
Performance:        0.012     1975.535    14223.850            0.006
```

When running with `KMP_AFFINITY=compact,verbose` we notice that the `OpenMP` runtime uses `48` `OpenMP` threads in `2025.3` but `1505` in `2026` (!).

FWIW a workaround is to explicitly `export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`

closed_issues.title: Fix HIP device arch setup with newer version of amdclang
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Newer versions of amdclang would fail to setup the device arch detection as the test input file would not be treated as HIP code.

**GROMACS version**

All versions since HIP support got added.

**Steps to reproduce**

Use bleeding edge version of amdclang and try to run CMake with this compiler as the CMAKE_HIP_COMPILER.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

CMake fails at is doesn't detect any valid offload-arch targets.

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

Configuration should succeed and offload-arch targets should be correctly identified.

**Possible fixes**

Add explicit -x hip to the command line in the CMake check, so files are treated as HIP input files

closed_issues.title: GPU Free Energy kernel yields incorrect energy values compared to CPU at lambda endpoints
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

The new GPU Free Energy kernel produces significantly incorrect `\xD\f{}H \xl\f{}` values compared to the CPU kernel. This discrepancy is most prominent in the final column of the output, where the GPU kernel returns massive outliers (e.g., -6.38e7 or 1.33e8) for values that should be effectively zero or consistent with the CPU calculation.

**GROMACS version**

2026.0

**Steps to reproduce**

Run a Free Energy perturbation simulation targeting the endpoints (Lambda 0 and Lambda 63) using both CPU and GPU kernels for comparison.

Lambda 0 (Zero step):
```
# GPU execution
gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm lambda_0/gromacs -nbfe gpu
# CPU execution
gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm lambda_0/gromacs
```
Lambda 63 (Last step):
```
# GPU execution
gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm lambda_63/gromacs -nbfe gpu
# CPU execution
gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm lambda_63/gromacs
```

**What is the current bug behavior?**

The .xvg output files show massive discrepancies in the calculated energy differences for the last window between CPU and GPU runs.

Case 1: Lambda 0 The CPU kernel produces a reasonable value for the last window (`~1164.8`). The GPU kernel produces a large negative value (`~ -63 million`).CPU Output (lambda_0/gromacs.xvg):

`... 1148.6625 1152.6930 1164.8236 22.375225`

GPU Output (lambda_0/gromacs.xvg):

`... 1148.6584 1152.6888 -63817586. 22.375225`

Case 2: Lambda 63 The CPU kernel produces 0.0000000 for the last window (as defined by the simulation setup). The GPU kernel produces a large positive outlier (`~133 million`).
CPU Output (lambda_63/gromacs.xvg):

`... 22.030062 9.4721044 0.0000000 22.324461`

GPU Output (lambda_63/gromacs.xvg):

`... 22.030055 9.4721046 1.3328709e+08 22.324461`

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

The GPU kernel should produce energy values identical (or within standard floating-point tolerance) to the CPU kernel.
For Lambda 0, the value should be approximately 1164.8236.
For Lambda 63, the value should be exactly 0.0.

closed_issues.title: gmx wham: Incorrect IACT calculation at large coordinates due to precision loss
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

`gmx wham` calculates incorrect Integrated Autocorrelation Times (IACT) when the `-ac` flag is used for solutes positioned at large coordinates in long trajectories (e.g., $z > 5.0$ nm, >320 ns simulation length) due to single-precision floating-point arithmetic limits.

This issue was observed in **GROMACS 2024.5** (vanilla) and persists in **GROMACS 2026.0** (source) (both mixed precision).

When accumulating position data to calculate the mean position of a solute far from the origin, single-precision `float` variables suffer from catastrophic cancellation (loss of significance). This results in a persistent error (DC offset) in the calculated deviation, which leads to the autocorrelation function plateauing at a non-zero noise floor rather than decaying. Consequently, the integration loop yields physically impossible correlation times (e.g., >25,000 ps) instead of the correct values (e.g., ~1-5 ps in bulk water).

## Exact steps to reproduce

1.  Set up an umbrella sampling simulation where the pull coordinate is far from the origin (e.g., a lipid membrane system where the solute is at $z \approx 5.5$ nm).
2.  Run the simulation to generate `pullf.xvg` files (e.g., >320 ns data).
3.  Run the analysis command:
    `gmx wham -it tpr-files.dat -if pullf-files.dat -ac -ac-trestart 100 -acsig 0.3 -o prof.xvg -hist hist.xvg -bins 300 -min -5.49998 -max 6.76418 -temp 310 -b 0 -cycl -nBootstrap 50 -bs-method b-hist -zprof0 -5.39998 -bsres bsResult.xvg -bsprof bsProfs.xvg`
4.  Inspect the output `iact.xvg`.

**Observation:**
*   Solutes near the center ($z \approx 0$) show reasonable IACT values (~1900 ps).
*   Solutes at the edges ($z > 5$ nm) show erroneous values (20,000 - 35,000 ps).

## For developers: Why is this important?

1.  **This is an actual issue.** It renders the error estimation for umbrella sampling invalid for large systems with long trajectories (e.g., membranes, large protein complexes) without the user realizing it (silent numerical error).
2.  I have identified the root cause in `src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_wham.cpp` in the calcIntegratedAutocorrelationTimes function and have a working fix ready to submit as a Merge Request.
3.  Fixing this requires promoting specific accumulators from `real` to `double` in the IACT calculation function.


## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

**(1) What happens:**
The autocorrelation function for distant solutes drops initially but plateaus at a value of approx ~0.15 (the square of the precision error) and never drops below the integration threshold. `gmx wham` integrates this noise floor up to `ntot/2`, resulting in massive overestimation of the correlation time.

**(2) What I expect to happen:**
The IACT should be consistent regardless of the solute's absolute position in space. Independent verification using Python (NumPy FFT) on the same raw data yields an IACT of ~1900 ps, confirming the `gmx wham` output is incorrect.

## Relevant input files, logs and/or screenshots

I have attached the simulation data of one window where this behavior was observed.
Additionally the iact.xvg of the buggy case before my fix (it contains the erroneously high IACT values at the box edges).
And the iact.xvg after my fix (it contains the the expectedly low IACT values at the box edges).

[iact_error.zip](/uploads/5f8ce966490b6fb3d38229d32ffec334/iact_error.zip)

## Possible fixes

I have developed and tested a fix. The issue lies in `calcIntegratedAutocorrelationTimes` in `src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_wham.cpp`.

The accumulators `av` (average), `corr` (correlation array), and temporary variable `tmp` are currently defined as `real` (float).
By calculating the mean:
`av += ztime[j];`
When `ztime` is large ($O(10^6)$) and fluctuations are small ($O(10^{-3})$), precision is lost.

**The Fix:**
I have modified the function to use `double` for `av`, `corr`, and intermediate calculations, casting `ztime` values to `double` before accumulation. This completely resolves the artifact and aligns the output with Python/FFT reference values.

I will submit a Merge Request shortly.

closed_issues.title: Remove hot path warp synchronizations from CUDA nonbonded kernels
closed_issues.description:
nvcc is failing to recognize that `widx`, and subsequently `imask` are uniform within a warp. In the nested if-blocks dependent on imask, unnecessary divergence/sync SASS instructions were being issued. Since this was in the hot path, there's a measurable performance hit for it. By using a shuffle broadcast, the compiler can see the values are identical and removes the extra operations.

Workaround applied in !5715

closed_issues.title: Enabling NNPot requires CUDA irrespective of whether the GPU platform is being used
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

When trying to link libTorch in a CPU-only platform, build fails because the NNPot code references CUDA functions directly.

**GROMACS version**

Current `main` as well as `release-2026`

**Steps to reproduce**

Buildin GROMACS with `-DGMX_NNPOT=TORCH` without CUDA.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

Failure to build `torchmodel.cpp` because it references CUDA functions directly.
```
home/runner/work/colvars/colvars/GROMACS-main-source/src/gromacs/applied_forces/nnpot/torchmodel.cpp:420:17: error: ‘cudaDeviceProp’ was not declared in this scope
  420 |                 cudaDeviceProp prop;
      |                 ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~
/home/runner/work/colvars/colvars/GROMACS-main-source/src/gromacs/applied_forces/nnpot/torchmodel.cpp:421:42: error: ‘prop’ was not declared in this scope
  421 |                 cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, device_.index());
      |                                          ^~~~
/home/runner/work/colvars/colvars/GROMACS-main-source/src/gromacs/applied_forces/nnpot/torchmodel.cpp:421:17: error: ‘cudaGetDeviceProperties’ was not declared in this scope
  421 |                 cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, device_.index());
      |                 ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

Because libTorch has CPU backends (useful for testing), linking it should not automatically trigger the building of CUDA code. Additionally, Colvars can uses libTorch even in the CPU platform without significant overhead (because the inputs are collective variables, computation is much more lightweight than with atomic coordinates).

**Possible fixes**

Linking libTorch could have its own CMake option, separate from `-DGMX_NNPOT` (but the latter could enable the former for backward compatibility).

closed_issues.title: PME gridsReadyForSpread event expectations are too restrictive
closed_issues.description:
`release-2026` has a bug in that PME spread expects each pipeline stage to wait on the PME stream before launching its spread kernel on its respective pipeline stream. But when a PP rank has no atoms, its pipeline stream doesn't wait on the PME stream. Then next step when PME spread starts, the check for complete consumption fails explicitly on non-CUDA builds. CUDA builds appear fine, because they don't check for satisfactory event consumption.

The simplest short-term fix is to allow the event to not be fully consumed. But the PME coordinate receiver already knows which PP ranks will send coordinates from the early messages after a domain repartitioning, so we always know how many pipelines will send non-zero particles and it is simple to use that information.

- [ ] @mark.j.abraham started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/5653#note_2935096431):  (+1 comment)

    > Part of your problem was having too much state in the class. It's easy to make a class contain memebers for "everything to do with *the thing*." But the only time a box is valid to use, it has just been provided by the ForceProviderInput. Its valid lifetime is short. It is not part of the what should be invariant of the class (e.g. "stuff needed *repeatedly* for calculating forces"), so should not be a member. Likewise pairlistForModel_ and shiftVectors_.     > Naturally one might also want to avoid allocating new storage every time one calculates forces, but perhaps that is negligible in the context of model inference. I suggest we make an issue to refactor this next year in the direction of "harder to have lifetime-validity bugs." Then if it gets noticeably slower, there are ways to optimize and avoid the repeated allocations.

closed_issues.title: SigFPE in PTX JIT Compiler with CuFFTMp
closed_issues.description:
In our CI (with T400 GPUs), using an image with CUDA 13.0.2 and NVHPC 25.9 (not in any regular pipeline yet), running a `Debug` build and invoking an FFT (even single-GPU one, via cuFFT API) causes an FPE deep inside CUDA's JIT compiler stack.

Does not seem to be readily reproducible on other systems, so perhaps specific to sm_75.

Should not affect release builds (unless the FPE indicates a genuine bug in the compiler, in which case something else can go wrong).

If we don't enable exceptions (cbf804e88144170b8f9cf859cbc1225a505357a7), the tests pass fine. This is likely the solution here.

closed_issues.title: Gromacs 2025.3 segfaults with ntmpi>2 and 2 GPUs
closed_issues.description:
Hello world,
I first posted this issue on the user forum, but @berkhess asked me to open an issue here as well: https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/segfault-with-ntmpi-2-with-2-gpus

I’m running into issues with Gromacs 2025.3 using a simulation (simple lysozyme in water) that worked on 2024.5.

If I run: `gmx mdrun -deffnm md_0_1 -nb gpu -pme gpu -npme 1 -ntmpi 4 -pin on -nsteps 1000` I get a segfault. If I run `gmx mdrun -deffnm md_0_1 -nb gpu -pme gpu -npme 1 -ntmpi 2 -pin on -nsteps 1000` the simulation runs to completion (eventually). With gromacs 2024.5 I don’t have this issue.

closed_issues.title: Energy discrepancy when running nnpot with 1 vs 2 MPI ranks
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

While experimenting with the Neural Network Potential (NNP) extensions, @HaoZeke and I observed an unexpected energy discrepancy when changing the number of MPI ranks. Running a simple Lennard-Jones (LJ) liquid argon system with a TorchScript-based NNP model produces different energies depending on whether GROMACS is launched with one or two MPI ranks.

**GROMACS version**

(Current main branch build)

<details>
<summary> gmx -quiet --version </summary>

```
             :-) GROMACS - gmx, 2026.0-dev-20251107-ed5b053201 (-:

Executable:   /home/loche/repos/gromacs/tmp/build/bin/gmx
Data prefix:  /home/loche/repos/gromacs (source tree)
Working dir:  /home/loche/repos/gromacs/tmp/nnpot
Command line:
  gmx -quiet --version

GROMACS version:     2026.0-dev-20251107-ed5b053201
GIT SHA1 hash:       ed5b0532017f8b8c6bc6ba41c61a4ee539e89a8f
Precision:           mixed
Memory model:        64 bit
MPI library:         thread_mpi
MPI version:         built in
OpenMP support:      enabled (GMX_OPENMP_MAX_THREADS = 128)
GPU support:         disabled
SIMD instructions:   AVX2_256
CPU FFT library:     fftw-3.3.10-sse2-avx-avx2-avx2_128
GPU FFT library:     none
Multi-GPU FFT:       none
RDTSCP:              enabled
TNG support:         enabled
Hwloc support:       disabled
Tracing support:     disabled
Colvars support:     enabled (version 2025-10-13)
CP2K support:        disabled
Torch support:       enabled (version 2.7.0)
Plumed support:      enabled
C compiler:          /usr/bin/cc GNU 13.3.0
C compiler flags:    -Wno-array-bounds -fexcess-precision=fast -funroll-all-loops -mavx2 -mfma -Wall -Wno-unused -Wunused-value -Wunused-parameter -Wextra -Wno-sign-compare -Wpointer-arith -Wpedantic -Wundef -Werror=stringop-truncation -Wshadow -Wno-missing-field-initializers -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -O3 -DNDEBUG
C++ compiler:        /usr/bin/c++ GNU 13.3.0
C++ compiler flags:  -Wno-array-bounds -fexcess-precision=fast -funroll-all-loops -mavx2 -mfma -Wall -Wextra -Wpointer-arith -Wmissing-declarations -Wpedantic -Wundef -Wstringop-truncation -Wshadow -Wno-missing-field-initializers -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -Wno-stringop-truncation -Wno-cast-function-type-strict SHELL:-fopenmp -O3 -DNDEBUG
BLAS library:        Internal
LAPACK library:      Internal
```

</details>

**Steps to reproduce**

The attached files run a short (100-step) NVT simulation of liquid argon at 94.4 K.
Lennard-Jones parameters are taken from [Phys. Rev. 136, A405 (1964)](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.136.A405).

[topol.tpr](/uploads/d94e50bbdd935d4fb35243973435d1ee/topol.tpr)

[topol.top](/uploads/c01542e8fb41823563ad4a62944f5dbd/topol.top)

[grompp.mdp](/uploads/a9225c012baf8d9d27d687ba702f9e84/grompp.mdp)

[conf.gro](/uploads/214152056d9b4e96119981c8b47b915f/conf.gro)

[gmx-lj.pt](/uploads/72536e18e277a259409c510a4415218b/gmx-lj.pt)


<details>
<summary> LJ "model" </summary>

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from typing import Optional


def displacement_vectors(positions, box: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None):

    disp = positions[None, :, :] - positions[:, None, :]

    if box is not None:
        inv_box = torch.inverse(box)
        disp_frac = torch.einsum("nij,jk->nik", disp, inv_box)
        disp_frac = disp_frac - torch.round(disp_frac)
        disp = torch.einsum("nij,jk->nik", disp_frac, box)

    # Extract only i < j pairs
    N = len(positions)
    indices = torch.triu_indices(N, N, offset=1)
    iu = indices[0]
    ju = indices[1]

    disp_pairs = disp[iu, ju]  # (N_dist, 3)

    return disp_pairs


class GmxNNPotModelWrapper(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cutoff, epsilon, sigma):
        super().__init__()

        self._cutoff = cutoff
        self._epsilon = epsilon
        self._sigma = sigma

    def forward(self, positions, atomic_numbers, box: Optional[torch.Tensor]=None, pbc: Optional[torch.Tensor]=None):
        distances = displacement_vectors(positions, box)

        sigma_r_6 = (self._sigma / torch.linalg.vector_norm(distances, dim=1)) ** 6
        sigma_r_12 = sigma_r_6 * sigma_r_6

        return torch.sum(4.0 * self._epsilon * (sigma_r_12 - sigma_r_6))

cutoff = 0.5
sigma = 0.33646
epsilon = 0.94191

gmx_model = GmxNNPotModelWrapper(cutoff=cutoff, sigma=sigma, epsilon=epsilon)
torch.jit.script(gmx_model).save("gmx-lj.pt")
```
</details>


**What is the current bug behavior?**

When running a single-threaded simulation (`gmx mdrun`), the summary section of the log shows:

```
   Energies (kJ/mol)
        LJ (SR)   Coulomb (SR)   NN Potential      Potential    Kinetic En.
    0.00000e+00    0.00000e+00   -5.86681e+02   -5.86681e+02    3.28788e+02
   Total Energy  Conserved En.    Temperature Pressure (bar)
   -2.57893e+02   -1.78290e+02    2.12603e+02    6.03256e+02
```

Here, the NN potential energy is `-5.86681e+02` and the LJ (SR) term is zero.

Running the same system with two MPI ranks (`gmx mdrun -ntmpi 2`) yields:

```
   Energies (kJ/mol)
        LJ (SR)   Coulomb (SR)   NN Potential      Potential    Kinetic En.
   -2.26697e+02    0.00000e+00   -6.26334e+02   -8.53031e+02    3.48793e+02
   Total Energy  Conserved En.    Temperature Pressure (bar)
   -5.04238e+02   -4.24599e+02    2.25538e+02    1.68953e+03
```

Now, the NN potential energy changes to `-6.26334e+02`, and the LJ (SR) term becomes nonzero.

We haven’t yet checked the forces, but this difference looks suspicious.

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

The total and component energies (especially the NN Potential term) should be consistent regardless of the number of MPI ranks.

**Possible fixes**

We encountered this issue while testing our [metatomic interface](https://github.com/metatensor/gromacs/pull/1), where we observe a similar behavior as it is close to the NNpot/QMMM implementation.
It could be related to how the NN potential is evaluated or reduced across ranks.

closed_issues.title: 1PME : 3PP with NVSHMEM enabled runs hang with STMV dataset
closed_issues.description:
Build with `GMX_NVSHMEM=ON` and run with `GMX_ENABLE_NVSHMEM=1`

run cmdline:

mpirun  -np 4 ./bin/gmx_mpi mdrun -s ../../stmv_pme/topol.tpr -npme 1  -ntomp 16 -nb gpu -update gpu -bond
ed gpu  -nsteps 25000 -nstlist 200 -resetstep 15000 -v  -pin off  -tunepme -dlb no -noconfout

It hangs after 200 timesteps at domain decomp step.

This regression is probably introduced from MR - https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/48f6b87988bc0c0f9cb8b15f2bb85fd1a78b4e43

call stack on the PME rank

```
#6  0x00007ffff5ebe81a in gmx_pmeonly(gmx_pme_t**, gmx_domdec_t const&, t_nrnb*, gmx_wallcycle*, gmx_walltime_accounting*, t_inputrec*, PmeRunMode, bool, bool, bool, gmx::DeviceStreamManager const*) () from /lustre/fsw/coreai_devtech_all/mdoijade/gromacs/build_main_nvshmem_debug/bin/../lib/libgromacs_mpi.so.11
#7  0x00007ffff5f59ad2 in gmx::Mdrunner::mdrunner() () from /lustre/fsw/coreai_devtech_all/mdoijade/gromacs/build_main_nvshmem_debug/bin/../lib/libgromacs_mpi.so.11
#8  0x000055555555f803 in gmx::gmx_mdrun(ompi_communicator_t*, gmx_hw_info_t const&, int, char**) ()
#9  0x000055555555f963 in gmx::gmx_mdrun(int, char**) ()
#10 0x00007ffff571177c in gmx::CommandLineModuleManager::run(int, char**) ()
   from /lustre/fsw/coreai_devtech_all/mdoijade/gromacs/build_main_nvshmem_debug/bin/../lib/libgromacs_mpi.so.11
#11 0x000055555555bf50 in main ()
```

Though this is now resolved in the MR !5501 this regression has happened due to redundant reinit()'s caused by redundant creation of `GpuHaloExchangeNvshmemHelper` object each time on the PP side without matching it with PME. https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/48f6b87988bc0c0f9cb8b15f2bb85fd1a78b4e43#87ab5a69a23a467f3dfa1dba09aa1a2023564a3f_3092_3094

closed_issues.title: MPI message mismatch for zero-sized PME force messages with GPU-aware MPI
closed_issues.description:
An MPI message mismatch occurs in simulations using GPU-aware MPI for PME. The issue arises when a particle-particle (PP) rank has no atoms to send to the PME rank.

In this scenario, [`sendFToPpGpuAwareMpi`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/e96d0a5e893608ca038761c8b309a3d45dfa5a1e/src/gromacs/ewald/pme_force_sender_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp#L156) sends a zero-byte force message, but the corresponding [`receiveForceFromPmeGpuAwareMpi`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/e96d0a5e893608ca038761c8b309a3d45dfa5a1e/src/gromacs/ewald/pme_pp_comm_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp#L191) function on the PP rank preemptively returns without posting a matching receive.

This leads to an accumulation of unreceived messages and test failures in case MPI is built with diagnostics enabled. The issue is observed in `ReproducesEnergies/PmeTest.Runs` tests when using a dedicated PME rank (`-npme 1`) and GPU acceleration for PME (`-pme gpu`), with HIP-aware MPICH (`gromacs:acpp-rocm-mpi:test` in CI). This can also lead to incorrect results if a previously empty domain gains some atoms: the PP ranks will start posting receives and will get forces from the past.

Fixing the issue is complicated by a divergence between libMPI and threadMPI treatment of such empty messages: the latter does not have any communications between empty domains.

closed_issues.title: Using PMX for ΔΔG on a glycosylated Fc (P238D back-mutation; PDB 3WJJ): viable workflows?
closed_issues.description:
Hi all,

I’d like to use PMX to compute ΔΔG of binding for an Fc that is N-glycosylated (structure based on PDB: 3WJJ) by reversing the mutation P238D. I know PMX supports Amber and CHARMM family protein force fields out of the box, but I’m unclear how best to proceed when linked glycans are present.

Concretely:

Amber/GLYCAM → GROMACS → PMX? If I build the glycoprotein in tleap with Amber+GLYCAM, then convert to GROMACS formats (e.g., via ACPYPE or similar), is that topology/coordinate set acceptable input for pmx mutate? Key requirement: the covalent N-glycosidic bond (Asn–GlcNAc) must survive the conversion and be represented as a bonded connection in GROMACS. Has anyone run PMX successfully on such converted glycoprotein systems? (Background: GLYCAM→GROMACS conversion with ACPYPE is documented, but I’m not sure about PMX compatibility and preserving cross-residue bonds. )

All-CHARMM36 route with pdb2gmx + PMX CHARMM-mut ff? Alternatively, prepare the glycoprotein entirely with CHARMM36 (jul2022) carbohydrate parameters in GROMACS (i.e., using carb.rtp/carb.r2b so mid-chain vs terminal sugar names map correctly), then use PMX’s CHARMM mutate workflow. Is there a recommended recipe (naming, r2b mappings for mid-chain GlcNAc, Man, Gal, Fuc, specbond.dat for linkages, etc.) known to work end-to-end with PMX? (GROMACS handles CHARMM36 glycans via carb.rtp + carb.r2b; correct residue naming and r2b mapping are critical. )

Any proven alternatives? If the above aren’t practical, are there known workarounds (e.g., splitting protein/glycans, then merging with manual bonds in topology; or specific PMX mapping files for common N-glycans) that people have used successfully for ΔΔG with glycoproteins?

Motivation / constraints: We prefer to avoid web services that require uploading proprietary coordinates (e.g., CHARMM-GUI), and we’re fine with some manual editing if that’s the current state-of-the-art. (We know CHARMM-GUI’s Glycan Reader/Modeler can produce GROMACS-ready glycoproteins; just checking for an offline/PMX-friendly path. )

Any pointers, example repos, or do/don’t tips (especially around PMX’s mutate step with carbohydrate-bearing topologies) would be hugely appreciated!

Thanks!

When mdrun is interrupted by a signal, crtl-C or TERM or USR1 signal, and stops at a step which is not a multiple of nstcalcenergy, the kinetic energy reported for the leap-frog integrator is incorrect. This would lead to incorrect kinetic energy, temperature and pressure reported in the last frame in the energy file and the log file, as well as an incorrect energy drift value in the log file. This issue does not occur when a run finishes normally.

closed_issues.title: Missing OpenMP_CUDA_FLAGS on Windows when building GROMACS with CUDA
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

CMake 3.31+ fails to build GROMACS 2025.0 with CUDA on Windows due to missing `OpenMP_CUDA_FLAGS` and `OpenMP_CUDA_LIB_NAMES`.

## Exact steps to reproduce

Reported on https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/cmake-error-missing-openmp-cuda-flags-on-windows-when-building-with-cuda/11545

CMake (3.31.5), CUDA 12.4.1, Visual Studio 2022.

```console
$ cmake .. "-DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=C:/GROMACS2025" "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:/FFTW;C:/OpenBLAS" "-DGMX_SIMD=AVX2_256" "-DGMX_GPU=CUDA" "-DGMX_HWLOC=ON" -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A "x64"

...
-- Performing Test HAVE_NO_DEPRECATED_COPY
-- Performing Test HAVE_NO_DEPRECATED_COPY - Failed
-- Performing Test HAS_WARNING_EVERYTHING
-- Performing Test HAS_WARNING_EVERYTHING - Failed
CMake Error at C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.31/Modules/FindPackageHandleStandardArgs.cmake:233 (message):
  Could NOT find OpenMP_CUDA (missing: OpenMP_CUDA_FLAGS
  OpenMP_CUDA_LIB_NAMES)
Call Stack (most recent call first):
  C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.31/Modules/FindPackageHandleStandardArgs.cmake:603 (_FPHSA_FAILURE_MESSAGE)
  C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.31/Modules/FindOpenMP.cmake:616 (find_package_handle_standard_args)
  src/external/muparser/CMakeLists.txt:28 (find_package)


-- Configuring incomplete, errors occurred!
```

## For developers: Why is this important?

This seems to be caused by `enable_language(CUDA)` called before `find_package(OpenMP)`, which causes the latter to try to find OpenMP flags for the NVCC compiler.

This _should_ work, and the problem indicates an issue with the environment.

However, it is not necessary for GROMACS 2025: Only `OpenMP::OpenMP_CXX` target is used, so detecting CUDA (or C or FORTRAN) flags is not necessary. OpenMP_CUDA is definitely not needed by muParser, which is where the reported error originates. Detecting OpenMP flags for compilers that are not used can cause other such issues, and, at the very least, wastest CMake time.


## Possible fixes

The following fix was confirmed by the used to fix the build and was accepted to upstream muParser: https://github.com/beltoforion/muparser/pull/157.

closed_issues.title: Empirical Transition Matrix formatting breaks with a large number of replicas
closed_issues.description:
When gmx calculates and prints the "Empirical Transition Matrix" to the log file, it appends the replica index at the end of each row.

For a small number of replicas, the formatting is correct, with a clear space separating the final probability from the replica index.

Correct output (few replicas):

Repl  0.0462  0.0520 ... 0.0002  0.0000  1
However, when the number of replicas is large (e.g., in the hundreds), the formatting breaks. The final probability value in the row is concatenated with the replica index, creating a single, incorrect number. This makes the output unreadable and breaks any script designed to parse this matrix.

Incorrect output (many replicas):

Repl  0.0322  0.0368247
In the example above, the last probability value was 0.0368 and the replica index was 247. They have been incorrectly merged into 0.0368247.
[gromacs.log](/uploads/445af2e5f8ad7f4d6d8e5312e1eab589/gromacs.log)

closed_issues.title: Introduce thread pinning mode respecting external CPU affinity masks
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

GROMACS's current CPU pinning is too rigid for modern hardware, failing to accommodate externally-set affinities needed for GPU runtimes or complex scheduler layouts. I propose a new `-pin inherit` option that pins threads within the existing process affinity mask, providing flexible and robust behavior without conflicting with the system environment.

# Detailed description

Currently, GROMACS supports two approaches to handling CPU thread affinity (with `-pin auto` selecting one of the two):
- `off:` don't do anything. This can mean either no pinning at all, per-process pinning (set by MPI / Slurm), or per-thread pinning (if `OMP_PROC_BIND` or the like is used, potentially in combination with per-process setting). The latter is safest performance-wise.
- `on`: pin everything manually, potentially respecting `pinoffset` and `pinstride` if we don't want to fully populate the cores.

Modern machines present the following challenges:
1. CPU-heavy GPU runtime threads (HIP HSA; NVSHMEM): we need to have some cores per process empty.
2. "Reserved" cores (LUMI, Frontier).
3. Too many cores (GH200): due to limited CPU parallelism, we can get better performance is we use less OpenMP threads than there are available cores.

They require pinning such that each rank is in the same CPU locality (chiplet, NUMA, etc), yet does not use all cores in it. It can't be done with existing mechanisms:

- The `-pin on` approach fails, because we cannot express "rank 0: cores 0-5, rank 1: cores 8-12, etc" with existing GROMACS mechanisms. Additionally, it can mess things if the scheduler sets unusual CPU affinities externally (e.g., [LUMI default scripts](https://docs.lumi-supercomputer.eu/runjobs/scheduled-jobs/lumig-job/)).
- Externally-set affinities (per-process + `OMP_PROC_BIND`) work okay with LLVM's `libomp`. [Except for Zen1 CPUs](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/40073), which are seen as single-core CPUs with N-way SMT (where N is the actual number of cores).
- Externally-set affinities (per-process + `OMP_PROC_BIND`) fail with GOMP (GNU OpenMP library), since it sets all per-thread affinities on library load, and thus all runtime worker threads inherit the affinity of thread #0, which usually means sharing a core with it.

## Possible fixes

1. We can make our custom affinity setting more elaborate to also include process stride (!4693).
2. We can launch an extra GROMACS thread with the desired affinity and use it solely to start runtime threads (does not handle reserved cores).
3. Do our own per-thread pinning, but each process only does it withing the externally set affinity mask.

The last option seems the best:

- Principle of least surprise: we don't mess with the scheduler settings.
- No dependency on OpenMP library behavior.
- Flexible: the external affinities (from Slurm, `hwloc-bind`, `taskset`, `numactl`, ...) can be set in any way, respecting whatever GPU numbering scheme there is, while we still prevent thread migration between cores.
- We set affinity after initializing MPI/GPU runtimes, so the worker threads inherit per-process affinity (and hopefully the OS migrates them to the non-GROMACS cores). AMD HSA thread likes to set its own affinities, mitigating the GOMP issue but potentially allowing it to migrate to a different chiplet/socket; now it will be ok as long as `HSA_OVERRIDE_CPU_AFFINITY_DEBUG=0` is set.

As such, a new option `-pin inherit` is proposed that does exactly that:
- If the affinity masks of all ranks are disjoint, each rank pins its threads consecutively within its set of cores. This is the expected libMPI case with the scheduler properly setting affinities.
  - E.g, for a 2-rank job on a LUMI-G node with `ntomp 6`, if the MPI runner assigns cores 1-7 to rank 0 and cores 9-15 to rank 1, `-pin inherit` will bind rank 0's threads within cores 1-6 and rank 1's within 9-14, leaving cores 7 and 15 for the HSA threads.
- If the affinity masks of all ranks are identical, we pin threads in consecutive non-overlapping block withing the mask. This is the expected threadMPI case with some externally-set affinity (e.g., if `taskset` was used).
  - E.g., a 2-rank threadMPI job launched with `taskset -c 0-15`, both ranks see an identical mask of cores 0-15. With `-ntomp 7`, `-pin inherit` will automatically divide the set, giving cores 0-6 to rank 0 and 7-13 to rank 1, leaving cores 14 and 15 empty.
    - One can have gaps; e.g., if there are 8 cores per NUMA, using `taskset -c 0-2,8-9 gmx -pin inherit -pinoffset 1 -ntomp 2` will have GROMACS threads pinned to cores 1,2,8,9 and core 0 left empty to be used by worker threads.
- In case the affinity masks between ranks overlap but are not the same, we bail out and don't touch affinities. This is in line with our current behavior of being cautious about affinity settings.
  - If rank 0 is assigned cores 0-8 and rank 1 is assigned cores 8-16 due to off-by-1 error in external affinity settings, GROMACS will not set any affinities to avoid incorrect behavior.

Additionally, the option `-pin on` can be deprecated in favor of more explicit `-pin force`, but that's optional.

An affinity reporting mechanism would facilitate debugging such issues.

closed_issues.title: H5MD: Implementation about the writing of topology
closed_issues.description:
### Implementation
String-based datasets are designed as `StringLookupTable` with the name field being an `int[NumAtoms]` looking into the lookup table `string[NumUniqueStrings]`. 

Since `particles` follow a hierarchical organization (atoms are put into their corresponding sub-groups), an `IndexGroup` or an `IndexMap` is passed to the topology writer functions to map the index. 

`BondPair` is deduced from the GROMACS molecule type object. Running the `cacheBondForNBlocks` generates the consecutive buffer writable for HDF writing.  
```
using  StringLookupTable  =  std::unordered_map<const  char*, int32_t>;
using  IndexMap  =  std::unordered_map<int64_t, int64_t>;
using  BondPairs  =  std::vector<std::pair<int64_t, int64_t>>;
```

#### Internal utility functions
* [x] `mapSelectionToInternalIndices`: Map the selection index group (global index) to the internal (local) index in the group. 
* [x] `deduceBondsFromMolecule`: Deduce bonds by interaction list from a GROMACS molecule type (`gmx_moltype_t`) object. 
* [x] `deduceDisulfideBondsFromMolecule`: Deduce disulfide bonds from a `gmx_moltype_t`. 
* [x] `cacheBondForNBlocks`: Write deduced bonds for `NumMolBlocks` with a global offset to correct the mapping of the atom ID. 

#### Topology writer functions
* [x] `writeAtomicProperties(AtomRange&, hid_t, IndexMap&)`

		Located in the particles container: 
		+-- nr_particles, int64
		\-- particle_id, int64[NumAtoms]
		\-- particle_name, int32[NumAtoms]
		\-- particle_name_table, string[NumUniqueAtomNames]
		\-- particle_species, int32[NumAtoms] - Atomic number
		\-- charge, float[NumAtoms]
		\-- mass, float[NumAtoms]

* [x] `writeResidueInfo(AtomRange&, hid_t, IndexMap&)`

		Located in the particles container: 
		+-- nr_residues, int32
		\-- residue_id, int[NumAtoms]
		\-- sequence, int32[NumResidues] - indices to lookup table in `residue_name_table`
		\-- residue_name, int[NumAtoms] - indices to lookup table in `residue_name_table`
		\-- residue_name_table, string[NumUniqueResidueNames]

* [x] `writeBonds(gmx_mtop_t*, hid_t, IndexMap&)` - `/connectivity/bond`

		Located in a bond base container: 
		+-- nr_bonds, int64
		\-- bonds, int64[NumBonds, 2]

* [x] `writeDisulfideBonds(gmx_mtop_t*, hid_t, IndexMap&)` - `/connectivity/special_bond`

		Located in a bond base container: 
		+-- nr_bonds, int64
		\-- bonds, int64[NumSpecialBonds, 2]

### Open questions
* [x] Whether we should define a version for it and how to version it? Start with GROMACS topology version 0.1. 
* [x] All identifier-based datasets (ends with `_id`) should be `1-based indexing`? Yes, 1-based index. 
* [x] Shall we, by default, renumber the `residue_id`? Renumber the residue ID for the experimental version. 

### Resources
* !5416: write atomic property and residue info
* !5545: write connectivity
* !5528: utility function to get AtomRange
* !5537: write molecule type
* !5570: hook topology writing to file setup

closed_issues.title: H5MD: Design of GROMACS internal topology
closed_issues.description:
This issue aims to discuss the details about how to design the GROMACS internal topology

### Structure of GROMACS internal topology 

The GROMACS internal topology objects should be an application-specific H5MD module and its base HDF container should be located in `/h5md/modules/gromacs_topology`. Since it is internal representation, it should respect the original organization of the data. 

The following is the major content in the **GROMACS internal topology**. 
```
Base container:
+-- version: int32[2], version of this definition
+-- system_name: string
\-- groups    // Internal groups
    +-- simulation_groups: string[NrSimulationGroup]
    \-- NameOfGroup1 (Flat structure or hierarchical?)
        +-- index_groups: string[NrIndexGroups]
        \-- ranges: string[NrIndexGroups+1]
\-- molecule_types    // Internal molecule representation
    +-- molecule_names
    \-- NameOfMolecule1
        +-- nr_atoms: int64
        +-- nr_blocks: int32
        +-- nr_residues: int32
        \-- particle_species: int[NrParticles]
        \-- particle_name: int[NrParticles]
        \-- particle_name_table: string[NrUniqueParticleName]
        \-- mass: float[NrParticles]
        \-- charge: float[NrParticles]
        \-- atomic_number: int[NrParticles]
        \-- internal_particle_type: int[NrParticles]  // GROMACS internal types, e.g. regular atom, virtual site or others
        \-- residue_index: int[NrParticles] // Look up residues in `sequence`
        \-- sequence: int[NrResidues]
        \-- residue_name_table: string[NrUniqueResidues]
        \-- interaction_list
		+-- interaction_names string[NrTypesInteraction]
		\-- BONDS
			\-- function_type int[NrInteractionBonds]
		        \-- value: float[NrInteractionBonds, 2]
		\-- SETTLE
			\-- function_type int[NrInteractionSettle]
		        \-- value: float[NrInteractionBonds, 2]
		... More interaction in list ...
	\-- exclusion
		\-- ranges int32[numRanges+1]
		\-- value: int64[numIndices]
	\-- position_restraint
		+-- nr_posres
		\-- position: float[NrPosRes, 3]
	... More molecule blocks ...
\-- forcefield
        +-- power_replusion: int32
        +-- factor_coulombic: float
        +-- nr_function_types: int32
        +-- nr_nb_atoms: int32
        \-- function_types: int32[NrForceFieldParams]
        \-- parameters
                \-- F_BONDS
                        b0A: float[numBondParams]
          	        b0B: float[numBondParams]
          	        cbA: float[numBondParams]
          	        cbB: float[numBondParams]

Function:    pmegrids_init(pmegrids_t*, int, int, int, int, int, gmx_bool, int, int, int, gmx::ArrayRef<std::vector<double, gmx::Allocator<double, gmx::AlignedAllocationPolicy> > >)::<lambda()>

closed_issues.title: Handle breaking of covalent bonds in ML/MM simulations
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

In QMMM simulations, some computational setups (e.g. in computational enzymology) require the cutting of covalent bonds between the QM and MM regions (i.e. in a bonded pair of atoms, one is part of the QM region and one is not). The most popular approach to deal with this are so-called link atom schemes, where a dummy atom (mostly hydrogen) is introduced at some position along the original bond, to complete the valence of the QM region.

We would like to enable these kinds of setups also with the `nnpot` module, and the approach is in principle completely analogous. However, in the `qmmm` module in GROMACS, these link atoms are handled almost entirely by CP2K, so that there is no machinery in place that can be re-used by the `nnpot` module. 

Tests with the `nnpot` module without introducing such a link atom approach result in unstable simulations, which is why it is currently discouraged in the manual.

## Possible fixes

Once the link frontier is identified (handled by the topology preprocessing), during each MD step, a dummy atom (of arbitrary type) can be placed at the appropriate position along the bond. A common choice for this position is the equilibrium length of a methyl C-H bond  (1.09 Å), but could be set by the user. There, we don't actually add any atoms to the topology, but just to the input vectors for the NNP. The NNP will then treat this dummy atom just like any other, with the difference being that we don't accumulate any forces on it. 
While we're at it, it might be worth considering issues with link atom schemes identified by [this paper](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01071) even in state-of-the-art QMMM simulations. In my understanding, this will become relevant mostly in the case of electrostatic embedding, though.

closed_issues.title: DSSP broken legends
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

The legends produced by gmx dssp -num do not render properly in XmGrace.

**GROMACS version**

2025.2

**Steps to reproduce**

Execute any gmx dssp command, specifying the optional -num output option.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

The use of Greek symbols in the strings in the source code leads to nonsensical rendering in XmGrace.

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

Correctly formatted legend strings are desirable for usability.

Faulty code found in src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/modules/dssp.cpp, lines 245-254.

Current code:

```//! String values (full) corresponding to secondary structures' types.
const gmx::EnumerationArray<SecondaryStructureTypes, const char*> c_secondaryStructureTypeNamesFull = {
    { "Loops",
      "Breaks",
      "Bends",
      "Turns",
      "PP_Helices",
      "π-Helices",
      "3⏨-Helices",
      "β-Strands",
      "β-Bridges",
      "α-Helices" }
};

Proposed fix (untested):

```//! String values (full) corresponding to secondary structures' types.
const gmx::EnumerationArray<SecondaryStructureTypes, const char*> c_secondaryStructureTypeNamesFull = {
    { "Loops",
      "Breaks",
      "Bends",
      "Turns",
      "PP\sII\N-Helices",
      "\xp\f{}-Helices",
      "3\s10\N-Helices",
      "\xb\f{}-Strands",
      "\xb\f{}-Bridges",
      "\xa\f{}-Helices" }
};

It would also be nice to reorder this list so the helical elements are all grouped, rather than having alpha-helices on their own. This requires reordering of other aspects of the code, e.g. enum class SecondaryStructureTypes.

closed_issues.title: Mdrun get stuck when number of MPI threads is significantly larger than number of physical cores
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

As I compile GROMACS on the main branch and perform an `mdrun` test on a tpr distributed with the source code, the `gmx mdrun` gets stuck. If I compile from release versions (e.g. v2024.4, v2025.2), the simple mdrun does not get stuck. 

This problem also seem like tpr-related: with a different tpr (e.g. `../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/clustsize.tpr`), the program does not get stuck. 

This seems like a bug. 

## To reproduce the problem

```
# simple build of GROMACS on dev mode
git checkout main
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake .. -DGMX_BUILD_OWN_FFTW=ON
make -j32

# hardware AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 16-Core Processor
# 16 physical cores, 32 logic cores
# gets stuck
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr   # default assign 32 MPI threads and 1 OMP threads per MPI thread
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntmpi 32
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntmpi 24
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntmpi 20

# does not get stuck 
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntmpi 18  # 18 mpi x 1 omp
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntmpi 16  # 16 mpi x 2 omp
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntomp 2   # 16 mpi x 2 omp
./bin/gmx mdrun -s ../src/gromacs/trajectoryanalysis/tests/trpcage.tpr -ntomp 4   #  8 mpi x 4 omp
```

## Call stack in gdb

closed_issues.title: Question about Changing DNA residues to Protein in residuetypes.dat for covalent bond
closed_issues.description:
Hello,
I have a single strand of DNA where both ends are modified nucleotides (named TO5 and TO3), and each of them is covalently bonded to a peptide.

The sequence looks like this in pdb file:
TO5 (modified nucleotide covalently bonded to peptide, marked as Protein in residuetype.dat) and peptide (chain A) → TER → 21 standard DNA base pairs (chain B) →TO3 (modified nucleotide, covalently bonded to peptide, marked as Protein in residuetype.dat) and peptide (chain C) → TER

I set both TO5 and TO3 as Protein in the residuetype.dat file so that GROMACS treats them as protein and the attached peptides as part of one chain.
I also added the following lines to the specbond.dat file:
```
TO5 C 1 ASP N 1 0.130 TO5 ASP
TO3 C 1 ASP N 1 0.130 TO3 ASP
TO5 O3’ 1 DT P 1 0.160 TO5 DT
TO3 P 1 DC O3’ 1 0.160 TO3 DC
```
I have 21 standard DNA base pairs in the middle of my structure. They are not terminal, but GROMACS still asks me to select terminal patches during pdb2gmx. I tried selecting “None” for both ends, but GROMACS still gives an error and does not generate the topology.
```
Fatal error:
There is a dangling bond at at least one of the terminal ends. Fix your
coordinate file, add a new terminal database entry (.tdb), or select the
proper existing terminal entry.
```
How can I tell GROMACS to treat these residues as internal, so it doesn’t ask for terminal patches?

solution:
If I rename DT/DC/DG/DA as Protein in the residuetype.dat file, the sequence in the pdb file will be:
TO5+peptide →TER → 21 base pairs +TO3 → TER,
and I don’t get any errors, even after minimization.

I used the CHARMM36 force field. I want to make sure I’m not missing anything important and that this approach is acceptable.

Any advice would be really appreciated, and I really appreciate any help you can provide.
Best regards,
Fatemeh,

closed_issues.title: expand parameters of void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::initAfterFirstFrame
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Currently GROMACS provides `void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::initAfterFirstFrame(const TrajectoryAnalysisSettings& settings, const t_trxframe& fr)` which provides access to the first frame before full trajectory analysis. It is useful in some cases, yet it misses `t_pbc* pbc`, which is available in `void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::analyzeFrame(int frnr, const t_trxframe& fr, t_pbc* pbc, TrajectoryAnalysisModuleData* pdata)`. Some operations might require `pbc`, like `gmx_rmpbc_apply(...)` function. Thus it would be nice to have access to `pbc` before `analyzeFrame`. Especially if such operations are required once per program run.

**Use cases**

Some operations, which require a `pbc` and a single execution during the program run either require an `if` statement in `analyzeFrame` or some `static` variable magic there. It would be nicer and cleaner to have a single run function like `initAfterFirstFrame` or it exactly, but with provided `pbc`.

**Impact**

This feature will make code cleaner, with less `if` statements or questionable `static` variables. 

**Detailed description**

I would like `void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::initAfterFirstFrame(...)` to have the same parameters as `void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::analyzeFrame(...)` or there to be an overload of it with `analyzeFrame` parameters. If it's complicated to implement such a change a `void TrajectoryAnalysisModule::analyzeFirstFrame(...)` function will do the trick.

**Requirements**

No.

**Links/references/implementations**

No

closed_issues.title: MPI_CXX_COMPILE_OPTIONS get added to build flags in non-MPI builds, enabling LTO
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Even when building with threadMPI, `MPI_CXX_COMPILE_OPTIONS` are added to GROMACS build flags. This is nasty since:

- these flags can be undesired;
- the behavior is unpredictable: in threadMPI build in a clean build directory, MPI is not searched the first time one runs CMake, but, if GMXAPI is enabled, is searched when reconfiguration happens. So, the clean build is done without MPI flags, but if you touch any of CMake files, new flags are added.

Specific example. MPICH from Ubuntu 24.04 repos enables LTO, which then gets applied to all files. It, on one hand, breaks CUDA builds (`Error: symbol fatbinData is already defined`), and, on the other, can lead to random performance fluctuations from one build to another without any meaningful changes in the code or the environment.

## Exact steps to reproduce

```
FROM ubuntu:24.04
RUN apt update && apt install -y build-essential cmake git libfftw3-dev mpich libmpich-dev python3 wget
RUN wget https://ftp.gromacs.org/gromacs/gromacs-2025.2.tar.gz && tar xf gromacs-2025.2.tar.gz && rm gromacs-2025.2.tar.gz
RUN mkdir gromacs-2025.2/build
RUN echo "First run of CMake"
RUN cd gromacs-2025.2/build && cmake .. && grep flto ./src/gromacs/CMakeFiles/libgromacs.dir/flags.make || echo "No mention of lto in Makefile"
RUN echo "Second run of CMake"
RUN touch gromacs-2025.2/CMakeLists.txt && cd gromacs-2025.2/build && cmake .. && grep flto ./src/gromacs/CMakeFiles/libgromacs.dir/flags.make && echo "Found lto in Makefile after reconfigure"
```

Shows that, after a re-run of CMake, we have `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects` added to the build flags:

```
C_FLAGS = -O3 -DNDEBUG -fPIC -fexcess-precision=fast -funroll-all-loops -mavx2 -mfma -Wno-missing-field-initializers -flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects
CXX_FLAGS = -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++17 -fPIC -fexcess-precision=fast -funroll-all-loops -mavx2 -mfma -Wno-missing-field-initializers -flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects -Wno-old-style-cast -Wno-cast-qual -Wno-suggest-override -Wno-suggest-destructor-override -Wno-zero-as-null-pointer-constant -Wno-cast-function-type-strict -fopenmp
```

## For developers: Why is this important?

Compiler flags should not randomly change. MPI-specific flags should not be added to non-MPI builds.

## Possible fixes

Probably all three need to be done:

1. Don't apply `MPI_CXX_COMPILE_OPTIONS` when not needed. - Done in !5367
2. Make sure second runs in the same directory don't change CMakeCache (can even be added to CI, by similarly touching CMakeLists.txt and comparing CMakeCache.txt files in all jobs?) - Done in !5484
3. Make sure CUDA works with LTO

closed_issues.title: Build fails with upcoming CUDA due to change in NVCC default
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

In CUDA 13, NVCC changes the default `-static-global-template-stub` from `false` to `true`, and this is causing GROMACS builds to fail with errors like:

```
/home/scratch.alang_sw/Gromacs/gromacs/src/gromacs/nbnxm/cuda/nbnxm_cuda_kernel_pruneonly.cuh(110): warning #20280-D: when "-static-global-template-stub=true" in whole program compilation mode ("-rdc=false"), a __global__ function template instantiation or specialization ("gmx::nbnxn_kernel_prune_cuda<(bool)0> ") must have a definition in the current translation unit. To resolve this issue, either use separate compilation mode ("-rdc=true"), or explicitly set "-static-global-template-stub=false" (but see nvcc documentation about downsides of turning it off)
...
/usr/bin/ld: CMakeFiles/libgromacs.dir/nbnxm/cuda/nbnxm_cuda.cu.o: in function `gmx::gpu_launch_kernel_pruneonly(gmx::NbnxmGpu*, gmx::InteractionLocality, int)':
tmpxft_0000ce5d_00000000-6_nbnxm_cuda.compute_53.cudafe1.cpp:(.text+0x615): undefined reference to `void gmx::nbnxn_kernel_prune_cuda<true>(gmx::NBAtomDataGpu, gmx::NBParamGpu, gmx::GpuPairlist, int)'
```

This can be fixed by explicitly setting `-static-global-template-stub=false` in CMake.

closed_issues.title: Incorrect shared memory calculation for Prune Only kernel
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

The calculation of requires shared memory for the CUDA Prune Only kernel does not account for the new [`sm_prunedPairCount`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/v2024.5/src/gromacs/nbnxm/cuda/nbnxm_cuda_kernel_pruneonly.cuh?ref_type=tags#L210-216) field (a single `int`), but always accounts for `cjs`, even when `cj` preload is disabled.

As a result,
- on devices < 7.0 (with cj preload), we have shmem buffer overrun;
- on device >= 7.0 (without cj preload), we request more shmem than needed.

The problem was introduced in 573fe18, which added `sm_prunedPairCount` to both NBNXM and PruneOnly kernels, but only updated shmem size calculation for the NBNXM kernel.

For other backends:

- HIP in 2025 does not do cj preloading and overlaps pruned pair counting buffer with the XQ buffer, but still [adds the size of cj buffer](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/v2025.2/src/gromacs/nbnxm/hip/nbnxm_hip_kernel_utils.h#L144-149). So, we overallocate memory, but no harm done.
- SYCL does not use cj preloading but uses pruned pair counting. Since we use separate local_accessors for them, we are fine.

closed_issues.title: Type convertions while working with AnalysisData and AnalysisDataHandle
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

While developing a new trajectory analysis module i found out that `AnalysisData` and `AnalysisDataHandle` accept `int` parameters on public methods. Logically speaking they are always meant to be `>=0` and in most cases original data comes from `.size()` and such. So to avoid unnecessary `static_cast<int>(...)` it would be nice to change the API or inner structure to accommodate such view. 

**Use cases**

This is pure developers issue and has no effect on end-user for developed software.

**Impact**

This should make developing cleaner: 

current example 1: `AnalysisData.setColumnCount(0, static_cast<int>(selection.size()));`

current example 2: `for (size_t i ... ) AnalysisDataHandle.setPoint(static_cast<int>(i), value);`

If change is applied such static casts should no longer be needed.

**Detailed description**

Public API of AnalysisData and AnalysisDataHandle and inner workings use `int` variables, while logic implies `>=0` values with some exception of `-1`, yet it seems to be leading to std::throw and not intended logic.

closed_issues.title: H5MD: Design of GROMACS topology and connectivity in H5MD format
closed_issues.description:
## Objective

H5MD should store the topology and the connectivity of the molecule for the following objective:

- Self-consistent and portable
- Straightforward and unequivocal
- Comprehensible for scientists from diverse backgrounds

## Design of topology

The proposed location for this field is in: **/particles/\<subgroup\>**. The \<subgroup\> here could be **system** (all particles in the simulation system) if no subgroup is defined.

### Attributes
* [x] nr_particles, int32
* [x] nr_residues, int32

### Datasets
* [x] id, int32 [numAtoms]: within H5MD 1.1 definition
* [x] charge, float [numAtoms]: within H5MD 1.1 definition
* [x] mass, float [numAtoms]: within H5MD 1.1 definition
* [x] species, int32 [numAtoms]: atomic number if all-atom simulation; within H5MD 1.1 definition
* [x] particle_name, int32 [numAtoms]: Enumeration of atom names
* [x] particle_name_table, string [numUniqueAtomName]: Lookup table for unique atom names. 
* [x] residue_id, int32 [numAtoms]
* [x] sequence, string [numResidues]: Lookup table for residue names
* [x] residue_name, int32 [numAtoms]: Enumeration of residue names
* [x] residue_name_table, string [numUniqueResidues]: Lookup table for residue name


### Questions to discuss

> Any thoughts on the above question marks?

> Any thoughts on whether there are any extra fields or attributes that we should add?

* [x] Storage of string-based fields with significantly duplicated entries (e.g., residue name, particle name):

  - **Enumeration** of possible strings, more efficient in space :white_check_mark: 

* [x] Do we need a version number for versioning topology information? 
  Start with an experimental feature. 

* [ ] How do we handle the second charge/mass (mass_b, charge_b, and type_b) designed for free energy calculation? 

---

## Design of connectivity

Connectivity Data Field under /connectivity/bond

### Attributes

* [x] nr_bonds, int64

### Datasets

* [x] bonds, int64 [numBonds, 2]: tuple of indices of bonded atoms

### Questions to discuss

* [ ] This form of connectivity field is flat; when sub-groups are used, shall connectivity follow the hierarchy, like in the atomic property list?

* [x] If a subset of the system is selected, atom indices in the bond field should be reordered. Otherwise, the original atom index is wrong.

  ```
  E.g. here are 3 selected water molecules. 
  bonds =  
  0,   1,  <not>  3415, 3416,
  0,   2,  <not>  3415, 3417,
  3,   4,  <not>  3418, 3419,
  3,   5,  <not>  3418, 3420,
  6,   7,  <not>  3421, 3422,
  6,   8,  <not>  3421, 3423,
  9,  10,  <not>  3424, 3425,
  9,  11,  <not>  3424, 3426,
  12, 13,  <not>  3427, 3428,
  12, 14   <not>  3427, 3429 
  ```

### Potential field in the future. 
* [ ] attr:nr_molecules, int
* [ ] chain_id, **int?string** [numAtoms] // **Need discussion: use int or string or char**
* [ ] molecule_id, int [numAtoms]
* [ ] terminal_residue, int [X] (Optional for biomolecular simulations)

closed_issues.title: PME to PP GPU force transfer suboptimal with lib-MPI
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

When running multi-GPU simulations with PME using lib-MPI, the PME to PP force transfer is being unnecessarily delayed by the PP halo exchange. This is contributing to the sub-optimal performance of lib-MPI as seen in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/5373.


## Details

The below profiles are for 4xGPU runs, with 1 PME GPU and 3 PP GPUs. The blue vertical lines show the CPU scheduling of the PME to PP force transfer, and the associated actual transfer. 

With thread-MPI, it can be seen that the transfer is scheduled early by the CUDA API on the PME CPU (bottom "CUDA API" row), and executed as soon as the PME GPU stream is ready (from bottom "[All Streams]" row to second bottom "[All Streams]" row):
![Screenshot_2025-06-19_at_10.51.06](/uploads/de52cb3e4dd41c3bcd608f6b215137e7/Screenshot_2025-06-19_at_10.51.06.png)



With lib-MPI, the PME CPU instead calls MPI_Isend (to each of the PP GPUs) and then waits in MPI_Waitall until the PP GPUs post their corresponding MPI_Recv before the data is actually transferred. But this is not done until after they finish the PP halo exchange.

![Screenshot_2025-06-24_at_17.00.12](/uploads/29c3781a59bf9e472ad7fb7ca53113b8/Screenshot_2025-06-24_at_17.00.12.png)

## Possible fixes

The force receive mechanism on the PP tasks can be split up into an init step which posts a non-blocking MPI_Irecv earlier than the PP halo exchange, such that the PME force data transfer can be overlapped with the PP halo exchange, plus a finalisation step to wait for the transfers to complete. This will require some refactoring of the schedule.

closed_issues.title: Unify H5md data set storage layout
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

H5md data sets for numeric data should all use C-style storage layout, e.g. float[N1][N2][N3], or more specifically for per-frame data sets of positions `float[numFrames][numAtoms][DIM]`. 

**Detailed description**

Currently the HDF5 storage of 1d data in the H5md module follows this layout (`float[numFrames]`) but rvec-lists (positions above) are 1d data sets too, where each value is a [numAtoms][DIM] compound array type. Internally the memory layout of this is identical to `float[numFrames][numAtoms][DIM]` but

1) This breaks the H5md specification, where such data sets should be explicitly 3d with the `float` (or other primitive) base type, and
2) It is easier for us long term to unify how data set dimensions are treated, with their HDF5 type always matching the base primitive type instead of being a compound type.

**Plan**

* [x] Extend data set helper functions to deal with any-dimension data sets instead of only 1D !5234
* [x] Update rvec-list data set creation functions (`createUnboundedFrameBasicVectorList()`, etc.) to create 3D data sets instead of 1D data sets with a compound type !5235
* [x] Fix reading and writing functions for 3D data !5235
* [x] Unify data set creation for 1D and 3D data sets: should be a common interface !5228
* [x] Clean up old code !5239

closed_issues.title: Metric for absolute performance
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

GROMACS currently uses two performance metrics, including `ns/day` and `hour/ns`. 
However, both of these metrics depend on the size of the system (number of particles) and the step size. 
A new metric, MASN (Mega-Atom steps per Second per Node), would help benchmark the absolute performance of a simulation on certain hardware. 


**Use cases and impact**

Before running production simulations, there is always a need for users to benchmark the simulation on certain hardware to make sure that the resources are used efficiently. However, the size of the simulation system differs from project to project. Comparing the ns/day requires the simulation system to be of a similar size.

Two typical use cases are that one has to run multiple simulations with similar simulation settings on a hardware, and different members in a research group working on different targets run their simulations on the same hardware. Ideally, the absolute performance should be close. If there is a large degeneration of this performance, the user shall immediately realize there are some problems in the simulation settings. 

Adding a metric for absolute performance would help users to easily benchmark the efficiency of certain simulation settings on certain hardware. It would also facilitate the effective comparison between researchers who work on similar hardware but with varied targets. 

If this metric is a good enhancement, I will take the responsibility to add it, and the addition of this metric will only require a very minor addition to the code for the reporting of performance. The MASN could easily be computed by the current ns/day with considering the size of the system, delta-t, and the number of nodes (see Detailed description). 

**Detailed description**

The number of atoms and the number of integration cycles in a fixed time are two major factors to reflect the absolute performance of a hardware. We could use the MASN (Mega-Atom steps per Second per Node) to quantify these two factors. The steps-per-second (Ts) in formula 1 quantifies the throughput of integration cycles and addresses the timestep disparities (dt). And the MASN could be calculated by formula 2: 

```
Ts = t / (dt * s)    (1)
MASN = (Ts * A) / (1e6 * N)    (2)
```

where t is the simulation time in ns, s is the clock time in seconds, dt is the delta-t in ns, A is the number of atoms in the simulation system, and N is the number of nodes. 

With the ns/day (r) metric being known, the MASN could simply be calculated with the following formula. 
```
MASN = (r * A) / (1e6 * N * dt * 86400)    (3)
```

For example, a system with 255,698 atoms, 1 femtosecond as a timestep (0.000001 ns) and run on 1 computing node, yielded a performance of 27.644 ns/day. Its MASN is 81.81. 
Another system with 33,885 atom, 2 femtosecond as a timestep (0.000002 ns) and run on the same computing node yielded a performance of 581.057 ns/day and its MASN is 102.12. 

For GPU tasks, the N (number of nodes) could be replaced by the number of GPUs (G). 

```
MASG = (r * A) / (1e6 * G * dt * 86400)    (4)
```

**Limitation**

Other performance-critical configures such as neighbor searching and cutoff are not considered in this metric.

closed_issues.title: Inconsistent behavior with too large -nstlist value
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

By default, mdrun selects nstlist in the runtime, using the value from TPR as the minimum. When a specific value is given via `-nstlist` flag, this automation is disabled.

As a result, when an unacceptable `-nstlist` value is passed, the flag is ignored, but the automatic selection is still disabled, and the simulation uses the nstlist value from the TPR. This behavior is kinda counter-intuitive: trying to increase nstlist over the default selection leads to a lower value being used.

## Exact steps to reproduce

Run 1.5k grappa or water box with `-nstlist 200`, see that the nstlist=10 is used:

```console
$ gmx mdrun -s ~/test_systems/grappa-1.5k-6.1M/0001.5/pme_v2.tpr -nsteps 1000 -nstlist 200
...
WARNING: Can not increase nstlist because the box is too small
$ grep nstlist md.log 
  gmx mdrun -s /home/aland/test_systems/grappa-1.5k-6.1M/0001.5/pme_v2.tpr -nsteps 1000 -nstlist 200
   nstlist                        = 10
Can not increase nstlist because the box is too small
      you might want to increase nstlist (this has no effect on accuracy)
$ grep 'Neighbor search' md.log 
 Neighbor search           1   24        101       0.018          1.369  14.4
```

Run the same system without `-nstlist` flag, see that the nstlist=80 is used:

```
$ gmx mdrun -s ~/test_systems/grappa-1.5k-6.1M/0001.5/pme_v2.tpr -nsteps 1000
...
Changing nstlist from 10 to 80, rlist from 0.903 to 1.072
$ grep nstlist md.log 
   nstlist                        = 10
Changing nstlist from 10 to 80, rlist from 0.903 to 1.072
$ grep 'Neighbor search' md.log 
 Neighbor search           1   24         13       0.003          0.204   2.7
```

## For developers: Why is this important?

The current behavior is logged correctly, but can lead to unexpected effets, e.g. when running through a range of box sizes.

## Possible fixes


It would be better to, either:
- make passing invalid `-nstlist` value a fatal error, thus ensuring the user requests are respected, or
- keep it a warning but don't disable automatic nstlist increase, making sure trying to increase nstlist won't decrease it.

closed_issues.title: NVCC check is broken
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

The CMake code for the ["Check for working NVCC/C++ compiler combination with nvcc"](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/release-2025/cmake/gmxManageNvccConfig.cmake?ref_type=heads#L84-110) is broken:

- it tries to use `CUDA_NVCC_EXECUTABLE` which is not set anymore by FindCUDAToolkit,
- but in the log output it reports in some places `CUDAToolkit_NVCC_EXECUTABLE`;
- it also does not respect the host compiler flags, which means that the check will fail if, e.g., `--gcc-toolchain` is needed (seems to be a [common problem with CMake](https://discourse.cmake.org/t/building-cuda-code-with-a-clang-host-compiler-which-uses-a-non-standard-gcc-installation/14058?u=al42and));
- however, the script does not properly check the error code, so the compiler is considered working even when `execute_process` fails with "file not found" (because `CUDA_NVCC_EXECUTABLE` is empty).

## Exact steps to reproduce

Compile with working CUDA, see `''` instead of compiler name in the log:

closed_issues.title: H5md: Unify data set creation functions
closed_issues.description:
H5md data sets are currently created using different functions for the cases of single-valued and multi-dimensional per-frame data. It would be ideal to unify these by refactoring common operations. 

This requires the code to have a notion of what individual "frames" represent for the data sets:

* For storing primitives, a "frame" is a single value of the primitive type
* For storing e.g. `ArrayRef<RVec>` which is a 2D data type we require knowledge about the dimensions

These could possibly be collected into a `FrameDescription` struct that defines the data dimensions and can be used directly to set up data sets. 

Possible use:

```cpp
hid_t dataSetValues   = createDataSet(parent, "singleValueDataSet", FrameDescription<float>());
hid_t dataSetRvecList = createDataSet(parent, "2dArrayDataSet", FrameDescription<RVec>(numAtoms));
```

- [ ] @mark.j.abraham started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/4962#note_2498475668): (+3 comments)

  > I think "buffer" is not a good noun for this name because it's generally used when talking about storing multiple things (see e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_buffer). Here we just have a value, so naming (and documenting it) `value` seems clearest.

closed_issues.title: Deal with restarts when writing TNG files
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Judging by the implementation of `gmxfio.cpp`, `checkpoint.cpp` and `mdoutf.cpp`, TNG files are flushed to disk before checkpointing, but because they are not
part of the list of open `t_fileio` files, no md5 sum is calculated and no
file-pointer position is stored in the checkpoint.

**GROMACS version**

All since TNG inclusion

**Steps to reproduce**

This assumed behaviour is unverified!

In principle, run mdrun writing TNG output, then kill mdrun after writing more TNG output after writing a checkpoint. Then attempt to restart with or without appending.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

It's possible that a restart with appending to a TNG file just doesn't work properly at all.

If a crash would happen after writing more output
* a restart with appending can't remove the output written after the checkpoint and before the crash, so does something undefined
* a restart without appending will leave the user with inconsistent data for the period after the checkpoint before the crash

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

Restarts with TNG output files should work as with other trajectory output, or be unsupported.

**Possible fixes**

Simplest for developers is to prohibit restarts with appending when writing TNG output. Users who have done restarts without appending can use `trjcat`, which will notice the duplicates and hopefully allow them to choose the write truncated output. This is probably the right approach given the presumed low adoption of TNG.

But first we should verify what the actual behaviour is

closed_issues.title: Build script for "own" FFTW3 ignores the compiler choice
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

With `GMX_BUILD_OWN_FFTW=ON`, FFTW3's build system defaults to the default compiler, ignoring what `CMAKE_C_COMPILER` says.

> I noticed that when FFTW3 is built, the compilation defaults to using `gcc`, instead of `gcc-11`. Only Gromacs itself is compiled with `gcc-11`. I can override this by setting the environment variable CC (e.g. ‘export CC=gcc-11’) before issuing the “cmake” command, but in my opinion users might expect the “CMAKE_C_COMPILER” setting to be propagated to the compilation of FFTW. (https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/wrong-compiler-when-installing-with-internally-built-fftw3/12024)

## Exact steps to reproduce

Build GROMACS with `cmake .. -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc-11 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++-11 -DGMX_FFT_LIBRARY=fftw3 -DGMX_BUILD_OWN_FFTW=ON`, while the default C compiler (or the one specified via `CC` env. variable) is _not_ `gcc-11`.

## For developers: Why is this important?

Silently using a different compiler for part of the build can lead to confusing errors and is messy in general.

## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

1. Default C compiler (in this case, `gcc`) is used
2. The same C compiler as used in GROMACS (specified via `CMAKE_C_COMPILER`) is used.

## Possible fixes

Passing the compiler manually in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/v2025.1/src/external/build-fftw/CMakeLists.txt#L113-119 should be enough, but requires testing.

In Gromacs 2025.0 modular simulator is disabled in expanded ensemble simulations, while all mdp parameters seem to be supported according to the docs. As a result the checkpoints are not written for unknown reason - the user has no idea what to change to make it work.
