closed_issues.title: Entropy calculation with gmx anaeig: inconsistent results with QH analysis
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

It seems that there is an issue with the entropy calculation by gmx anaeig, where the results calculated using Schlitter's formula and QH analysis differ by even one order of magnitude and are thus inconsistent. The issue is with the QH calculation. 

**GROMACS version**

Verified to exist in 2022.5 and 2024.1

**Steps to reproduce**

This issue appears to happen when using gmx covar + gmx anaeig to perform entropy calculations on trajectories. Specifically, gmx anaeig -entropy outputs two entropy values, one calculated using Quasi-Harmonic analysis and one using Schlitter's formula, which appear to be inconsistent, and differ by up to an order of magnitude. I was able to reproduce this with different molecular systems, e.g. a simple protein simulation in water in the NPT ensemble, as well as simulations of nanoparticles such and dendrimers (different systems, different force fields, and no obvious issues or instabilities in the simulations themselves). To reproduce the bug, it seems to be sufficient to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a given system using gmx covar and then performing entropy analysis using gmx anaeig with the -entropy flag.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

The entropy result by gmx anaeig using the two calculation methods is inconsistent. In one example protein simulation in water (CHARMM36m FF, NPT ensemble), the result of gmx anaeig -entropy is:

Schlitter: 3228.01 J/molK

QH: 34517.5 J/molK

Again, I was able to confirm this behaviour on very different simulations, so it should not depend on the specific simulation being analyzed.

**What did you expect the correct behavior to be?**

Entropy values should be consistent, or at the very least differ by a small value (as reported e.g. in https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1401821 )

**Possible fixes**

I suspect that this issue might be connected with the one that was briefly reported in issue #3481.
By looking at the gromacs source code, the calculation of the entropy starting from the eigenvalues is performed in /src/gromacs/gmxana/thermochemistry.cpp. It seems to me that the calculation of frequencies starting from the eigenvalues performed in the function eigval_to_frequency is not correct.
In recent versions (i think 2019 onwards), the conversion is performed by taking the square root of the product of the eigenvalues times a factor (called "factor_gmx_to_omega2") equal to 1e21/(NA*AMU), where NA is Avogadro's number and AMU is the conversion between a.m.u. and kg. In the current versions, the calculation of the frequency is thus performed as:

std::sqrt(std::max(0.0, eigval) * factor_gmx_to_omega2)

I think the issue might be that the correct way of calculating omega is by first calculating the factor as:

factor_gmx_to_omega2 = k*T*1e18 / AMU

where k is the Boltzmann constant, T the temperature, 1e18 is the reciprocal of the conversion factor between nm^2 (unit of the non-mass-weighted eigenvalues as produced by gmx covar) and m^2 (SI). Omega should be then given by using this corrected factor in:

w = sqrt(1/lambda * factor_gmx_to_omega2)

where lambda is the eigenvalue in nm^2. This should be the correct implementation of the equation relating eigenvalues to frequencies as reported e.g. in https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1401821, and indeed gives realistic values.

I think the issue might not be present in versions before 2018, since there the calculation is performed in /src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_anaeig.cpp and the corresponding function, calc_entropy_qh, indeed calculates the frequencies as follows:

lambda = eigval[i]*AMU;

w      = std::sqrt(BOLTZMANN*temp/lambda)/NANO;

which should be the same as the suggested solution above.

closed_issues.title: Performance analysis for gpu macro removal
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

The performance impact of removing the gpu macros used to stub the implementations of the GPU specific methods in CPU builds should be quickly tested to ensure that it doesn't create major performance regressions.

**Use cases**/**Detailed description**

Removing the macros will make it easier to port the accelerator layer to new targets, as it will be more clear which methods are implemented where based on the CMake inputs, instead of having the rather cryptic macros defined for it in one place. The macros are also not consistently used throughout the codebase.

We need to make sure that this doesn't create performance regressions because the function calls will no longer be inlined stubs in the CPU only build.

**Impact**

Avoid performance regressions for users

    > So, almost all of them are already backend-specific! The only file where we actually enjoy the advantages these wrappers offer is `src/gromacs/ewald/pme_gpu_internal.cpp`.
    > 
    > Would we not be better off ditching these helpers altogether and just having backend-specific functions for invoking each kernel? My feeling is that they add more complexity than brevity (and yes, I perhaps should have removed them myself when adding SYCL, but alas).

closed_issues.title: NBNxM CPU kernel loop unroll issue
closed_issues.description:
Some compilers, in particular the LLVM backend for ARM, do not unroll some short, fixed length loop in the innermost loop of the NBNxM CPU SIMD kernels. There loops were introduced in commit 0ad4a2ed in 2022, so the performance of release-2023 and release-2024 is affected by this.

This is part of #4752, where a lot of performance results are discussed.

closed_issues.title: Replace gmxManageCcache.cmake with CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_LAUNCHER

CMake since version 3.4 supports specifying [CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_LAUNCHER](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/variable/CMAKE_LANG_COMPILER_LAUNCHER.html) and, since 3.17, this is [also supported as environment variable](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/envvar/CMAKE_LANG_COMPILER_LAUNCHER.html).

Our minimum required version is already 3.18 and we should consider removing `gmxManageCcache.cmake` in favor of this approach.

If I try to use the pdb file as the input for ```-s```, which the documentation says is ok, I get no error but CONECT records do not appear in the output pdb. The solution is to generate a tpr file for my pdb which takes multiple extraneous commands (pdb2gmx, editconf, grompp, then trjconv). 

In [editconf](https://manual.gromacs.org/current/onlinehelp/gmx-editconf.html), it is noted that CONECT records require a topology file but not in trjconv (and an error is thrown if you try to use -f input.pdb, but it is a null pointer error). Documentation says I can use pdb for ```-s``` so I try to do that: `gmx trjconv -f input.pdb -s input.pdb -o input-conect.pdb -conect yes`. I get no error, but the output pdb (input-conect.pdb) has no CONECT records in it.

I run energy minimization of the system using the l-bfgs algorithm with energy dumping every frame. I use long range dispersion corrections for energy and pressure. gmx mdrun -deffnm min  ; run 10-step minimization

```

log = np.loadtxt('./min.xvg', comments=['#', '@'])
energy1 = log[:, 1:-1].sum(axis=1)  # sum of all energy terms
energy2 = log[:, -1]  # potential energy from log

dE = energy2 - energy1  # difference (should be zero)

```

The potential energy includes dispersion correction term only 1 time.

closed_issues.title: Race condition on GPU halo exchange scheduling events in extreme corner case runs
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

In extreme run conditions (e.g. high numbers of thread-MPI tasks running on each GPU), the tasks can become so out of sync that there is a race condition on the event used to schedule synchronization of X and F GPU halo exchanges, causing a seg fault in cudaStreamWaitEvent. 

More explicitly, 
 - a given rank can mark it's halo event and send it to it's lower neighbor
 - the rank will receive the corresponding event from its upper neighbor and proceed to scheduling it's F halo exchange
 - it will send the same event (reused for X and F halo exchanges) to its upper neighbor 
 - the event has not yet been processed by the lower neighbor, which is way behind. 

## Exact steps to reproduce

So far I've only reproduced it with 8 thread-MPI tasks running on 1 or 2 GPUs, with CUDA graphs enabled (for both STMV and ADH Dodec). Note the issue is not directly related to CUDA Graphs (it happens on non-graph steps), but use of graphs seems to help the tasks get further out of sync.

## For developers: Why is this important?

GROMACS shouldn't crash.

## Possible fixes

Use separate events for X and F GPU halo scheduling. Fix incoming.

closed_issues.title: Template doForce methods on GMX_GPU build
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Currently, the doForce method and its children contain a large number of branches that can be dead code depending on the build configuration, but still need to be evaluate during the loop. Eliminating these dead branches through the use of templating and `if constexpr` might lead to further optimization options and subsequent performance improvements.

**Use cases**/**Impact**

Possible performance boosts for users due to better code optimization by the compiler, guidance for developers for how to further improve methods.

**Detailed description**

The doForce kernel and where useful some of the child methods should be changed to be templated on the current GROMACS build type, in this case whether it is a GMX_GPU build or not. Then all the GPU specific branches can be locked behind `if constexpr` expressions that (in optimized builds) will be removed by the compiler when preparing the different template versions.

**Requirements**

Performance investigation to see if this results in any actual improvements beyond code cleanup.

closed_issues.title: OpenMP is disabled for bonded list update in Clang-CUDA builds
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

With CUDA-Clang build, we pass `-fno-openmp` flag to all GPU-related files to work around an old Clang bug under the assumption that no CUDA file uses OpenMP. But that assumption is not valid anymore.

- Our CMake code: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/bbe83e52dda31475f634993fb5c587753ac24154/cmake/gmxManageClangCudaConfig.cmake#L123-124

- LLVM bug: https://bugs.llvm.org/show_bug.cgi?id=45533

- MR introducing the OpenMP region in a GPU source file: !3899

- Similar issue: #4747 / !3540

## Exact steps to reproduce

```console
$ cmake ../.. -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-17 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++-17 -DGMX_GPU=CUDA -DGMX_CLANG_CUDA=ON -DGMX_CUDA_TARGET_SM=86
[...]
$ make -j$(nproc)
[...]
$ touch ../../src/gromacs/listed_forces/listed_forces_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp
$ VERBOSE=1 make
[ 16%] Building CXX object src/gromacs/CMakeFiles/libgromacs.dir/listed_forces/listed_forces_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp.o
[...] /usr/bin/clang++-17 [...] -Wno-source-uses-openmp [...] -fopenmp=libomp [...] -fno-openmp [...]
```

In this case, `-fno-openmp` overrides the earlier `-fopenmp=libomp` and disables the use of OpenMP on the host, which can be seen if we remove `-Wno-source-uses-openmp`:

```
/home/aland/gromacs/src/gromacs/listed_forces/listed_forces_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp:192:9: warning: unexpected '#pragma omp ...' in program [-Wsource-uses-openmp]
  192 | #pragma omp parallel for num_threads(gmx_omp_nthreads_get(ModuleMultiThread::Bonded)) schedule(static)
      |         ^
1 warning generated when compiling for sm_86.
/home/aland/gromacs/src/gromacs/listed_forces/listed_forces_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp:192:9: warning: unexpected '#pragma omp ...' in program [-Wsource-uses-openmp]
  192 | #pragma omp parallel for num_threads(gmx_omp_nthreads_get(ModuleMultiThread::Bonded)) schedule(static)
      |         ^
1 warning generated when compiling for host.
```

The first warning, for the sm_86 pass is expected and is the reason to keep `-Wno-source-uses-openmp`. The second indicate that OpenMP gets disabled for the host.

## For developers: Why is this important?

We should use OpenMP whenever we intend to use it.

## Possible fixes

The easiest solution is making the CMake flag addition more narrow. Per https://bugs.llvm.org/show_bug.cgi?id=45533, the bug is fixed in Clang 11, so there is no need to add `-fno-openmp` with new versions.

Clang-CUDA is not widely used and the performance benefit of !3899 is not huge, so we can keep it as-is (without parallelization) with Clang 9-10.

closed_issues.title: Discrepancy in GROMACS 2024 mdp options for mass repartitioning
closed_issues.description:
Hello GROMACS development team,

In GROMACS 2024, a new mdp option to allow for easy hydrogen mass repartitioning was added.

- In the documentation (https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/user-guide/mdp-options.html#mdp-mass-repartitioning-factor) this new mdp option is referred to as 'mass-repartitioning-factor'
- In the release notes (https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/release-notes/2024/major/performance.html#flexible-hydrogen-mass-repartitioning-using-grompp), this new mdp option is referred to as 'mass-repartition-factor'

When using the grommp command, including the mdp option 'mass-repartitioning-factor' yields the following warning:

```
WARNING 1 [file ../enmin.00.mdp, line 68]:
  Unknown left-hand 'mass-repartitioning-factor' in parameter file
```

When using the mdp option 'mass-repartition-factor' instead, no such warning occurs.

It seems that the mdp option 'mass-repartitioning-factor' is labeled incorrectly in the documentation.

 

Thank you for your support,

Michael Robo

Computational Chemistry Staff Scientist

Indiana Biosciences Research Institute

closed_issues.title: 2024 with AdaptiveCpp crashes when building ACPP with clang
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

If I am following the build instructions to build Gromacs 2024 for AMD GPUs, the make check phase crashes if I am using the ROCm provided clang to build AdaptiveCpp. Building AdaptiveCpp with gcc 11 works. This was tested with ROCm 5.7.1 and 6.0.2

## Exact steps to reproduce

Follow the guide: https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/install-guide/index.html#sycl-gpu-acceleration-for-amd-gpus
Configure AdaptiveCpp (latest version) with its compilers set to use ROCm's LLVM:

Step 1:
cmake .. -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=${ROCM_PATH}/llvm/bin/clang \
         -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=${ROCM_PATH}/llvm/bin/clang++ \
         -DLLVM_DIR=${ROCM_PATH}/llvm/lib/cmake/llvm/
make; make install

Step: configure and build GROMACS:

closed_issues.title: DPC++ build targeting NVIDIA/AMD devices is not properly testing compiler flags
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

[In the code](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/release-2024/cmake/gmxManageSyclOneApi.cmake?ref_type=heads#L124-136), we were setting flags using `SYCL_WARNINGS_CXX_FLAGS` variable, but when checking for their validity, we were using uninitialized variable `SYCL_WARNING_CXX_FLAGS`. This caused the flags to always be accepted, regardless of the compiler reaction.

So far, all compiler versions support the flags, so the bug was not causing any negative impact.

## For developers: Why is this important?

When we test compiler flags, we should test them.

## Possible fixes

Fix the typo.

## Summary

When an atom is outside the box, [index calculation in `computeEffectiveAtomDensity`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/71d0092693a303ac5633b2d458f1602217139a6b/src/gromacs/mdlib/calc_verletbuf.cpp#L1133) produces negative values, and GROMACS crashes due to heap corruption.

Specifically, the problem seems to be caused by negative coordinates (-8.229) of magnitude larger than the box size (6.2), so that our `+ numCells[d]` is not enough to make the value positive.

## Unit test

For `src/gromacs/mdlib/tests/calc_verletbuf.cpp`:

```cpp
// Issue #5002
TEST(EffectiveAtomDensity, LargeValuesHandledWell)
{
    const std::vector<RVec> coordinates      = { { 13.132, -8.229, -2.700 } };
    const matrix            box              = { { 6.2, 0, 0 }, { 0, 6.2, 0 }, { 0, 0, 6.2 } };
    const real              cutoff           = 1;
    const real              referenceDensity = (1) / (coordinates.size() * gmx::power3<real>(6.2/6));

    const real density = computeEffectiveAtomDensity(coordinates, box, cutoff, MPI_COMM_NULL);
    EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(density, referenceDensity);
}

closed_issues.description:
## Summary

!3952 introduced `gmx_simdcall` into the GPU compiler pass. While such functions are note called from the GPU, they cause problems:

- warnings with DPC++ (worked around in !3952)
- build failures with CUDA + Clang due to handling of `vectorcall` attribute (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/jobs/6222737148)
- build failures with CUDA + GCC due to handling of `vector_size` attribute (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/3952#note_1785134310)
- build failures with Clang + SYCL when targeting NVIDIA/AMD devices due to the workaround above causing invalid cluster sizes to be reported (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/3964#note_1785086331)

closed_issues.title: oneMKL FFT: Remove the workaround requiring a single backend
closed_issues.description:
Currently (February 2024), oneMKL with DPC++ crashes when not linked directly to the backend library due to an issue in Unified Runtime. The fix is expected in oneAPI 2024.2, and, currently, the workaround requires linking to a single backend (cuFFT/rocFFT/MKL), negating the benefit of oneMKL as a compatibility layer.

Since we are unlikely to need a deep backward-compatibility for oneMKL, we are better off removing this workaround when possible.

The following discussion from !3964 should be addressed:

- [ ] @acmnpv started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/3964#note_1784577908):  (+2 comments)

    > is there a version where this is fixed so we know when the workaround here can be removed?

closed_issues.title: More force fields in the default distributions
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Users have expressed interest in GROMACS including more force fields, for use with `gmx pdb2gmx` in the distribution. This is listed as one of our high-priority development goals in the Bioexcel development plan:

"Force fields are continuously evolving and are continuously updated to account for the variety of the complex biomolecular systems. The most recent versions of the force fields are usually recommended by the force field developers. With newer versions of force fields included in the default GROMACS distribution it would be easier for users to enjoy the recent developments. However, this comes with the burden of converting the force fields to a format suitable for GROMACS and subsequently testing the conversions in order to ensure correctness. In addition, it would also be important to retain old versions of force fields for backward compatibility. A balance between usability and sustainability will have to be found, in dialogue with the force field developers and/or contributors involved in the conversion process."

The first priority would be to try to include CHARMM36 and recent Amber force fields (19 and/or 14).

## For developers: Why is this important?

This is a user requested feature. The force fields we ship should, if possible, be up-to-date and reflect what is recommended.

## Possible fixes

We should contact the force field developers and/or those who are converting the force fields into GROMACS formats to investigate if we can include the force fields directly or if we should find other solution that are good both for the GROMACS users and the force field developers.

## Progress

- [ ] ~~CHARMM36~~ cannot be added in the distribution. A download link is presented instead.
- [x] Amber 19/14

closed_issues.title: CPU nonbonded performance regression due to new pairlist settings
closed_issues.description: For the 2024 release the minimum pairlist pruning interval was increased from 4 to 10. This was to reduce the overhead of the pruning kernel cost. But this decision was based on setting with smooth Coulomb cut-off (PME). For other settings, such as reaction-field, there can be a 5% performance loss.

closed_issues.title: Document local Windows testing workflow
closed_issues.description:
**Follow-up description**

https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/january-24-biweekly-gromacs-developer-meeting/8060/3

I have written a draft version of the guide for setting up a local Windows/MSVC build and test environment for GROMACS in a virtual machine without requiring a license from Microsoft and I am adding it below.

**Impact**

Developers will have an option of testing Windows builds locally without having to maintain a Windows installation.

Ideally, workers for our CI/CD on GitLab can be set up in the same way using some automation tool that performs the actions below without requiring user intervention. In such case, this automation tool would periodically redownload and resetup the virtual machine as a CI/CD worker.

**Other contributors**

CI/CD infrastructure maintainers, anyone who can help with installation and configuration automation.

**Draft version of the guide**

Microsoft provides time-limited [Windows virtual machines for developers](https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/downloads/virtual-machines/) that include Visual Studio Community Edition and last for approximately 3 months. In that time frame, Microsoft releases a new version that again lasts for approximately 3 months. Supported virtualization platforms are VMware, Hyper-V (Gen2), VirtualBox, and Parallels.

To get an image that can be used with QEMU/KVM via e.g. [Virtual Machine Manager](https://virt-manager.org/), one can convert either VMware or VirtualBox image to QCOW2:

Option 1) After downloaded VMware archive:

``` shell
$ unzip WinDev2404Eval.VMWare.zip
Archive:  WinDev2404Eval.VMWare.zip
  inflating: WinDev2404Eval-disk1.vmdk
  inflating: WinDev2404Eval.mf
  inflating: WinDev2404Eval.ovf

$ qemu-img convert -O qcow2 WinDev2404Eval-disk1.vmdk WinDev2404Eval-disk1.qcow2
```

Option 2) Alternatively, after downloading VirtualBox archive:

``` shell
$ unzip WinDev2404Eval.VirtualBox.zip
Archive:  WinDev2404Eval.VirtualBox.zip
  inflating: WinDev2404Eval.ova

$ tar xvf WinDev2404Eval.ova
WinDev2404Eval.ovf
WinDev2404Eval-disk001.vmdk

$ qemu-img convert -O qcow2 WinDev2404Eval-disk001.vmdk WinDev2404Eval-disk001.qcow2
```

Note that `host-passthrough` CPU model might cause Windows to give a BSoD on some CPUs. Using `host-model`, a [named models](https://qemu-project.gitlab.io/qemu/system/qemu-cpu-models.html), or QEMU Virtual CPU (`qemu64`), might work better in such cases.

After starting Windows 11, there might be error notices regarding VMWare or VirtualBox VM tools, which can be safely ignored.

Run the Terminal app, open `Windows PowerShell` preset and use winget package manager to obtain Git, Python, and CMake:

``` shell
> winget install -e --id Git.Git --source winget
> winget install -e --id Python.Python3.12 --source winget
> winget install -e --id Kitware.CMake --source winget
```

The installations will ask for admin permissions. Confirm them.

Create the directories for the source code:

``` shell
> md .\source\
> md .\source\repos\
```

Afterwards, open `Developer PowerShell for VS 2022` preset in Terminal app, change into the previously created directory, download the GROMACS sources with Git, change into GROMACS source repository root directory, and use CMake to configure and build the source:

``` shell
> cd C:\Users\User\source\repos\
> git clone https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs.git
> cd .\gromacs\
> cmake -B .\build\ -S .\ -D GMX_DEVELOPER_BUILD=ON -D GMX_FFT_LIBRARY=fftpack
> cmake --build .\build\ --parallel 4
```

In the last command, CMake runs MSBuild with up to 4 workers. This can be increased on machines with more cores allocated to the virtual machine.

Since CTest is broken on Windows (#4097), use a small inline PowerShell script to run the tests and Notepad to check their output:

``` shell
> cd .\build\
> foreach ( $file in Get-ChildItem -Filter *.exe -Path .\bin\Debug\ ) { & .\bin\Debug\$file >> out.txt 2>> err.txt }
> notepad .\out.txt
> notepad .\err.txt
```

Note that Windows build type is set to Debug by default (#4688).

To work around a broken CTest and have more Unix-like build experience, get Ninja using winget:

``` shell
> winget install -e --id Ninja-build.Ninja --source winget
```

And then build GROMACS with Ninja instead of MSBuild:

``` shell
> cmake -G Ninja -B .\build-ninja\ -S .\ -D GMX_DEVELOPER_BUILD=ON -D GMX_FFT_LIBRARY=fftpack
> cmake --build .\build-ninja\
> cmake --build .\build-ninja\ --target test
```

Builds using Ninja tend to be faster than those performed with MSBuild, but testing with MSBuild would still a preferred way to test Windows/MSVC compatibility since Ninja is a third-party tool.

closed_issues.title: Build with GMX_USE_COLVARS=NONE segfaults in MdrunTests
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

When configured without Colvars support, mdrun tests for GROMACS 2024.0 segfault while calling `grompp`, apparently while handling mdp fields that should be handled by the colvars module. Presumably `grompp` itself will segfault similarly.

## Exact steps to reproduce

```
cmake .... -DGMX_USE_COLVARS=None
make mdrun-test
bin/mdrun-test
```

## For developers: Why is this important?

Configuration options should work. We should also have a build in CI that tests `GMX_USE_COLVARS=NONE` so that it stays working.

## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

Unrelated test cases segfault while trying to handle colvars mdp options. They should behave gracefully.

My guess is that in this case the colvars module is not constructed, so one of the getters in the backtrace below is returning a nullptr that is dereferenced. closed_issues.title: Implement sorting of neighbour list on GPU with SYCL
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Support for pairlist sorting on GPU was originally implemented in AMD HIP fork, and later was added to mainline GROMACS's CUDA backend (#4872, !3809). For simplicity and feature parity, it should be implemented in SYCL too.

The code is rather straightforward. `exclusive_scan` is implemented in oneDPL (which has *some* compatibility with ACpp too) and there are talks with Aksel about getting native support in ACpp for prefix sum.

Performance checking is a broad task, so we should have an easy way to toggle between the old and the new codepath.

closed_issues.title: In the spread force of virtual_site1, the force of i atom is added to the virtual site.
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

In the spread force of virtual_site1, the force of i atom is added to the virtual site. But actually, we should add the forces on the virtual site to atom i.

**GROMACS version**

2025-dev-20240201-3732873364

**What is the current bug behavior?**

This might be a code error. We should add the forces of the virtual site atom to the constructing atom, rather than adding the forces of the constructing atom to the virtual site atom.
https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blame/main/src/gromacs/mdlib/vsite.cpp?ref_type=heads#L1267
![image](/uploads/d22356b3e571c0cc448554cc468c6a2f/image.png)

reference：https://manual.gromacs.org/current/reference-manual/functions/interaction-methods.html#on-top-of-an-atom

**Possible fixes**

Use "f[ai] += f[av];" to replace "f[av] += f[ai];" in spread_vsite1.

closed_issues.title: New versioning scheme for 2024.0
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

We decided to change the major release version number from 2024 to 2024.0. During the release process we noticed that this introduced some issues:

- The files were uploaded to `https://manual.gromacs.org/2024/` instead of `https://manual.gromacs.org/2024.0/`.  This has been addressed by Stefan.
- The uploaded file names are not correct, e.g. `https://ftp.gromacs.org/gromacs/gromacs-2024.tar.gz` and `https://ftp.gromacs.org/regressiontests/regressiontests-2024.tar.gz`, `https://manual.gromacs.org/current/manual-2024.pdf`. These have not been fixed and it is probably safer to leave them for now.
- cmake with REGRESSIONTEST_DOWNLOAD=ON will download `regressiontests-2024.tar.gz`
- When extracting the file archive, the directory is called gromacs-2024 and regressiontests-2024. This is potentially the biggest issue, since this will probably be the name the, e.g., HPC centers will use.
- In the PDF of the documentation it says "Release 2024".
- gmx binary outputs `gmx, version 2024`
- The link in the [manual](https://manual.gromacs.org/current/index.html) points to `manual-2024.pdf`

These issues should be fixed automatically in 2024.1, as far as I can see. But we must make sure that we address them before 2025.0. We must keep our eyes open to see if there are other problems.

closed_issues.title: gmx nmtraj: Invalid value: '0.0'; expected an integer
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Trying to run `gmx nmtraj` on any trajectory fails with

```
Program:     gmx nmtraj, version 2025-dev-20240126-fd7fd2facf-dirty
Source file: src/gromacs/utility/strconvert.cpp (line 88)
Function:    int gmx::intFromString(const char*)

Error in user input:
Invalid value: '0.0'; expected an integer
```

This is because we are using [the default value of `0.0` for `phasevec`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/f8bb8c99907c2cf95ccfca69c01ae9ebe9d9a46d/src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_nmtraj.cpp#L83) but then [try to parse it as `int`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/f8bb8c99907c2cf95ccfca69c01ae9ebe9d9a46d/src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_nmtraj.cpp#L145).

`git log` suggests that the error has been there since 2020 (658819431c0dabdb13ef01f32bf59e0c0eca82ff). Before that, we were using `strtod`, but is was changed to `gmx::fromStdString<int>` during refactoring.

## Exact steps to reproduce

`gmx nmtraj -s topol.tpr -v traj.trr` on any TPR+TRR file.

For a full run, the file with eigenvectors must be present, but this error happens before that file is read.

## For developers: Why is this important?

User report: https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/nmtraj-issue/8171

## Possible fixes

Using `gmx::fromStdString<real>` instead seems like the most logical thing to do, but we would need to run at least some tests afterward.

closed_issues.title: RISC-V: use RDTIME instead of RDCYCLE
closed_issues.description:
Reported by @aurel32:

> Starting with Linux 6.6 [1], RDCYCLE is a privileged instruction on
> RISC-V and can't be used directly from userland. There is a sysctl
> option to change that as a transition period, but it will eventually
> disappear.
> 
> Use RDTIME instead, which while less accurate has the advantage of being
> synchronized between CPU (and thus monotonic) and of constant frequency.
> It is somehow similar to the virtual timer that is used by GROMACS on
> Aarch64.
> 
> NB: it might be better to use the RDTIME pseudo instruction instead of
> using the CSRRS instruction with the CSR addresses, but there might be
> a reason for not using it.
> 
> [1] https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=cc4c07c89aada16229084eeb93895c95b7eabaa3

The issue is fixed in %"2024.release" with !4040. We need to backport it to %2023.5. In `main`, perhaps we can consider changing our asm code to use `rdtime`

closed_issues.title: NbnxmTests crash with MSVC in reduce_energies_over_lists
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

`NbnxmKernelTest.type_plain-C_TabNo_CoulombReactionField_VdwCutCombNone` (846702ee517a89724c4f39975ee25d1dbcb048dd) tries to access an out-of-range std::vector element in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/bf703ffad53f366f1b54a9677bb88ef638bc4606/src/gromacs/nbnxm/kernel_common.cpp#L124.

In particular, the test set-up code resizes `nbv_->nbat().out[0].Vvdw` to 1 to trigger non-energy-group kernels. This works ok with the most of [`nbnxn_kernel_cpu`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/bf703ffad53f366f1b54a9677bb88ef638bc4606/src/gromacs/nbnxm/kerneldispatch.cpp#L241), except, at the very end, `reduce_energies_over_lists` is called which thinks that there are 3 energy groups based on `nbat->params().nenergrp` and assumes that the `nbv_->nbat().out[0].Vvdw` vector is appropriately sized. Since the vector was shrunk to 1, it triggers and assertion failure (surprisingly, only with MSVC, although the logic seems to be platform-independent).

As far as I can tell, this only affects tests. I have not bisected, but it looks like the issue has been there since the tests were introduced in d855abac1c9241475d54c7827a632586696f037b (!3673).

**Use cases**/**Impact**

Ability to run GROMACS with HIP through the common gpu abstraction layer without having to write everything from scratch.

**Detailed description**

Currently, the abstraction layer for GPU backends only covers CUDA, SYCL and OpenCL. To be able to use AMD devices with HIP later on we need to extend this to also include HIP.

closed_issues.title: Set up testing infrastructure to cover builds with HIP backend
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

We want to make sure that the HIP specific code gets tested in the same way as for the other accelerator backends.

**Use cases**

Avoid broken software that annoys users :smile_cat: 

**Impact**

Users will be able to expect a working HIP backend and be able to rely on the accuracy of their simulations.

**Detailed description**

To be able to cover the new code that the HIP backend will add, we will need to add backend specific testing and build images to ensure that we cover the new runtime. To do this, build images with different versions of the ROCm backend should be added to the GROMACS container registry, and new test cases need to be introduced that use those images.

One issue could be that this stresses the current infrastructure too much, and that total build times would become too long. In this case I'm open to work on reducing build times also for unrelated configurations so that this doesn't become a blocker.

**Requirements**

This will likely need additions to the current CI infrastructure, to be able to test newer hardware as well. AMD is open to help there (in a reasonable manner) with at a minimum expertise in setting up relevant systems.

closed_issues.title: MSVC build broken with Colvars and OpenMP
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

After !3966 enabled OpenMP for Colvars, the MSVC build fails with `error C3016: 'i': index variable in OpenMP 'for' statement must have signed integral type` errors for three `parallel for` loops in `src/external/colvars/colvarproxy.cpp`: [this one](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/d5f5830a127a54deacc19b809f220dc2cdde5311/src/external/colvars/colvarproxy.cpp#L303-304) and two just below.

## Exact steps to reproduce

Try building recent `release-2024` (after !3966) on Windows with MSVC 2022 and `GMX_OPENMP=ON`.

## Possible fixes

1. This is [a genuine limitation of OpenMP 2.0](https://stackoverflow.com/q/2820621/929437), so the easiest solution would be changing the iterator variable to `int` (or `std::int64_t`) in these loops.
2. According to [a recent discussion of the same problem in Tesseract OCR project](https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract/issues/3285), adding `/openmp:llvm` compiler flag should lift this restriction. I don't know whether this will have any other side-effects, either good or bad.
3. OpenMP 2.0 is ancient. We can refuse to support it, and just add a CMake check preventing it. Given how easy fix (1) is, I think this is an overkill. On the other hand, I'm not 100% OpenMP on MSVC has been working well before (it is disabled in our CI), so perhaps this combination should have been forbidden long ago.
4. Forbid only OpenMP && MSVC && Colvars (as opposed to OpenMP && MSVC, see (3)). If we can't do anything else before the %"2024.rc", this is the minimal thing that should be done.

closed_issues.title: complex/nst_mismatch fails with hipSYCL, GPU-aware MPI, 2 ranks, -nb gpu -pme cpu -update cpu
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Seen in CI with weekly CI, can be reproduced quite reliably when running manually in the same docker image (`registry.gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/ci-ubuntu-22.04-llvm-15-cuda-11.7.1-hipsycl-0.9.4-rocm-5.3.3:latest`) on our infrastructure with a single GPU.

```console
$ /usr/local/cmake-3.18.4/bin/cmake ../ -DGMX_GPU=SYCL -DGMX_MPI=ON -DGMX_SIMD=AVX2_256 \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithAssert -DGMX_SYCL=ACPP -DGMX_SYCL_HIPSYCL=ON \
  -DHIPSYCL_TARGETS='cuda:sm_50,sm_52,sm_60,sm_61,sm_70,sm_75' -DGMX_GPU_FFT_LIBRARY=VkFFT \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER= -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER= \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-15 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++-15 \
  -DGMX_USE_NVTX=ON -DGMX_CYCLE_SUBCOUNTERS=ON \
  -DNVTX_INCLUDE_DIR=/usr/local/cuda-11.7/targets/x86_64-linux/include/ \
  -DNVTX_LIBRARY=/usr/local/cuda-11.7/targets/x86_64-linux/lib/libnvToolsExt.so
...
$ cd tests/complex/nst_mismatch
$ GMX_ENABLE_DIRECT_GPU_COMM=1 GMX_FORCE_GPU_AWARE_MPI=1 HIPSYCL_MAX_CACHED_NODES=0 \
  mpirun -np 2 ../../../bin/gmx_mpi  mdrun -notunepme -npme 0 -ntomp 2 -pme cpu -update cpu
```


The energies match well on steps 0 and 14, but on steps 28 and 30 "Coul. recip" energy (and, as a consequence total energies) fluctuate from run to run:

- [md.log](/uploads/37802e3483548df29769e43d48d6aa07/md.log)
- [reference_s.log](/uploads/10b08204f8ccf5d5274faf4604dbc829/reference_s.log)

Observations:

- Setting `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` fixes the problem
  - Up to (and including) Step 26, the input coordinates for PME calculation are identical (a few differences of 1e-4 absolute) and so are per-rank long-range energies (up to 1e-3 absolute); on Step 27, coordinate differences become much more numerous and larger (up to 4e-4) and the per-rank long-range energies start differing by ~1e0 (absolute).
- Disabling GPU-aware MPI / GPU-direct communications fixes the problem
- Running under `compute-sanitizer --tool=(sync|init|mem)check` or `valgrind` fixes the problem
  - racecheck hangs
- Issue reproduces fine when running under nvprof (no nsys in the image).
  - Two ranks recorded with energy not matching the reference: [fail_143399.nvprof](/uploads/7b32509c6b321c87bf34a65cc38993fa/fail_143399.nvprof) [fail_143401.nvprof](/uploads/57c50d0a7916ea827501f77e138ed5ad/fail_143401.nvprof)
  - Re-ran same build until energy matched the reference: [good_143348.nvprof](/uploads/4d9a34225f09c35f3fcd9a3c79345a7c/good_143348.nvprof) 
[good_143350.nvprof](/uploads/b3b087cd63235614bdf6e4d00ca5fd89/good_143350.nvprof)
- Changing `HIPSYCL_MAX_CACHED_NODES` does not seem to affect the behavior.
- Setting `-dlb no` does not seem to affect the behavior.
- Does not reproduce with native CUDA in the same container.
- Reproduces with hipSYCL 0.9.4 and 23.10.0
- Setting `HIPSYCL_ALLOW_INSTANT_SUBMISSION` fixes the issue (supported in 23.10.0 only)
- Reproduced in the same docker image on a different system (with sm_86 GPU).
- Changing `nstlist` from 13 to 5/8/10/12/14/15/17/26 fixes the problem. Setting it to 11 or 9 or 7 still exhibits the bug. Other `nst*` variables do not seem to have huge effect.
- Synchronizing with the Halo stream after (but not before) submitting [indexMap H2D copy in `reinitHalo`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/abf1d54bc933802fb4ec94b6374177e68e60a61e/src/gromacs/domdec/gpuhaloexchange_impl_gpu.cpp#L152-153) seems to help.
- Something wrong with F-Halo on step 26 (NS), pre-integration forces are way off.
  - Host forces are lost, sometimes on one rank, sometimes on both.
  - Disabling `StepWorkload.useGpuFBufferOps` on NS steps helps

Affected commits:

- ce8024bbf912e1be89389f99e5c356cbf54b2f38 (recent release-2024)
- 94882102a54dec84cb92f8e415194e854fbeadb9 (v2024-beta)
- 7494d1b0200ef1eb4ee3503927c2c7ab81f9535b (late September)
- cd348c8aa928409650f92e4ffdbce2230595472a (late July)

closed_issues.title: Topology generation suggestions in "System preparation" chapter are outdated
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Our [System preparation](https://manual.gromacs.org/current/user-guide/system-preparation.html) chapter from the User Manual looks quite dated.

It makes some questionable recommendations:

- PRODRG is not available anymore and, according to Justin Lemkul, [was never a good tool to use](https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/prodrg-server/7782/2). Yet we recommend it for preparing GROMOS topology: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/98af5014ec72e7674dd9740873319394d9c5d298/docs/user-guide/system-preparation.rst#L57-58
- MKTOP website has been down for a two years already, yet we still recommend it for building OPLS/AA topologies: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/98af5014ec72e7674dd9740873319394d9c5d298/docs/user-guide/system-preparation.rst#L61. One can find the source code around, but hopefully a 9-year-old Perl script is not the best tool out there?

And does not mention other widely used tools, such as CHARMM-GUI (used even in our own [Membrane protein tutorial](https://tutorials.gromacs.org/docs/membrane-protein.html))

## Exact steps to reproduce

Look at our user guide: [System preparation](https://manual.gromacs.org/current/user-guide/system-preparation.html)

## For developers: Why is this important?

Bad documentation confuses users and makes them less likely to refer to said documentation in the future.

closed_issues.title: Updating build instructions for Grace
closed_issues.description:
The following two sections of text add recommendations for running on Grace (ARMv9). Advice on where in the documentation this should go would be appreciated. For now I've split this into two sections, 1) updating the existing [SIMD support section](https://manual.gromacs.org/2023/install-guide/index.html#simd-support) and 2) additional stand alone section. 

## update to existing [SIMD support section](https://manual.gromacs.org/2023/install-guide/index.html#simd-support)

Updates bolded. It is likely that the recommendations for Grace generalise to other ARMv9 architectures, but as I don't have data for other architectures I've left the text Grace specific in this draft. 

> 11. `ARM_NEON_ASIMD` 64-bit ARMv8 and later. **For maximum performance on NVIDIA Grace (ARMv9), we strongly suggest at least GNU >= 13, LLVM >= 16. Avoid GNU 12 on NVIDIA Grace, as it can cause bugs on that platform.** 
> 
> 12. `ARM_SVE` 64-bit ARMv8 and later with the Scalable Vector Extensions (SVE). The SVE vector length is fixed at CMake configure time. The default vector length is automatically detected, and this can be changed via the GMX_SIMD_ARM_SVE_LENGTH CMake variable. **If compiling for a different target architecture than the compilation machine, GMX_SIMD_ARM_SVE_LENGTH should be set to the hardware vector length implemented by the target machine. There is no expected performance benefit from setting a smaller value than the implemented vector length, and setting a larger length can lead to unexpected crashes.** For ARMv8, Minimum required compiler versions are GNU >= 10, LLVM >=13, or ARM >= 21.1. For maximum performance we strongly suggest the latest gcc compilers, or at least LLVM 14 or ARM 22.0. Lower performance has been observed with LLVM 13 and Arm compiler 21.1. **For maximum performance on NVIDIA Grace (ARMv9), we strongly suggest at least GNU >= 13.2 or LLVM >= 16 with best performance seen from GNU. Avoid GNU 12 on NVIDIA Grace, as it can cause bugs on that platform.**

## Grace specific recommendations

> Summary: For best performance on Grace, run with GNU >= 13.2 with the `-mcpu=neoverse-v2` gcc flag and choose the `GMX_SIMD=ARM_NEON_ASIMD` GROMACS compilation flag. 
> 
> It is important that any compiler being used for Grace implements neoverse-v2, such as GNU >= 13.2 and LLVM >= 16. There is a significant performance improvement between gcc-13 and gcc-11. Avoid gcc-12, which has been seen to cause bugs on Grace. GNU 13 moderately outperforms LLVM 17. The `-mcpu=neoverse-v2` flag ensures that the compiler is not defaulting to the older Armv8-A target. 
> 
> On both GNU and LLVM, the GROMACS version implemented with `NEON SIMD` instructions significantly outperforms the SVE version. This can be selected by setting `GMX_SIMD=ARM_NEON_ASIMD` at compilation.   
> 
> `GMX_SIMD_ARM_SVE_LENGTH` should be 128, the vector length implemented by Grace. This value will be autodetected at compile time so only needs to be set if compiling on hardware which implements a different vector length. 
> 
> These Grace specific config optimisations are most important when running in CPU only mode, where much of the run time is spent in SIMD instructions.

    > 
    > If we move on to requiring MPI 3, then we can also remove the `const_cast` from `sbuf`.
- [x] Update tmpi interfaces to conform to MPI 3
- [x] Remove workarounds for MPI 2 conformance (see e.g. reverted commits in the branch for !3976)

closed_issues.title: GROMACS 2023 does not work properly when using AWH with multidir
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

AWH in **GROMACS 2023** does not work properly when the option `-multidir` is used on **CPU-only** nodes (1 node, `--tasks-per-node=32` and `--cpus-per-task=4`). The log file is created, but no step is written, although the job is running (10 minutes of simulation).[awh_1.part0001.log](/uploads/014439b8cbc07f0e5d60c72d4e52a488/awh_1.part0001.log)

The issue is still present when using the same input files and settings with **GROMACS 2023** on **GPU** nodes (1 node, 1 GPU, `--tasks-per-node=32` and `--cpus-per-task=4`). [_awh_1.part0001.log.5_](/uploads/423a27f5dce47c88c0df212ad1277ecc/_awh_1.part0001.log.5_)

**GROMACS 2023** works correctly on **GPU** if `--tasks-per-node` and `--cpus-per-task` are not specified and the execution is limited to two tasks (`srun -n 2`). [awh_1.part0001.log](/uploads/76f12bc687877d72130c57b99b0c54d1/awh_1.part0001.log)

**GROMACS 2023** works on **CPU** if `--tasks-per-node` and `--cpus-per-task` are not specified and the execution is limited to two tasks (`srun -n 2`). However, the performance is strongly affected (0.4 ns/day).[awh_1.part0001.log](/uploads/dca236051169aaf3ca5b7733c1fe36cd/awh_1.part0001.log)

 The issue is absent when using the same input files and settings (1 node, `--tasks-per-node=32` and `--cpus-per-task=4`) with **GROMACS 2021** or **GROMACS 2022** on **CPU-only** nodes (25 ns/day, 29 ns/day).[awh_1.part0001.log](/uploads/6617e649b082a15b7d7e42d64f2b9df8/awh_1.part0001.log)[awh_1.part0001.log](/uploads/a1fe081a310b7d760d3be0ee1c15aaee/awh_1.part0001.log)

I am using GROMACS `-multidir` to run AWH with two walkers sharing the bias.


## Exact steps to reproduce

The issue can be reproduced running `gmx_mpi mdrun -deffnm awh_1 -multidir walker_1 walker_2 -maxh 0.1 -noappend` using the following input files:[gmx2021.5.zip](/uploads/856778060121b7f6208013c0b9ea8c71/gmx2021.5.zip)
[gmx2022.6.zip](/uploads/f75fe3022b68c4c6560e80fb5fe5db88/gmx2022.6.zip)
[gmx2023.zip](/uploads/1ab1b875940854caa7b6c8ce3ef8b692/gmx2023.zip)


## What should happen

Several MD steps with a performance close to 25-30 ns/day on one CPU-only node.

## What happens

Reduced performance (0.4 ns/day) or no MD step performed (during 10 minutes of simulation).

## Update

The issue is not present when using the `multidir` function without AWH (problem in the processes communication?)

closed_issues.title: GROMACS 2024 beta maybe need fix some issues for Windows Visual Studio compile
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Some compile issues for WIndows 

**GROMACS version**

GROMACS version:    2024-beta

**Steps to reproduce**

Use Visual Studio 2022 compiles gromacs can reproduce below issues

**What is the current bug behavior?**

1. the function `colvarproxy_io::rename_file` in colvarproxy_io.cpp maybe have issue:
We need check the `newfilename` if exists while remove_file:

2. Some declarations `extern template NbnxmKernelFunc nbnxmKernelSimd<KernelLayout::r4xM, ... ` in `kernels.h` is unsupported, given error like: `'function' : typedef cannot be used for function definition`
3. A typo in `hbond.cpp` in line ` fprintf(fp, "[ hbonds_%s_frame_№%i ]", selects.c_str(), i.frameNumber_);`

**Possible fixes**

1. A fix for issue 2:
```C++
#if defined(_WIN32) && !defined(__CYGWIN__)
  // On straight Windows, must remove the destination before renaming it
  if (_access(newfilename, 00)==0) {
    error_code |= remove_file(newfilename);
  }
#endif
```
2. A fix for issue 2: 
Turn off all `extern template ...` or do not use typedef for Windows compile?

3. A fix for issue 3:
 Maybe `fprintf(fp, "[ hbonds_%s_frame_%i ]", selects.c_str(), i.frameNumber_);` ?

A patch:
[fix2024.patch](/uploads/a89ba2b3d36e6e0ed19a23a8b5870844/fix2024.patch)

closed_issues.title: setupLocalGpuForceReduction() is called before gmx_pme_send_coordinates() in doPairSearch() resulting in reduceKernel not been called in PP side for PME forces
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

The culprit commit is - https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/22c3b31348edd02daf93cc67292f29f8751504a5
Here setupLocalGpuForceReduction() is called before `gmx_pme_send_coordinates()` in `doPairSearch()`.
Due to this pmePpCommGpu->reinit is not called which is done by `gmx_pme_send_coordinates()`,
this results in pmeForces not getting allocated before setupLocalGpuForceReduction().
This results in reduceKernel not been called in PP side for PME forces as  rvec buffer is not registered on PP side.

This is a blocker for my NVSHMEM enabled PME to PP force transfers MR to work correctly https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/3872


## Possible fixes

I believe calling gmx_pme_send_coordinates() before setupLocalGpuForceReduction()  in  doPairSearch() should fix this.

closed_issues.title: Suggested new list splitting values for Ampere, Ada, Hopper
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Improve performance of nb force kernel by ~2-5% depending on architecture, for input sizes in the range 48k-96k on single GPU, by increasing GMX_NB_MIN_CI defaults on those architectures. 

**Impact**

This is a couple of line code change. Main work involved is testing to make sure there is no perf regression for particular architectures/inputs. 

So far tested water box (pme) with 24k to 768k on H100, L40, A100, A40, A4000. Note GMX_NB_MIN_CI is similar to the number of blocks launched for the nb force kernel but not a one to one mapping; for inputs <24k increasing GMX_NB_MIN_CI above the default has no impact on block count so these weren't benchmarked. Likewise for sizes >768k number of blocks >> GMX_NB_MIN_CI so increasing this has no effect. Suggested splitting factors were chosen conservatively such that there was no significant perf degradation for all problem sizes benchmarked, rather than choosing the optimum value for any particular size. 

**Detailed description**

GMX_NB_MIN_CI is a parameter that controls splitting of the neighbour list to increase the amount of parallelism in the nb force step for small problem sizes. Other than for very small and very large sizes, if set it is approximately equal to the number of blocks used in the nb force step. If not set, this value is chosen by the heuristic `gpu_min_ci_balanced_factor` x number of SMs in GPU where `gpu_min_ci_balanced_factor`=44.

The following graphs show perf results of varying GMX_NB_MIN_CI on various architectures. This is tested for gromacs before and after introducing gpu sorting of the neighbour list (see #4872). 

horizontal axis: GMX_NB_MIN_CI

vertical axis: speedup relative to original (cpu sort) version for the default list splitting value. Where the default list splitting value would be too small to have an effect on number of blocks, the smallest value benchmarked was used as a baseline instead. 

Black line: default splitting value

H100. 

![image](/uploads/4a3bc730070d3cbde403452fc356b62c/image.png){width=70%}

L40

![image](/uploads/f3f5f265fff25451ebde8f6e7bc4a3ca/image.png){width=70%}

A100

![image](/uploads/3d88ff427638ad3b25fafca8694d6b6a/image.png){width=70%}

A40

![image](/uploads/2bda1c5b6982699146d8349126ca54f9/image.png){width=70%}

A4000

![image](/uploads/5480424a041ea2ec8593f2be570c63f4/image.png){width=70%}

Summary of results:

| Arch | Chip |  SMs | Default splitting val |  Optimum splitting val | Optimum gpu_min_ci_balanced_factor|
| ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ |
|  H100 | GH100 | 132 | 5808 | 8000 | 61 |
|  L40  | AD102 | 144 | 6336 | 9000 | 63 |
|  A100 | GA100 | 108 | 4752 | 8000 | 74 |
|  A40  | GA102 | 84  | 3696 | 7000 | 83 |
|  A4000 | GA104 | 48 | 2112 | 3000 | 79 |

TODO decide whether to use one updated gpu_min_ci_balanced_factor (conservative value would be 61) or set a different value for each architecture?

closed_issues.title: Lennard-Jones Particle Mesh Ewald Summation (LJ PME) routine gives incorrect long-range forces and potential energies
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

The forces and energies resulting from the Lennard Jones Particle Mesh Ewald summation for long-ranged, non-bonded forces are incorrect. This I have reproduced on single-precision GROMACS 2019.1 and 2023.0. I saw this first in a simulation of a water molecule and a graphene sheet, and in the attached minimal example, it is shown for 2 argon atoms. The results are similar for the two systems.

This has a major impact when simulating surfaces and interfaces, where long-range LJ forces become important.

I do not have time to help to fix this.

## Exact steps to reproduce

I can see this by simulating 2 argon atoms in vacuum together and then doing scatter plots of their energies and forces over the argon-argon distance. I attach files to run the system and then plot the results. Simply run the shell script 'run' and then run the jupyter notebook to produce the plots.

## For developers: Why is this important?

## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

Potential energies/forces deviate from the Lennard-Jones potential/forces

See attachments.

I am not a developer, so I don't have any suggestions.

closed_issues.title: K8s allocates one physical NVIDIA GPU when two are requested, gromacs:gcc-11-cuda-11.7.1:testMPI-NVSHMEM  fails
closed_issues.description:
Often, `gromacs:gcc-11-cuda-11.7.1:testMPI-NVSHMEM` job in CI fails:

```
The following tests FAILED:
	 30 - GpuUtilsUnitTests (Failed)
	 31 - NvshmemTests (Failed)
```

The reason for it is that the job requests two GPUs, but instead gets two slices of the same physical GPU, which is treated inside the container as a single device. This fails `DevicesAvailable.ShouldBeAbleToRunOnDevice` and `NvshmemTests.NvshmemSimplePut` tests since they require two GPUs.

Besides obvious job failures, this also partially compromises our regression tests, since tests that are supposed to run on two devices and thus test device communication can end up running with a single device. They still use the expected number of ranks, so it is not too bad.

Here is a copy of the discussion on this topic in !3569; the issue still persists as is 2023-10-25

- Andrey Alekseenko @al42and · 4 months ago
> @mdoijade: Turns out, with GPU sharing enabled, NVIDIA K8s GPU Operator sometimes allocates two virtual devices on the same physical device, and thus the test fails (since both NVSHMEM and plain CUDA see only a single device). Do you know if there is any way to make sure two different devices physical devices are used (without disabling the GPU sharing)?

- Mahesh Doijade @mdoijade · 4 months ago
> I am not sure about K8s need to investigate this, from what I see in the [logs](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/3569#note_1424004828) `nvidia-smi` shows a single GPU so as expected both `DevicesAvailable.ShouldBeAbleToRunOnDevice` and nvshmem test fails due to expecting 2 GPUs. Where can we see k8s logs and how it is calling the docker run? perhaps that'll give some hint.
> 
> Here are some [info](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/gpu-sharing.html#about-configuring-gpu-time-slicing) on K8s GPU operator, does setting `replicas: 2` help ?


- Mahesh Doijade @mdoijade · 4 months ago

> after further reading about K8s GPU sharing with time-slicing feature it seems that in K8s oversubscription of NVIDIA GPU devices is disallowed as scheduling API advertises them as discrete integer resources by K8s which the time-slicing feature solves. But it does not provide a separate GPU instance like MIG provides due to which we see only 1 GPU in nvidia-smi as well as seen by CUDA app.
> 
> So the only solution I can think of is to waive the launch on such a config similar to what is done with cuFFTMp PME decomp [launch](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/main/admin/ci-scripts/gromacs-base-test.sh#L22). should we do that?

- Andrey Alekseenko @al42and · 4 months ago
> > So the only solution I can think of is to waive the launch on such a config similar to what is done with cuFFTMp PME decomp [launch](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/main/admin/ci-scripts/gromacs-base-test.sh#L22). should we do that?
> 
> 1. That's a good idea, but I'd rather avoid that (I did not like the original solution either). Tests randomly skipping is a pain to deal with. We can do it as a last resort, though.
> 2. Looking at the code you linked: Now we only have T400's in the CI with 4GiB of memory, so that test is always running without FFT MPI Decomposition test. That is, we're skipping `FFTMpiUnitTests`. Not great and illustrates my previous point: a change in our CI caused the tests to be skipped, and no one noticed it. Filed #4806.
> 3. Random thought: for dual-GPU tests, with 8 slices per GPU, we can request 16 "virtual" GPUs, so that we definitely get 2 physical devices. Or even 9 "virtual" GPUs. That is a huge hack, but might work. What's your opinion here?
> 4. Is there any way to ask NVIDIA people responsible for the GPU operator to add an option to require the slices to be on different devices? In nvidia/kubernetes/device-plugin!224, the heuristic is implemented to _prefer_ this behavior, but it's not required (and I can see reasons other projects might be okay with slices being on the same GPU, so perhaps keeping the current behavior as the default is okay).

- Mahesh Doijade @mdoijade · 4 months ago

> regarding 3.) can you further clarify what you mean by 8 slices per GPUs? do you mean slices for a MIG supported GPU? AFAIK getting physical 2 devices is only possible in MIG supported GPUs, T400 does not support MIG.

- Andrey Alekseenko @al42and · 4 months ago

> > regarding 3.) can you further clarify what you mean by 8 slices per GPUs? do you mean slices for a MIG supported GPU? AFAIK getting physical 2 devices is only possible in MIG supported GPUs, T400 does not support MIG.
> 
> We're not using MIG, but [time-slicing](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/gpu-sharing.html. Sorry that I did not make it clear.
> 
>    `"nvidia.com/gpu.replicas": "4",`
> 
>    `"nvidia.com/mig.capable": "false",`
> 
>    `"nvidia.com/mig.strategy": "single"`
>
> And it's 4 slices per GPU, not 8, as I claimed earlier.

- Evan Lezar @elezar · 4 months ago

> Thanks for the questions and raising this issue @al42and. At first glance, this doesn’t seem like too complex a feature request to implement, but would require some thought on how to expose this to the user. There may also be side-effects in terms of how the kubelet behaves if the plugin is not able to fulfil an allocation request or returns an error when requesting a preferred allocation.
> 
> One question would be, for example if we allow multiple "slots" to be consumed on any device at all.
> 
> Then, since this is not something we have run into ourselves, how much flexibility do you have to test a proposed solution on your end?

- Andrey Alekseenko @al42and · 4 months ago

> @elezar, thank you for chiming in!
> 
> > would require some thought on how to expose this to the user.
> 
> I was imagining something like the `TimeSlicing.Strategy` (nvidia/kubernetes/device-plugin!144), with an optional flag to mark it as either a requirement or a recommendation.
> 
> But the `TimeSlicing.Strategy` setting was soon removed, so I suspect it was not all that great?
> 
> > Then, since this is not something we have run into ourselves, how much flexibility do you have to test a proposed solution on your end?
> 
> We would gladly test it, but perhaps not immediately. We're entering the summer break season in Sweden. And even during the normal times, the number of people with k8s expertise in our team is not high :(
> 
> But I think our problem would not be too hard to mock in tests: have a node with two physical GPUs with 2 slices each, occupy all 2 slices with two single-GPU tasks on the same physical GPU, then try to launch a new container requesting 2 virtual GPU slices.

closed_issues.title: Improve release-notes conflict resolution
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

When two merge requests both add a note to the same release-notes file, we get a conflict that needs to be manually resolved, which necessitates re-approval of the MR. This creates extra friction when multiple MRs are submitted for a patch release.

## Possible fixes

https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect/issues/2311 seems to have a comprehensive list:

- Add a custom merge strategy for the CHANGELOG.md file (merge=union) to better handle these conflicts. This will usually work, but may run into issues if concurrently added features have very similar lines.
  - The original discussion mentions that it is not supported by GitHub, but GitLab claims to support it.
- Split the changelog into file-per-feature, and use a tool (towncrier is popular) to generate the final changelog from this before release.
  - Or manually? Creating more manual work for the release manager is not good, but I feel it will be less time wasted overall than the constant bother with MR.
- Add a bunch of filler entries (e.g. empty - list rows), and rely on developers adding entries in different spots to avoid merge conflicts.
  - We don't have a list, but perhaps having a number of placeholder records or just blank lines would work?


## References

- https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2015/02/10/gitlab-reduced-merge-conflicts-by-90-percent-with-changelog-placeholders/
- https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2018/07/03/solving-gitlabs-changelog-conflict-crisis/
- https://github.com/handsontable/handsontable/issues/7405
- https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect/issues/2311

closed_issues.title: Incorrect default for GMX_USE_RDTSCP in GitHub macOS CI
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Our GitHub "macOS latest Clang" jobs fail because the (virtual?) hardware lacks support for `rdtscp` instruction.

The same error has been observed by [Conda-forge](https://github.com/conda-forge/gromacs-feedstock/issues/23)

## Exact steps to reproduce

https://github.com/gromacs/gromacs/actions/runs/6534344557/job/17741321464

```
Fatal error:
The mdrun-mpi-pme-test executable was compiled to use the rdtscp CPU
instruction. However, this is not supported by the current hardware and
continuing would lead to a crash. Please rebuild GROMACS with the
GMX_USE_RDTSCP=OFF CMake option.
```

## For developers: Why is this important?

Our CI should not fail, even on Mac.

More importantly, since we're running both CMake and tests in the same container, and we don't set any specific value in our scripts, this means that our logic for enabling RDTSCP is not correct; we should not enable it when the hardware clearly does not support it.

## If this is a bug, (1) what happens, and (2) what did you expect to happen?

1. Tests fail because an unsupported hardware instruction is used.

2. Tests pass

## Relevant input files, logs and/or screenshots

Logs from the GitHub job linked above: [logs_2545.zip](/uploads/c0481772ce5f0f5ab2363725d8eb6f7a/logs_2545.zip)

## Possible fixes

- Improve RDTSCP detection to disable it automatically if the host does not support it, or
- Set `-DGMX_USE_RDTSCP=OFF` for the macOS Clang build ([that's what conda-forge did](https://github.com/conda-forge/gromacs-feedstock/pull/24)).

closed_issues.title: Verlet buffer calculation slow due to O(N^2) operations
closed_issues.description:
For systems with many different atom types the Verlet buffer calculation code can become very slow, up to many minutes, see https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/t/the-issue-of-slow-tpr-generation-speed-and-slow-running-simulation-speed-of-15-million-atoms-system/7357

There are two issues:
One is finding all the different atom types. This is an O(#atoms_in_molecule_types * #verlet_atom_types) operation. This can be changed to O(#atoms_in_molecule_types) by using std::unordered_map.
The drift calculation itself is O(#verlet_atom_types^2). Here the number of types can be reduced for cases with many types by storing properties, in particular the charges, with limited precision.

closed_issues.title: grompp memory leak on massive system
closed_issues.description:

I was able to reproduce her observation of massive memory consumption during `grompp` (it completely exhausted memory on my 128 GB Desktop) after checking with:

`mprof run gmx grompp -f alchembed.mdp -c virion_box.gro -p virion_box.top -o alchembed.tpr -n virion.ndx -maxwarn 20`

closed_issues.title: NBNxM Verlet buffer estimate needs to take into account higher order LJ derivatives
closed_issues.description:
Currently the Verlet buffer drift estimation code only takes the first derivative of the LJ potential into account. For atomistic systems this is usually fine, as the electrostatic interaction fully dominate the energy drift. But for LJ only or Martini coarse-grained systems the second and third derivative can contribute up to 40% extra. So we need to take this into account.

This was discovered while investigating #4861

closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

I am simulating simple nucleic acid systems to test new virtual site parameters. Early tests with 2021.1 worked fine, but now that I am making more extensive tests I use a newer version of Gromacs and the simulations usually segfaults within a few minutes or tens of minutes, usually without any signs of instability. Restarts from checkpoints work well and go beyond the time step where the segfault happened.

These simulations use a timestep of 5 fs, and I have reduced the p-coupling frequency due to someone reporting segfaults possibly related to that (cannot find that issue now). I use the following constraints parameters:

```plaintext
constraints = all-bonds
constraint-algorithm = Lincs
continuation = yes
lincs-order = 6
lincs-iter = 1
lincs-warnangle = 30
```

**GROMACS version**

Tested and failing on the following versions. Time until segfault in parentheses 2022.2 (3 min) 2022.5 (3 min) 2023 (14 min) 2023.2 (50 min, ran again and got 5 min)

These were all centre-provided at the Dardel supercomputer (PDC, Stockholm). I have seen the same behaviour for centre-provided 2021.1 on Rackham (Uppmax, Uppsala) and my own build of 2023 and 2023.2 on Rackham. Dardel is AMD-based, Rackham is Intel. The compilers used seem to differ between the 202\[12\] and 2023 versions, the former used clang and the latter gcc.

**Steps to reproduce**

```plaintext
gmx grompp -f run.mdp -o run_2023.2.tpr -c npt.gro -p salty.top -n xna.ndx
gmx mdrun -deffnm run_2023.2 -maxh 24 -cpi -cpo -nt 8
```

Note that this system doesn't use any new parameters, so no FF modifications needed. Angle constraints already defined in the FF.

**What is the current bug behavior?**

The steps above caused segfaults within a few minutes (1-15) with all the 202\[23\] versions I have tested, but my 2021.7 run finished its 24 hours without problems.

In one simulation (version 2023) I do get a warning:

> WARNING: Listed nonbonded interaction between particles 2 and 4 at distance 3.857 which is larger than the table limit 2.158 nm.
>
> This is likely either a 1,4 interaction, or a listed interaction inside a smaller molecule you are decoupling during a free energy calculation. Since interactions at distances beyond the table cannot be computed, they are skipped until they are inside the table limit again. You will only see this message once, even if it occurs for several interactions.
>
> IMPORTANT: This should not happen in a stable simulation, so there is probably something wrong with your system. Only change the table-extension distance in the mdp file if you are really sure that is the reason.

No segfault

closed_issues.title: Implement sorting of neighbour list on GPU (with CUDA)
closed_issues.description:
**Summary**

Sorting the neighbour list by number of neighbour atoms speeds up the non bonded force kernel by allowing blocks with the most work to launch first and therefore reducing kernel tail effects. Performing this sorting on the gpu after the prune kernel allows the sorting to be done with more accurate neighbour counts by ignoring atoms which will be masked out in the nb force kernel. 

**Use cases**

This will speed up use cases with a small amount of work per GPU (which are more sensitive to tail effects in the nb force kernel). For example, adh_dodec (95k atoms) on a single H100. 

**Impact**

On a single H100, this gives a ~2% end to end speedup for adh_dodec, ~1% speedup for cellulose. No impact for larger workloads. 

There may be a performance degradation for atom counts smaller than adh_dodec, eg a possible ~2% performance degradation for rnase_cubic (24k atoms) is seen on H100. This is still being investigated. 

**Detailed description**

Open issues:
- Should this feature be controllable with an env variable or can the cpu sorting code path be removed entirely (currently commented out)?
- Potential performance degradation for very small atom counts, seemingly related to an increase in time in the 'Rest' performance counter 

Description:

The pruning kernel is updated to count neighbours for each supercluster, taking into account masked out neighbours, and binned into a histogram. 

CUB exclusive scan is used to calculate a prefix sum on the histogram. The new kernel `nbnxn_kernel_bucket_sci_sort` performs a count sort using the prefix sum. Both these kernels are launched just after the pruning kernel in `gpu_launch_kernel_pruneonly`.

-- GROMACS is being built without library MPI support (-DGMX_MPI=no). However MPI is potentially useful for the gmxapi Python API, so we will search for MPI anyway.  If this causes problems, disable the check with -DCMAKE_DISABLE_FIND_PACKAGE_MPI=on.
-- Could NOT find MPI_C (missing: MPI_C_LIB_NAMES MPI_C_HEADER_DIR MPI_C_WORKS) 
-- Could NOT find MPI_CXX (missing: MPI_CXX_LIB_NAMES MPI_CXX_HEADER_DIR MPI_CXX_WORKS) 
-- Could NOT find MPI (missing: MPI_C_FOUND MPI_CXX_FOUND) 
    Reason given by package: MPI component 'Fortran' was requested, but language Fortran is not enabled.
```

We are not building with CP2K, so Fortran should not be requested: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/b8ac0d61b39bf0f00843049311a0f9471a41cb46/cmake/gmxManageMPI.cmake#L60-75

As I understand, the problem if we don't set `GMXAPI` explicitly, the `GMX_REQUIRED_MPI_COMPONENTS` is empty (because `gmxManageMPI` is called earlier in the top-level CMakeLists.txt then `add_subdirectory(api)`), and CMake apparently interprets it as "all components".

Re-running `cmake` in the same directory works correctly, since `GMXAPI` value is cached from the previous run, and `GMX_REQUIRED_MPI_COMPONENTS` is correctly set to just `CXX`.


## Exact steps to reproduce

Run `simple-build` job manually in a docker container.

## For developers: Why is this important?

- Our CMake logic relies on a potentially unitialized variable, so it's wrong
- Simply running `cmake` again in the same directory without any internal or external changes forces re-detection of MPI library, which is not nice
- An annoying warning about Fortran is printed

closed_issues.title: MoleculeTests/ScatteringModule.DirectMode/SAXS is too slow
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

It looks like the DirectMode SAXS test is responsible for >50% of the total runtime of the TAF unit tests.

Current `main` (410134cecc22577269921b83cff153a24d466d9b), GCC 12.3, release mode, i9-12900K:

```console
$ ./bin/trajectoryanalysis-test
...
[       OK ] MoleculeTests/ScatteringModule.DirectMode/1 (3275 ms)
...
[==========] 244 tests from 23 test suites ran. (5855 ms total)
```

The whole test suite in this configuration takes ~45 seconds, so that's ~7% of all the `make check` time for a single test.

## Exact steps to reproduce

Build tests, run `./bin/trajectoryanalysis-test --gtest_filter=MoleculeTests/ScatteringModule.DirectMode/1`, see that it takes a few seconds.

## For developers: Why is this important?

All in all, three seconds are not a lot, but that's on a fast machine with all optimizations on. If we look at the `TrajectoryAnalysisUnitTests` times in some slower configs, here's how they changed since 6713ccec was merged:

- ASAN: [18.80 sec](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/jobs/4926163447) -> [99.48 sec](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/jobs/4945861920) :crying_cat_face: 
- TSAN: [78.49 sec](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/jobs/4926163450) -> [436.86 sec](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/jobs/4945861948) :scream_cat: 

That is quite bad. It wastes CI resources and annoys the developers who run unit-tests regularly.

It also kinda hints that the code is not particularly fast.

## Possible fixes

1. Use smaller protein for unit tests? It's O(N^2) algorithm, so less atoms would help a lot.

2. Optimize the code?

Unordered maps have fast lookups, but it looks like a lot of time is spent there anyways:

![Screenshot_20230901_183839](/uploads/7c75737b94263b9112dc250499625dc9/Screenshot_20230901_183839.png)

  - Partially flatten the map by using `std::unordered_map<double, gmx::EnumerationArray<Isotope, double>>`?

closed_issues.title: Too high pressure due to missing dispersion interactions in systems with no or weak electrostatics
closed_issues.description:
The estimate for the buffer of the Verlet pair list is, currently, based on energy drift only. When there are no electrostatic interactions, i.e. uncharged particles, or extremely weak electrostatics or PME with very small ewald_rtol, this Verlet buffer size can become so small that missing dispersion interactions can lead to a measurably lower pressure towards the end of the pair list life time. We have only observed a measurable effect, i.e. more than 0.1 bar (and less than 1 bar), in coarse-grained systems and atomistic systems without charge. Because of how the NBNxM algorithm construct the cluster-pair list, the effect is often larger in the z-dimension that along x and y. This can lead to deformation with anisotropic pressure coupling.

Note that nearly all atomistic simulations are unaffected, as they nearly always contain mainly atoms with charged particles and therefore use a sufficiently larger buffer and/or pair list lifetime.

Solutions to this problem:
* Decrease the verlet-buffer-tolerance mdp parameter, a value of 1e-4 should be sufficient in most cases.
* Make sure that nstpcouple is a multiple of nstlist, note that nstlist is tuned at runtime unless you use the -nstlist option of mdrun.

Measures to be taken:
* For 2023.4: include a print of the (over)estimate of the pressure error in the log file and potentially  a warning when using semi-isotropic or anisotropic pressure coupling.
* For 2024: add a mechanism to control this error.

closed_issues.title: SYCL Nbnxm kernels and the fCi buffer splitting
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

Short version of the long discussion in !3172:

- AMD MI250X (gfx90a) GPUs can only achieve full floating-point flops when using packed floats (2-wide SIMD). The compiler tends to do a decent job of optimizing things when it sees `Float3` by using packed math for the first two components. Packed math requires moving the data to special registers, so keeping the data as Float3 is good. That's why `fCiBuf` should be array-of-structures. See !3172. Called **contiguous** later.
- The compiler for Intel GPU tries to allocate the arrays as contiguous chunk of register file, even when access indices can be inferred in compile time. This makes the register allocator choke on large arrays, producing suboptimal code. That's why `fCiBuf` should be three separate arrays (not even structure-of-arrays, since structures must be contiguous too). See !3104. Called **split** later.

## Performance starting point

Based on `main` ca. May 2023 (1e2b7fd99526dfae57034bbc8615a84d5925e865, "split"), Grappa 1.5M. "Contiguous" version was hacked on top for testing.

F-only kernel timings on MI250X (hipSYCL 0.9.4, ROCm 5.3.3), ns:

|                      | TAB     | ANA     | TAB rel | ANA rel |
|----------------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
| Split (1e2b7fd)      | 4258346 | 3975012 |         |         |
| Contiguous (cd4ec77) | 4075048 | 4071100 | 0.957   | 1.024   |

With the contiguous buffer, the kernel performance (both TAB and ANA) can be further improved by ~5 p.p. by using a custom Float3 type.

F-only kernel timings on PVC 1100 (oneAPI 2023.2), relative to "split":

|                      | TAB rel | ANA rel |
|----------------------|---------|---------|
| Split (535c87a)      |         |         |
| Contiguous (cd4ec77) | 1.009   | 1.004   |

FV kernel timings on PVC 1100 (oneAPI 2023.2), relative to "split":

|                      | TAB rel | ANA rel |
|----------------------|---------|---------|
| Split (535c87a)      |         |         |
| Contiguous (cd4ec77) | 1.0     | **2.4** |

In terms of performance, analytical F-only kernels are ~6% faster than tabulated ones on PVC 1100, so slowing down energy kernels 2x is not good.

closed_issues.title: Non-multiple GPU counts should be allowed
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

GROMACS forbids run configurations where the number of GPUs requested on each node is not an exact multiple of the available number of GPUs on the node. But some use cases (in particular with PME GPU decomposition) benefit from such non-multiple configs. An example is below.

## Exact steps to reproduce

- STMV 28M from https://repository.prace-ri.eu/ueabs/GROMACS/2.2/GROMACS_TestCaseC.tar.xz 
- Selene cluster, using 4xA100 and 2x64-core AMD Rome per node
- The best config is 7 MPI tasks per node (16 OpenMP threads per task): 6 for PP (using 3 GPUs) and 1 for PME (using 1 GPU).
- The 6 MPI tasks for PP give a better MPI/OpenMP balance for CPU update and constraints (noting this case doesn't support GPU update and constraints). MPS is used to allow overlapping kernels.
- We don't want 8 tasks per node, because we want 1 PME GPU per node, and don't want that to be shared with a PP task.

Walltime comparison using 2-nodes (5000 steps):

4 MPI tasks per node, 32 OpenMP tasks per MPI task:
- Update 43.254 s
- Constraints: 77.571 s
- Total: 270.782 s

7 MPI tasks per node, 16 OpenMP tasks per MPI task:
- Update 29.437 s
- Constraints: 51.878 s
- Total: 229.252 s

## For developers: Why is this important?

GROMACS should allow optimal run configs.

## Possible fixes

Remove this restriction.
