closed_issues.title: Angle potential with k=0 and theta=0 produces nan and eventually crash
closed_issues.description:
I found a rare crash of GROMACS on ~2020.6. I have not tested but from the source code 2021 series seems fixed the issue at least for the SIMD case. (Commit 132f5c9f fixes the issue).

Steps to reproduce: on GPU-installed machine run the simulation from the attached tpr file. Around 80% of the time the run crashes (the most typical crash is SEGV occurring on ca. 2ns, but the program may sometime stop silently) 
`gmx mdrun -deffnm nptA.tpr`
I confirmed the crash on gcc 7.4.0 + CUDA 11.0 and icc + gcc 7.4.0 + CUDA 11.0.

After investigating into the problem I found the cause is the following line in the `[ angle ]` section of the topology file:

```
;ai aj ak f theta_0A    kA          theta_0B    kB
 30 14 17 1 1.11100e+02 0.00000e+00 1.11100e+02 5.27180e+02
```

This line indicates k=0 when lambda=0 (because this atom becomes a dummy atom in the state A).
But when the angle (theta) is 0, the force becomes nan. This behavior is documented in the source comment (src/gromacs/listed_forces/bonded.cpp, angles(), in simd flavor) but I could not find in the PDF manual.
(Example case I found while running is as follows:
```
x[ai] 2.88292313 1.18869507 1.56111658
x[aj] 2.76677704 1.22401822 1.65273976
x[ak] 2.88373399 1.18847489 1.56050110 
```
)

This problem should not occur on typical runs, but may arise when FEP is run on a single precision (on double precision case, theta~=0 is much less likely to happen).
The fix I can suggest is backporting commit 132f5c9f (if ver. 2020 line is still alive).

[topol_nan_angle.top](/uploads/b4c67f2b932ee0ce9e83c48264c76ff8/topol_nan_angle.top)

closed_issues.title: Help forks and packaging tools declare that they patched and/or built GROMACS
closed_issues.description:
We have had a tool that checks whether the code has been modified. Most packaging libraries do modify GROMACS, often in trivial ways like fixing typos, changing test timeouts, disabling tests on weird architectures, etc. Sometimes they also have to patch issues that we haven't fixed yet (e.g. bioconda had to have a patch to support OpenCL on Darwin) They were being detected by the checker as having modified GROMACS. This means that users might have been concerned about that and avoided using that version. It also means that developers handling forum posts or bug reports can't tell the difference between a real fork and something built by a packaging tool.

We should help downstream projects consume GROMACS in ways that help our users by setting `GMX_VERSION_STRING_OF_FORK` to show that they handled the build and/or patched GROMACS.

Packaging projects to persuade to use GMX_VERSION_STRING_OF_FORK:
- [x] Spack https://github.com/spack/spack/pull/25869
- [x] EasyBuild https://github.com/easybuilders/easybuild-easyblocks/pull/2571
- [x] DebiChem has been already using it since 2020
- [x] Fedora (currently using 2019, which doesn't support GMX_VERSION_STRING_OF_FORK, so need to wait for upstream update)
- [x] openSUSE https://build.opensuse.org/request/show/930679
- [x] MacPorts https://github.com/macports/macports-ports/pull/12184
- [x] HomeBrew https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/85158
- [x] Bioconda https://github.com/bioconda/bioconda-recipes/pull/30491

I looked at conan and vcpkg but they don't have GROMACS ports yet. PyPi has one but it's orphaned a few years ago.

Forks to persuade to use GMX_VERSION_STRING_OF_FORK:
- [X] PLUMED https://github.com/plumed/plumed2/pull/739
- [X] Colvars https://github.com/Colvars/colvars/pull/423

closed_issues.title: PME GPU FEP sometimes does not calculate splines correctly

However in the spline computation there is a check for whether `atomCharge` is zero, and the spline computation is omitted if so. Since that charge can be different in the two FEP states, the splines should be computed differently. Simplest is probably to compute the spline for all atoms when doing FEP, but that means we need to template the spline computation accordingly.

closed_issues.title: Modularize PME grid, FFT grid management
closed_issues.description:
With new GPU PME-decomposition, there are different cases we need to handle wrt PME and FFT grids-

1. PME grid and FFT grids can be same - Current GPU implementation with no-decomposition.
2. PME grid and FFT grids cannot be same due to memory on different devices - PME hybrid mode
3. PME grid and FFT grids cannot be same due to extra overlap regions in PME grid - new decomposition implementations based on HeFFTe/cuFFTXt.

More details here: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1903#note_670398177

All this is handled in `src/gromacs/ewald/pme_gpu_internal.cpp` currently. 

Following are few design goals-
- Create a separate component that handles different cases (using same or different PME/FFT grid, copy between different grid) and provides cleaner abstraction to PME classes. 
- Cleaner interface to FFT abstraction. It might be better to just allocate FFT grids in FFT classes and then let another component decide whether to share or not same grid with PME spread/gather operations.
- Support for resizing when PME tuning is enabled

closed_issues.title: incorrect GPU update dependency with PME ranks, GPU update and staged comm
closed_issues.description:
With separate PME ranks, staged communication and GPU update, the PME forces are reduced on the CPU with the rest of the GPU forces after the GPU reduction's results and copied to the CPU. The result of this is copied back to the GPU prior to update, but there is a mismatch in the [event produced](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/gromacs/mdrun/md.cpp#L1523) and [the one passed to update](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/gromacs/mdrun/md.cpp#L1538). Hence, on such steps the GPU update waits on the GPU reduction rather than the H2D copy of final forces ~~and therefore PME force contributions can be missing at the time of update.~~

This is only a logic bug and does not affect correctness because the copy in question happens on the update stream, but it leads to incorrect synchronization.

closed_issues.title: Allow for more clarity on disposition of merge requests
closed_issues.description:
## Summary

New labels and practices are proposed for handling merge requests. In particular, we try to provide strategies for handling stale merge requests.

## Background

A merge request may go stale for many reasons. The author may not have responded to feedback or may not have received feedback from reviewers. An accompanying issue may have gone stale because of unclear priority or timeline. It can be hard to tell whether a merge request is still "active" but there are no guidelines for public two-way communication of whether an MR is on track to be reviewed, and whether the contributor or reviewers have any intention of following up.

It does not help the contributor or the reviewer to simply rebase the MR periodically. Rebasing is often not a true requirement for an issue or merge request to receive initial feedback or even complete review, and is a false indication of how "active" an issue is.

If developers try to prescreen merge requests to determine which old merge requests are simply overlooked versus those that are not likely to receive further attention, there has not been a clear action to take while reviewing the issues.

A merge request can be closed without deleting the branch from which it is made and without affecting the issue status. A closed MR remains linked from issues whether closed or not.

Many merge requests will never be reviewed. When it seems clear to a number of potential reviewers that a merge request is not likely to be reviewed any time soon, the merge request will be closed in order to indicate that it is not actively under review or consideration. The merge request may be reopened, but the contributor should respond to review threads, resolve merge conflicts, and communicate with other developers before doing so.

## A working proposal

The following process may be partially or fully automated, but can be carried out by a group of developers.

A merge request that has had no updates for six months or more can acquire the status label "Status::Stale"

If the proposed change still seems important and the next steps are unclear, contributors with stale issues are encouraged
* to contact existing reviewers (or potential reviewers),
* to participate in the developer mailing list, and
* to attend the biweekly teleconference to coordinate.

If the future of the merge request has not become clear within a month (especially if it has become stale multiple times), developers may close the merge request with a label indicating why it has entered a "closed" state.

"Status::Stale" and "Status::Closed, <reason>" should not be assumed to imply that the merge request has been reviewed unless it is explicitly rejected.

The above notes will be added to the contributing guidelines and to the documentation on GitLab labels (in a merge request in preparation by @eirrgang). New labels will be created and described by @eirrgang shortly.

- [ ] @mark.j.abraham started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1876#note_654824639): 

    > The doxygen does not say the second parameter is an equilibrium constant.
    > 
    > It's not something to fix in this MR, but note that all the types like `LinearAngle` could have a method `tuple scalarForce(dr)` so that one layer of functions is eliminated (along with the possibility of mis-ordering the unpacking of `angle` into parameters of type `T` and busywork documentation to which little attention is paid when reading, writing, or reviewing). The caller is still fine to call `threeCenterInteraction.scalarForce(theta)` rather than the current `threeCenterKernel(theta, parameters)` because the only times `computeThreeCenter` is instantiated is for a `ThreeCenterType` and those should all have such a `scalarForce` method. Each `scalarForce` method can `\copydoc` their documentation from another `ThreeCenterType`. This is a strength of the duck-typing capabilities of templates. Both the current and my suggested approach rely on the existence of a function defined for each concrete type like `LinearAngle`, so why not simplify?
    > 
    > The simplification might also mean better encapsulation, since currently LinearAngle (and similar types) need getters that are probably only called here and also for a kernel that also computes the forces. Methods that access the private members directly make the type easier to use correctly and less busy work to implement. Perhaps the comparators also need the getters, but if that's all then they can be declared as friends.

closed_issues.title: The second column of atomtype shoud accept string begin with a number
closed_issues.description:
There is nothing in doc that says that this is wrong.

```
[ atomtypes ] 
; name      at.num  mass     charge ptype  sigma      epsilon
2C 6 12.01 0.0000 A 3.39967e-01 4.57730e-01 
2C_ 2C 12.01 0.0000 A 0.339967 0.45773 
```

But this would give 
```
ERROR 1 [file biased_1.0.top, line 1723]:
  Atomtype 2C_ not found
```

I think that when reading the second column, it is assumed that if the first character is a number, it would not be recognised as an atomtype.

By the way, this would work:
```
[ atomtypes ] 
; name      at.num  mass     charge ptype  sigma      epsilon
Br 35 79.90 0.0000 A 4.64693e-01 2.45414e-01 
Br_ Br 79.90 0.0000 A 0.464693 0.245414  ; scaled
```

closed_issues.title: Consider guidelines for "TODO comments"
closed_issues.description:
## Update
This issue is in follow-up to several conversations in past telcos and MRs that may or may not lead to new guidelines on whether and how to use "TODO" comments in code.

## Original issue

@mark.j.abraham and @ejjordan recall adopting a "No TODO comments" policy. However, the policy does not appear to be documented or enforced. (If no such policy decision has been made, then I suggest closing this issue.)

If such a policy change has been made, we should make sure that the GROMACS 2022 release (and current `master` branch) reflect the update.

- [ ] Update contributor guidelines regarding inline code comments. (Note that many editors provide a feature to warn before pushing commits containing "to do" comments.)
- [ ] Update reviewer guidelines.
- [ ] Apply some automated check(s), if possible.

Automated enforcement may not be possible and will almost certainly not be robust without an inappropriate amount of new custom infrastructure. Note that `clang-tidy` has `google-readability-todo` but the `.clang-tidy` files in `master` disable this check. However, the clang-tidy code is not sufficient to catch "to do"s as we typically format them for Doxygen comments. Doxygen has https://www.doxygen.nl/manual/config.html#cfg_generate_todolist but to try to leverage it before removing all current "to do"s would be an unrewarding rabbit hole.

closed_issues.title: Normalize branch naming policy
closed_issues.description:
Suggestions at https://manual.gromacs.org/current/dev-manual/change-management.html#naming-branches and https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/wikis/home#naming-of-branches are inconsistent. There is also a practice of prefixing branch names with developer initials.

We should clarify our branch naming policy, and update the developer guidelines. We can also take the opportunity to prune the repository of stale or inappropriately named branches.

## Considerations

An unwieldy number of stale branches accumulate, and even active branches are hard to sort through.
* Sometimes branches are not deleted after being merged or abandoned, and it can be hard to identify these.
* Some branches are pushed without reference to a tracked issue.

## Proposals

### Branch naming schemes

* Encourage/require tracked issues, and prefix branch names with issue numbers.
* Prefix branch names with author identifier. Suggest GitLab ID rather than initials for convenience of the project manager.

I can't think of a rationalization for branch names without an easily-tracked prefix, as currently recommended in the dev guide. If someone has one, please update this section of the issue description.

### Practices
Use https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/branches/stale periodically to identify and delete stale branches and remove those without an active issue and/or merge request.

closed_issues.title: Improve robustness and user-friendliness of gmxapi 0.2 package.
closed_issues.description:
(Follow up to #4078)

The delay in the GROMACS 2021.3 release revealed that the publication of gmxapi 0.2.1 to PyPI was premature and revealed some versioning and packaging aspects that warranted urgent attention.

@eirrgang has uploaded a gmxapi 0.2.2 package to PyPI to improve compatibility and user experience for the `gmxapi` Python package and for the `sample_restraint` sample code.

This issue coordinates the several merge requests needed to incorporate the updates into the release branch. There is not any particular reason to rush these merges for 2021.3. (It is completely reasonable for these changes to exist only in the git branch until GROMACS 2021.4.)

- [x] Add API version checks so that 0.2.x Python package can build against any GROMACS 2021 release.
- [x] Add a `long_description` to improve appearance on pypi.org.
- [x] Add a `LICENSE` file per Python packaging guidelines.

## Deferred

These changes can be back-ported to gmxapi 0.1.x, but the current consensus among developers seems to be to do this in a `2020-dev` fork (e.g. https://github.com/kassonlab/gmxapi).

Expanded test coverage (API regression testing) for library client code is clearly appropriate, but can be pursued in `master`, and warrants separate issue tracking.

closed_issues.title: Optimize CUDA PME Decomposition
closed_issues.description:
These issues will be applicable to both hybrid mode and full-GPU decomposition.
Two issues:

1. Reported by @pszilard at https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1711#note_638922484. Two Packing/reduction kernels are launched for left and right neighbor. These are independent tasks so, can be moved to different stream or packed in a single kernel.
2. Currently, we create a full PME grid on GPU on each rank to avoid doing co-ordinate transformations in spread/gather kernel. The side effect of this is that grid data that needs to be communicated between X-domain neighbors in not contiguous in case of pencil-decomposition. For the time being, I send the full data along y-dimension but, this can be optimized either by packing/un-packing non-contiguous data or we can allocate smaller grids in each local rank and do necessary co-ordinate transform in spread/gather kernel. I am inclined towards the later.
3. Experiment with different block size and decide on optimal configuration for kernels use in halo exchange and PME grid <-> FFT grid conversion. https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/2117#note_718564376

closed_issues.title: Set required versions for GROMACS 2023
closed_issues.description:
For GROMACS 2023, specify minimum support versions of dependencies, tools, and interacting software. Document and confirm test coverage.

Remember that they start being relevant to users when we release in 2023.There is a trade-off between what new things we can do (because we support a smaller range of things) vs what things we might require some users to do (because GROMACS no longer builds out of the box for them). Your workload as a GROMACS developer goes up for each extra version we support, even if that only shows up in what you have to do to keep CI happy, or how hard it is for you to get access to others’ feedback because they are thinking about something that is mysteriously broken in some CI combination. Also, versions that may or may not be the bases for forks that support hardware that GROMACS users might have that isn’t already shipping in early 2023 really shouldn’t factor highly.

**CMake**
We have previously generally adopted the minimum version of the then-latest Ubuntu LTS ie 22.04, which we don't know yet, but will know in good time to do the work to test it and require it.

**C++ version**
Not enough need to change from C++17. C++20 was standardized just before 2021 started and we are still waiting on the std library implementations to support all of C++17 well.

**Compilers**
Minimum supported versions are currently generally implied by the requirement for C++17 support. Note that support in the respective standard libraries often lags years behind support in the compiler (sometimes because they need the compiler to support language features before it is efficient to complete the library development).

**gcc**
We currently require 7, but increasing (e.g. to 8) could be good as

* gcc 7 does not have the proper C++17 flag, CUDA code currently has to compile in C++14 mode.
* #3041 could be finally solved
* If we increased it to 9.4 (released may 2021) we could fix #3951 
* gcc 8.1 (released may 2018) first supports std::filesystem in the non-experimental namespace
* gcc 9.1 (released May 2019) first supports std parallelism, which we might use if someone is e.g. going to work on the analysis tools, but clang has no such implementation yet

Decision: adopt 9 and 9.4 for stdlib **edit** but 20.04 provides only 9.3.0 by default, so perhaps it's better to support that OS version easily and leave #3951 for later

**clang**
We currently we say we support clang 5 even though clang 7 is the earliest that we test (resolve #4081 accordingly). Upgrading the minimum could be good as 

* clang 9 (released Sep 2019) first supports std::filesystem in the non-experimental namespace

**msvc**
We require 19.15 (ie Visual Studio 2017), no need to change. 
* We should decide how much we support/test it. It has been suggested in #4161 that we stop supporting it. It has much less OpenMP support.

Decision: support Visual Studio 2019. For GPU support with OpenMP we should document use WSL. 
Updated (11/11): We support Visual Studio 2019 with OpenMP.

**icpx**
Since it is based on recent enough clang, no need to set a minimum version for non-SYCL builds. (See below for SYCL)

**icc, xlc, pgi**
Not supported because either problematic, not conformant, or not relevant

**cray**
Since CCE 9.0 (Sept 2019) both classic and clang compilers claim C++17 support so that makes sense as a minimum to require, but we have not documented that anywhere so far.

**CUDA**
Currently we require 11.0 (for C++17 compatibility.) For approx CUDA release dates, see https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit-archive. Generally we have supported two major versions at the time of release, but CUDA no longer has an annual release cadence. Is there any reason to increase it past 11.0?

**SYCL**
We require SYCL2020 and suggest latest available compilers and SDKs, in particular for Intel where there's no relevant hardware out yet. hipSYCL and codeplay implementations are still maturing, so it only makes sense to pick a hard minimum version of these SDKs in late 2022.

**MPI**
Currently 2.0, no plans to change

**Python interpreter**
Python 3.7 EOL is 27 Jun 2023 so is a reasonable choice for min version for GROMACS 2023

**Doxygen**
Some people want to update but the risk vs reward and available effort needs to be understood.

**Sphinx**
No need to change

**GoogleTest**
There will not be formal releases of this in future ("live at head" adopted). We updated in mid 2021, so no reason to plan to update unless someone will do the work and knows of a new feature that someone will then use. 

**clang-format**
No need to change, we updated in 2021

**clang-tidy**
No need to change, we updated in 2021

**CI container base**
Adopt 22.04 and use it for all CI containers (where it is possible, and after it comes out in April).

We currently bundle pybind 2.5 and require only pybind 2.2 for the gmxapi Python package C++ extension module. For robust compatibility with Python 3.9, we should update the pybind requirement to pybind>=2.6 before the 2022 beta release.

Optionally, we could update the way the pybind dependency works, but we may want to tackle that in a separate issue. pybind has updated support for CMake and scikit-build, and has moved toward dependency fulfillment through Python package import rather than bundled git subtrees.

The `sample_restraint` code remains compatible with GROMACS 2019 and gmxapi >= 0.0.7. We may not need to add a hard requirement there, but might consider updating the compatibility checks. This is probably a separate issue, too.

Related to #3716 and #3708.

There are also still references in the repository to issue #2896. These should be updated.

closed_issues.title: HtoD force transfer on critical path for heterogeneous DD cases
closed_issues.description:
For DD cases with GPU halo exchange and CPU forces, the per-step HtoD force transfer is unnecessarily on the critical path and exposed in the profile, shown here for one of the PP GPUs in a 4-GPU EAG1 run:
![July13before](/uploads/5bcf15d06693b5583723d8dce164c508/July13before.JPG)

This is because it is scheduled in the local non-bonded stream, so must wait for local non-bonded GPU force calculations to complete.

A solution is to instead schedule it in a stream managed by its consumer: the GPU halo exchange (with appropriate sync) so it can initiate earlier and overlap with GPU compute. This gives ~5% overall performance improvement for the above-mentioned EAG1 case (on DGX-V100):

```
export GMX_GPU_DD_COMMS=1
export GMX_GPU_PME_PP_COMMS=1
gmx mdrun -s topol.tpr -ntomp 10 -pme gpu -nb gpu -ntmpi 4 -npme 1 -nsteps 10000 -resethway -v -notunepme -pin on -bonded gpu -noconfout -nstlist 200 -update gpu

before:
Performance:       64.381        0.373

after:
Performance:       67.517        0.355
```

- [ ] Implement transfer in halo stream, retaining fork/join of non-local stream in each halo exchange to ensure correct dependencies for multiple pulses and dimensions
- [ ] Refactor stream and event dependencies out of halo exchange and into caller functions in domdec.cpp, for a more elegant solution.

closed_issues.title: Restore gmxapi._gmxapi.add_mdmodule() Python functionality.
closed_issues.description:
Some functionality was orphaned and forgotten in the last-minute changes to core gmxapi infrastructure as the Python package was merged to GROMACS 2020. Issue #3145 remains to be addressed, but we should restore some of the gmxapi 0.0.7 functionality that was lost in gmxapi 0.1.

A logic error was introduced as `gmxapi::System` was deprecated, in which `IRestraintPotential` providers added to the system are not attached to the simulation that is launched. This was possible because of some confusing redundancy that was introduced, in which a container was duplicated in the `gmxapi::System` and `gmxpy::PyContext` proxy, but roles were not completely updated.

## Background
A working updated protocol is demonstrated in the C++ tests, illustrated in the following sequence diagram.
```plantuml
'https://plantuml.com/sequence-diagram

'autonumber

autoactivate on
client -> libgmxapi: gmxapi::fromTprFile()
libgmxapi -> "gmxapi::System" **: create
return "gmxapi::System"
client -> libgmxapi: gmxapi::createContext()
libgmxapi -> "gmxapi::Context" **: create
return "gmxapi::Context"

client -> "gmxapi::Context": setMDArgs()
return

client -> plugin: create
plugin -> restraint **: create
return restraint

client -> "gmxapi::System": System.launch(gmxapi::Context)
"gmxapi::System" -> "gmxapi::Context": launch(systemimpl.workflow_)
return session
loop foreach member in systemIml.spec_->getModules()
"gmxapi::System" -> libgmxapi: addSessionRestraint(session, member)
note right
spec is empty!
end note
return
end
return "gmxapi::Session"

client -> libgmxapi: gmxapi::addSessionRestraint(session, restraint)
libgmxapi -> sessionImpl: addRestraint(restraint)
sessionImpl -> "gmx::MdRunner": addPotential(restraint)
return
return success
return success

client -> "gmxapi::Session": run()
"gmxapi::Session" -> "gmx::MdRunner": run()
return
return
```

It took an extra few years to enable automated testing of Python code in the GROMACS CI pipelines, during which time development and test coverage languished.

The broken protocol is illustrated in the following sequence diagram.
```plantuml
@startuml
'https://plantuml.com/sequence-diagram

'autonumber
autoactivate on
context.py -> _gmxapi: Context()

deactivate

return system

return this->workNodes_
"gmxpy::PyContext" -> restraint: bind(pycontext.workspec)
restraint -> "gmxpy::PyContext": gmxapi::MDWorkSpec::addModule(module)
note right
restraint added to PyContext member.
end note
deactivate
deactivate
deactivate
deactivate

context.py -> _gmxapi: system.launch(context)
_gmxapi -> "gmxpy::PyContext": get()
return gmxapi::Context
_gmxapi -> "gmxapi::System": System.launch(gmxapi::Context)
"gmxapi::System" -> "gmxapi::Context": launch(systemimpl.workflow_)
return session

@enduml

```

## Proposal

* Make minimal changes to the gmxapi interfaces related to `gmxapi::System` and `gmxapi::Context` at this time.
* Update the `gmxapi._gmxapi.add_mdmodule()` function in the Python bindings to allow the target of the plugin `bind()` behavior to target the correct instance of the container.
* Add a test to `python_packaging/sample_restraint` to confirm that IRestraintPotental code is actually called in GROMACS 2020+ / gmxapi 0.1+.
* Follow up in issue #4079 to migrate to using a `SimulationInput` and expanded `SimulationContext` interface, and remove `gmxapi::System`, `gmxapi::Workflow`, and `gmxapi::WorkSpec`

closed_issues.title: Issues with trjorder using TIP5P water model
closed_issues.description:
I hope this is the correct place to post this - I've been directed to the gitlab site from the gromacs forums where I initially brought up this issue...

This issue is affecting 2020.4.

I’m encountering an issue with trjorder when trying to order TIP5P water molecules based on their distance from a polymer.

I’ve never had any issue when using trjorder to order SPC/E water, here’s an example of the ordered PDB file:

```
ATOM  49740  OW  SOL  6484      66.620  68.720   5.780  0.00  0.30           O
ATOM  49741  HW1 SOL  6484      67.530  69.050   6.030  0.00  0.30           H
ATOM  49742  HW2 SOL  6484      65.930  69.350   6.110  0.00  0.30           H
ATOM   8022  OW  SOL  2578      63.370  68.640  13.180  0.00  0.31           O
ATOM   8023  HW1 SOL  2578      64.240  69.140  13.270  0.00  0.31           H
ATOM   8024  HW2 SOL  2578      63.490  67.710  13.520  0.00  0.31           H
```

However, when using the TIP5P water model, I suspect the two dummy atoms for the lone electron pairs (LP1 and LP2) are causing issue:

```
ATOM   8550  HW1 SOL  1659      80.520  69.850  40.270  0.00  0.25           H
ATOM   8551  HW2 SOL  1659      80.830  69.080  39.000  0.00  0.25           H   
ATOM   8552  LP1 SOL  1659      80.870  70.440  39.090  0.00  0.25
ATOM   8907  LP1 SOL  1730      82.400  68.810  44.120  0.00  0.25
ATOM   8908  LP2 SOL  1730      82.410  68.500  45.220  0.00  0.25
ATOM   8909  OW  SOL  1731      58.440  65.660  29.770  0.00  0.25           O
ATOM  14493  LP2 SOL  2847      74.260  53.470  22.730  0.00  0.26
ATOM  14494  OW  SOL  2848      77.200  45.790   7.490  0.00  0.26           O
ATOM  14495  HW1 SOL  2848      77.850  45.550   6.840  0.00  0.26           H
```

In both cases, I’ve specified that trjorder used the COM as the coordinate to calculate the distance. So one would expect that you’d see five consecutive entries, e.g. OW, HW1, HW2, LP1, LP2 all from the same molecule. However, as you can see above, the first three entries are from molecule 1659, then two entries from molecule 1730, etc. It seems that trjorder is writing out groups of three atoms with consecutive atomic indices (i.e. 8907, 8908, 8909) which would work for a three-point model such as SPC/E but not a five-point model such as TIP5P. I’m aware that you can specify the number of atoms per molecule using the -na flag, however specifying -na 5 for TIP5P yields an error that the number of atoms in SOL isn’t a multiple of 5 (the number specified is a multiple of 3 however).

closed_issues.title: Issue with dihedral parameter cited in oplsaa.ff/ffbonded.itp from Amber
closed_issues.description: https://github.com/gromacs/gromacs/blob/master/share/top/oplsaa.ff/ffbonded.itp#L1669 has an issue. For opls style torsions, they must sum to 0. Looking at the cited Amber forcefield, the parameter seems to be pulled from https://github.com/openmm/openmmforcefields/blob/ca9319f15d0c5d8565853c0f525b54373cfffae1/amber/ffxml/ff94.xml#L5242. Applying the [gromacs conversion](https://manual.gromacs.org/current/reference-manual/functions/bonded-interactions.html#proper-dihedrals-ryckaert-bellemans-function) to RB torsion parameters from the opls style, the correct parameters should be [-8.9956 3.138 10.0416 -4.184 0.0 0.0]. See https://github.com/mosdef-hub/mbuild/pull/916#issuecomment-859073283 for more information.

closed_issues.title: Fujitsu fx1000: Crashes in hardwareTopologyPrepareDetection() function when using more than 8 MPI ranks per node.
closed_issues.description: We are executing GROMACS on the Fujitsu FX1000. It works great if we do not use more than 8 MPI ranks per node, but it crashes on the hardwareTopologyPrepareDetection() function when we use more than 8. Every single rank executes that function, so when there are many ranks on a single node, a considerable number of threads are spawned, and it seems that the FX1000 can not handle that. I guess the easiest solution is that only one process per node executes the hardwareTopologyPrepareDetection() function.

closed_issues.title: evaluate hipSYCL with native HIP kernels
closed_issues.description:
In case if SYCL native code would not produce the desired performance on AMD with hipSYCL, we can use native HIP kernels:
- using SYCL kernel invocation with native HIP kernel body
- hipSYCL backend iterop calling a separately compiled HIP kernel object

On the device-side there the difference between the above two is in the upstream clang vs ROCm clang HIP compilers which may or may not behave significantly differently, something we should verify.
In the host-device code there may be differences (especially if explicit multipass is used), but I'm hoping that these will not have a major performance impact.

closed_issues.title: Properly do event-based synchronization in hipSYCL
closed_issues.description:
With DAG-based scheduling, the only standard-compliant way to synchronize in SYCL is to either use task-associated events or wait here and now on host for all the tasks submitted to the stream. That does not play well with the `GpuEventSynchronizer` class.

DPCPP has [SYCL_INTEL_enqueue_barrier](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/sycl/sycl/doc/extensions/EnqueueBarrier/enqueue_barrier.asciidoc) extension that allows inserting barrier events, like `cudaEventRecord` or `clEnqueueBarrierWithWaitList` do.

A hack was introduced in !1185 that does over-zealous synchronization in hipSYCL's version of `GpuEventSynchronizer`.

Some of the extra synchronizations can be avoided by setting `GMX_GPU_SYCL_NO_SYNCHRONIZE=1` environment variable (!1404). 

Overall, since CUDA (and HIP) have full access to the CUDA Event API, it can be used directly, avoiding all the troubles with trying to fit SYCL into the CUDA-inspired synchronization model.

See `SYCL-TODO`s in `gpueventsynchronizer_sycl.h`.

closed_issues.title: sycl::buffer::reinterpret and hipSYCL
closed_issues.description:
When working with force buffers on device, we `reinterpret` them from `Float3` to `float` to allow creating atomic accessors.

However, at the moment hipSYCL does not support reinterpreting buffers to an element of a different size. This triggers an assertion in Debug build but works perfectly fine in Release mode.

Possible solutions:

- Use pointers instead of accessors.
- Add extended support for buffer reinterpretion to hipSYCL. Not trivial due to hipSYCL page state tracking.
- Add `atomic_ref` support to hipSYCL, so that we can work with buffer of Float3, and only get references to its elements.

Affects at least NBNXM and SETTLE kernels (so far)

Partially fixed by !1606

closed_issues.title: Introduce the support for a new communication mechanism in MiMiC QM/MM module
closed_issues.description:
Currently, the MiMiC communication module in GROMACS is using only the older mechanism based on the MPI client-server mechanism, which turned out to be poorly supported by MPI implementations. The additional, new mechanism is using the MPI MPMD capabilities. Here two applications are run with a single `mpirun` command forming a joint `MPI_COMM_WORLD`. This joint communicator is then split according to `MPI_APPNUM` property and is used instead of `MPI_COMM_WORLD` within GROMACS.

The splitting has to be done before the first collective over `MPI_COMM_WORLD` is invoked (otherwise, this will result in a deadlock). This is achieved with a call to `MCL_init` function in the MiMiC communication library. According to the discussion with @eirrgang the most suitable place for the splitting is in:
programs/mdrun/mdrun.cpp after line 82.

closed_issues.title: Exclusions not treated correctly for the interactions beyond rcoulomb
closed_issues.description:
If an interaction between two atoms is excluded in the topology, but the interatomic distance between the atoms is larger than rcoulomb, the interaction will not be properly excluded.

Example:
Below are the energies calculated for a system of two atoms with charges q1=+1 and q2=-1. The distance between the atoms is 1.0 nm. The cases where interaction between the atoms is excluded explicitly in the itp file are marked as "_excl". For rlist=rcoul=1.2 nm the exclusions are subtracted properly. For rcoul=0.9 nm, the exclusion is not applied.

Total Coulomb energy\
rlist1.2_rcoul1.2_noexcl   -141.403107\
rlist1.2_rcoul1.2_excl      -2.467650

rlist1.2_rcoul0.9_noexcl   -141.406036\
rlist1.2_rcoul0.9_excl     -141.406036

rlist0.9_rcoul0.9_noexcl   -141.406036\
rlist0.9_rcoul0.9_excl     -141.406036

A similar bug regarding the excluded atoms that are further than rcoul apart was recently resolved for the exclusions including perturbed atoms https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/3403

For the perturbed atom exclusions that are further than rlist, the following solution was introduced: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/861

Maybe a similar fix could be applied to any exclusion, i.e. not only those where perturbed atoms are involved? 
Alternatively, maybe it would be reasonable to check every excluded interaction explicitly irrespectively of it being in the neighbourlist? Some of the discussion on this is already started here: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/3844

closed_issues.title: GPU communication scheduling code has blocking behavior
closed_issues.description:
For each timestep, the GPU direct communication code has 2 stages

1) CPU performs scheduling of GPU communication operations
2) GPU operations execute asynchronously

Stage 1 involves CPU-side blocking MPI communications of pointers and events. This has no impact for those fully-GPU-offloaded cases since the scheduling is all done long in advance of the actual GPU communications, but we need to assess potential impact for those cases that involve CPU-side force calculations, and move towards a more asynchronous (from the CPU perspective) implementation if necessary.  

Includes following comms associated with https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1591:
- [x] send location of force pointer from PP to PME task (can be made non-blocking, moved earlier and doesn't need to be done every iteration)
- [x] receive location of force pointer on PME task from PP task (doesn't need to be done every iteration) 
- [x] receive event pointer on PP task from PME task, which signals force has been transferred ((can be made non-blocking, moved earlier)


Quoting @pszilard from https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/5fd12f7205bfb54dc0da93cfea5a6f204c2b097d:

This feels like a somewhat heavy-handed approach, so I'd like us to improve it. We require a "handshake" using a blocking send with each PP rank on the critical path when we should ideally be progressing with the reduction. Even if the PME rank is ready to send, it has to wait until the PP rank arrives to the end of the step and sends this ptr. I'd prefer if we do this using a nonblocking send in the beginning of the step, e.g. after sending X to the PME rank. Even better, we could set up an array of pointers for the next `nstlist` steps at decomposition.

...

As the above, I think and we should at least use an nonblocking recv issued early; if we send both `localForcePtr` and `eventptr` in the same place, we could do that with a single MPI operation to cut down on latency. However, to make the whole step more async even with CPU work on the critical path, it would be useful to not have to send around events every step, but this would require some additional mechanism to make sure the event is consumed only when it is ready (so either a sa"fe event" that one can poll on until it's been recoded or a memops-based solution).

closed_issues.description: A persistent annoyance when sharing/debugging Gromacs simulations between multiple users is that on Linux (and perhaps other platforms), `gmx solvate` and `gmx genion` create topology files without world-readable permissions. If one has root privileges those permissions can be overridden, but that is not an option for normal users. Notably, both `gmx pdb2gmx` and `gmx editconf` create/modify topology files with what I would argue are the correct permissions (i.e. `644`). It would be great if `gmx solvate` and `gmx genion` could be changed to behave like `gmx pdb2gmx` and `gmx editconf`.

closed_issues.title: G96Angle Parameter not converted to cosine in radians in listed-forces
closed_issues.description:
This was an issue that got discovered when support for more concrete listed forces types came under development in the NBLIB project. The tests and the ref data in `src/gromacs/listed_forces/tests/bonded.cpp` were examined and it was found that the results for the g96 angles were off by a large margin compared to data from NBLIB's compute pipeline.

On further examination, we found that the equilibrium angle parameter is passed to the compute pipeline in degrees, as seen in line 3583 onward in `bonded.cpp`. For harmonic angles, it was observed that explicit conversion takes place to radians in line 1043 of the same file. For g96angles, it should passed in as cosine of radians.

However, in the preprocessor file, `src/gromacs/gmxpreprocess/convparm.cpp`, we see that this is accounted for. 

To resolve this inconsistency, I suggest two approaches:

1. Change things inside the kernel, the way it is done for harmonic angles. Remove special cases from `convparm.cpp`.
2. Pass the cosines of the angles in radians as params only in the listed-forces tests, with the `iListInput` data structure. This approach would mean that any alternative caller to the g96angles kernel should be mindful of this parameter processing step.

The first approach is certainly cleaner and helpful for APIs that want to reuse older code. But it would mean that a redundant cosine, and deg2rad conversion takes place each step.

closed_issues.title: Update ensureNoPendingDeviceError
closed_issues.description:
Currently, CUDA has the `ensureNoPendingDeviceError` function that potentially helps localize the source of CUDA errors. This function has the following problems:

- only declared for CUDA, so can not be used in backend-agnostic code;
- always does CUDA API calls -- it might make sense to make this function no-op in release builds to avoid the overhead.

Besides, if we want to make sure this function actually helps with tracking down errors, it should be consistently used at every module boundary. It was removed from `LincsGpu::apply` in !1428, and, if I recall correctly, is used sporadically in general.

The following discussion from !1428 should be addressed:

- [ ] @al42and started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1428#note_556352097):  (+1 comment)

    > Shall we bring back the `ensureNoPendingDeviceError`, which was removed from the very top of `void LincsGpu::apply`?

- 2 sockets Intel Xeon Platinum 8160 CPU with 24 cores each @ 2.10GHz for a total of 48 cores per node
- L1d 32K; L1i cache 32K; L2 cache 1024K; L3 cache 33792K

closed_issues.title: SYCL: D2H copy of temperature scaling factors cause GPU stalls when using GPU update
closed_issues.description:
When using GPU update, the code (!1329 + !1404) has an unintended host synchronization with the GPU local stream. This only affects SYCL + DPCPP + OpenCL configuration.

Repro: 76e984a522b71150be8d3f08dfde9604dc7e16d2, `SYCL_DEVICE_FILTER=opencl:gpu gmx mdrun -ntmpi 1 -ntomp 4 -nb gpu -pme cpu -update gpu -resethway -nsteps 1000 -nobackup -pin on`, Ar-157k system, Intel Xe iGPU.

When running **without** manual synchronizations between GPU streams (`GMX_GPU_SYCL_NO_SYNCHRONIZE=1`):

![image16](/uploads/f7094fa35c5a4b81535e0a6a6cac1fe0/image16.png)

When running with manual sync (notice the third GPU utilization drop, causing 7% performance loss):

![image17](/uploads/6c3ec4e238aa7bb535cf6dede41928f1/image17.png)

<hr/>

The stall is caused by the following behavior:

- In `UpdateConstrainGpu::Impl::integrate`, we call `fReadyOnDevice->enqueueWaitEvent(deviceStream_)` prior to calling `LeapFrogGpu::integrate`. This places a barrier into the local stream.
- In `LeapFrogGpu::integrate`, we request a host accessor to write updated temperature scaling factors.
- In OpenCL, the request for the host accessor, despite not being associated with the local stream, waits for the barrier. See https://github.com/intel/llvm/issues/3539
- The host thread is forcibly synchronized with the GPU local stream, instead of submitting the async copy.

Possible solutions:

1. Use manual host buffer and async copy (as done in CUDA).
2. Remove explicit synchronization (ref. #3895).

For now, the first solution seems safer, and should aid with #2608.

closed_issues.title: GpuForceReduction waits for itself (from previous step), not for data copy
closed_issues.description:
[Here](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/d8f269b41e49e0a132bff754631f54ad75d3af75/src/gromacs/mdlib/sim_util.cpp#L1169), we make `gpuForceReduction[NonLocal]` wait for `getForcesReadyOnDeviceEvent(AtomLocality::NonLocal)`.

The intent seems to be that it has to wait for the forces to be copied from CPU to GPU.

Except, this call returns the completion marker of the reduction itself, not of any copies: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/d8f269b41e49e0a132bff754631f54ad75d3af75/src/gromacs/mdtypes/state_propagator_data_gpu_impl_gpu.cpp#L501

Changing `true` to `false` in the call to `getForcesReadyOnDeviceEvent` will probably fix the issue, but I'd prefer to hear the opinions of @pszilard and @artemzhmurov first.

Related to #3988, but is not about a mismatch _per se_.

closed_issues.title: Gromacs-FEP proposal
closed_issues.description:
Dear Gromacs developers, 

    Based on Gromacs-2020.2, we've done a series of development related to FEP in following aspects . We would like to contribute our codes to Gromacs and we're looking forward to hearing your opinions first.

    High-performance implementations: 

    1.  Offload FEP-PME to GPU.  Our status: finished. We've also noticed that this function has been implemented in commit f7be07e3cc901eb03700d93248fc09b573370282 by M. Lundborg et. al. and has been merged in Gromacs-2021. So we won't commit this. 
    2.  Offload non-bonded free energy kernel to GPU. Our status: finished. 
    3.  Offload bonded free energy kernel to GPU. Our status: finished.
    4.  Support GPU updates for FEP. Our status: finished md-integrator. We've noticed that this has also been implemented in Gromacs-2021, but we'are still interested in supporting GPU updates of sd-integrator.  Similar discussion can be found in issue  #3258 on gitlab. 
    5.  Support GPU replica exchange. Our status: finished.

    New features: 

    1.  Support "Soft Bond Potential" in FEP, which is proposed in  DOI: 10.1021/acs.jctc.6b00991 and allows a more smooth change of bond topology when there is bond formation or breaking in a FEP transformation, such as 5-member ring to 6-member ring.  Our status: finished. 
    2.  Split softcore parameters for VDW and Coulomb interactions.  We noticed that currently Gromacs supports only one parameter "sc-alpha" to modify soft-core interactions.  After our tests, this will cause a phase-transition-like phenomenon at middle lambdas in some cases.  Our status: finished.  We also noticed recently there have been some new forms of softcores  like gapsys softcore (DOI:  dx.doi.org/10.1021/ct300220p and discussed in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/882 ) and Amber SSC2 softcore (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jctc.0c00237.)  And we would like to ask if you consider it's necessary to support such new softcore potentials. 

    These terms are all that we want to contribute to Gromacs. But we have to admit that there is still a lot of work to test and standardize our codes to meet all requirements of Gromacs.  Is there any suggestion? 


    Best wishes!
    Happy Simulating!

    Yuzhi & Junhan 

See discussion as https://mailman-1.sys.kth.se/pipermail/gromacs.org_gmx-developers/2021-March/011044.html

closed_issues.title: PME-PP force transfers serialized on thread-MPI path
closed_issues.description:
With PME-PP GPU communications, each PP task is responsible for pulling the remote PME GPU force buffer directly from the PME GPU memory, but CUDA is serializing these multiple transfers. We can instead have the PME task pushing the buffers to each PP task explicitly in parallel (in multiple streams), allowing overlap, as implemented in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/tree/ag_pme_force_push

**Performance**

Cellulose, 4xV100 on DGX-1

export GMX_GPU_DD_COMMS=1
export GMX_GPU_PME_PP_COMMS=1
gmx mdrun -s topol.tpr -ntomp 10 -pme gpu -nb gpu -ntmpi 4 -npme 1 -nsteps 10000 -resethway -v -notunepme -pin on -bonded gpu -update gpu -noconfout -nstlist 400

Before: 111.016 ns/day      
After: 118.934 ns/day

closed_issues.title: GROMACS docs should provide more effective navigation to forums.
closed_issues.description:
https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/ and https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs are the clear entry points for current GROMACS information, but neither effectively directs users to https://gromacs.bioexcel.eu/c/gromacs-user-forum

The [install guide](https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/install-guide/index.html?highlight=forum) provides the only link I could find. (Note it is not formatted correctly in the online version).
https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/dev-manual/contribute.html?highlight=forum mentions the forum without a link.

There is no link at https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/index.html or through obvious trees like "User guide", "Short How-To guides", or "Reference Manual"

Searches such as https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/search.html?q=support, https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/search.html?q=help, and 
https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/search.html?q=getting+help
are not effective.

At https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs neither the banner, the README, nor the wiki mention the forum.

# Suggestion

Sprinkle in some links to the forum both to help users discover it and to encourage users to actively navigate back and forth between the docs, the issue tracker, and the user forum.

closed_issues.title: Reduce leak suppressions
closed_issues.description:
[`admin/lsan-suppressions.txt`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/main/admin/lsan-suppressions.txt) has a lot of items to get regression tests to pass, some of the cleanup is probably trivial.

Testing locally involves building with `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=ASAN` and running tests with the following environment variables (adjust the path to the suppressions file):

```bash
export LSAN_OPTIONS="suppressions=../admin/lsan-suppressions.txt:print_suppressions=0"
export ASAN_OPTIONS="check_initialization_order=1:detect_invalid_pointer_pairs=1:strict_init_order=true:strict_string_checks=true:detect_stack_use_after_return=true"
```

As the suppression is removed, the `gromacs.clang-ASAN` CI job could be used to check that the test now passes (see https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/main/admin/gitlab-ci/gromacs.matrix/gromacs.clang-ASAN.gitlab-ci.yml).


ASAN/LSAN docs: https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerLeakSanitizer

closed_issues.title: GPU tests do not set the list of devices used correctly
closed_issues.description:
#3980 revealed that the tests do not implement the step which in the [task assignment reduces the list of GPUs to the ones used in the run](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/gromacs/taskassignment/taskassignment.cpp#L302). In that case this manifested in `gpuIdsToUse` containing devices that were in fact not used and therefore peer access was manipulated for these.

I think this is a shortcoming of the test design that would be good to address, namely that e.g. if we pass 
```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 bin/mdrun-mpi-test -ntmpi 2
```
we know that _by design_ we can not use >2 GPUs, so (after the detection) we should not touch GPUs 2,3, i.e. the above should behave as if we passed
```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 GMX_GPU_ID=0,1 bin/mdrun-mpi-test -ntmpi 2
```

closed_issues.title: Properly set sub group size for AMD RDNA(2) devices in SYCL kernels
closed_issues.description:
In `src/gromacs/nbnxm/sycl/nbnxm_sycl_kernel.cpp`, we always set `subGroupSize` to 64 for hipSYCL build on AMD. But newer RDNA and RDNA2 devices support 32-wide execution.


The following discussion from !1221 should be addressed:

- [ ] @al42and started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/1221#note_522340285):  (+3 comments)

    > [HIP docs](https://rocmdocs.amd.com/en/latest/Programming_Guides/HIP-GUIDE.html) say they always return `warpSize = 64` for AMD devices, but the [code](https://github.com/ROCm-Developer-Tools/HIP/blob/2080cc113a2d767352b512b9d24c0620b6dee790/include/hip/hcc_detail/device_functions.h#L309) seems to indicate that global `warpSize` constant is properly set for newer hardware.
    > 
    > I would expect using `warpSize` here to behave sanely with explicit multipass in hipSYCL, but that's an open question.
    > 
    > That said, hipSYCL currently ignores the `reqd_sub_group_size` attribute, so we don't have to care much about the value of this variable.

Parent: #3934

* <s>At the same time, we need to</s>
  * <s>skip CPU-side force buffer clearing if there are no CPU forces computed</s>
  * <s>check all code-paths and make sure we can not end up with reduction kernels accumulating into non-initialized buffers.</s>. 

Done:

-------------
If CPU forces exist: 
   - cleared in setupForceOutputs

else if no CPU forces exist: 
   - if DD and GPU halo:
        - cleared before GPU halo
   - if DD and not GPU Halo:
        - cleared in setupForceOutput
   - if not DD and GPU buffer ops
        - uses set rather than accumulate
   - if not DD and not GPU buffer ops
       - cleared in setupForceOutputs
-------------

* consider inline transform function for on-the-fly transform within the nonbonded kernel; in particular for high parallelization the performance hit in the nonbonded kernel may be less than the cost of launching an extra kernel.
 - May not be relevant if #3921 goes ahead

closed_issues.title: std::aligned_alloc not available on all platforms
closed_issues.description:
!1206 abandoned our aligned memory allocation in favor of the C++ standard library implementation. I am not sure the standard implementation as broadly available as we would need, though. Notably, compilation on Mac OS 11.1 (using clang 8, 9, 11 or gcc 8) fails with error `no member named 'aligned_alloc' in namespace 'std'; did you mean simply 'aligned_alloc'?`

This lead me to investigate some more. I didn't come to a full conclusion yet, but I'm opening this issue to collect thoughts.

https://godbolt.org/z/r1j3h9 might be helpful to play around with different compilers. Based on godbolt, it seems we'd need to bump minimal versions (current → new)
* GNU (gcc/libstdc++) 7 → 7.4 (probably due to https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=83662, we could likely have a workaround, see below)
* LLVM (clang/libc++) 5 → 7
* Microsoft is unlikely to support it, by their own docs (https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/overview/visual-cpp-language-conformance?view=msvc-160#note_C11):
  > C11 Compiler support for C11 requires Visual Studio version 16.8, or higher. C11 library support requires Windows SDK version 20211, or higher. The Universal CRT implements the parts of the C11 Standard Library that are required by C++17, with the exception of C99 strftime() E/O alternative conversion specifiers, and C11 aligned_alloc(). **The latter is unlikely to be implemented because the Windows operating system doesn't support aligned allocations.**

  (emphasis mine)

Playing around with godbolt also indicates that compilation passes by using `aligned_alloc` instead of `std::aligned_alloc` (which probably means we're using the C implementation?).

The problem on MacOS might be due to the MacOS libc++. I haven't (yet) found clear information online as to what that might be though, although these threads https://forum.qt.io/topic/100242/aligned_alloc-is-not-available-despite-c-17-flag, https://github.com/marian-nmt/marian-dev/issues/227, https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=69680 seem to indicate it might be a problem of the implementation (or the lack thereof) of aligned_alloc for MacOS. In my tests locally, however, using `aligned_alloc` instead of `std::aligned_alloc` at least compiles.

closed_issues.title: port GROMACS to AMD GPUs
closed_issues.description:
AMD GPUs will provide most of the FLOPs in several upcoming machines of interest to GROMACS users (LUMI in Finland, Dardel in Sweden, Frontier in USA) so we will deliver a port in GROMACS in version 2022 intended to supsersed the (now deprecated) OpenCL-based support for AMD GPUs.

AMD has made available their working port of (currently) GROMACS 2020.3 as the basis for a HIP port. Further work will be needed, as considerable improvement and extension to our GPU infrastructure took place since that branch forked in January 2020. (*Update* I hear  they have updated that to 2021.x.) As HIP works very much like CUDA, most of the porting work can be automated with AMD's source-to-source translation tools (e.g. hipify-clang). However, GROMACS doesn't want to maintain >14k LOC of both a CUDA port and its near-duplicate HIP port. So we will explore a version that produces the HIP source code at configure time for developers. GROMACS developers will continue to develop on the CUDA port as the primary source for both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. If this approach is adopted, users will eventually get a tarball containing static HIP files produced by the hip-ification process.

As GROMACS is also adding a SYCL port primarily targeting Intel GPUs via SYCL compiled with DPCPP, it is interesting to consider whether SYCL compiled with hipSYCL to target AMD GPUs provides an attractive long-term end point. Naturally performance and maintainability will be two big factors in that decision.

hipSYCL

closed_issues.title: Incorrectly large pressures at lambda=1 with perturbed masses

We get incorrectly large pressures in FEP simulations in the lambda=1 state if we perturb the masses of all hydrogen atoms. Specifically, we simulate a pure-water box and perturb the masses of all H atoms from 1amu to 2amu. This happens with Gromacs 2019.6, 2020.5, and 2021, but NOT with 2018.6.

The pressures are shown in a PDF here:

https://cloud.hiz-saarland.de/s/NH6Mz8QKi39qBH7

(The relaxation in the problematic cases is due to rapid box expansion).

We have a test system here:

https://cloud.hiz-saarland.de/s/oJXPp5BRnTgRxg9

This does NOT happen if:

- masses are not perturbed
- using Gromacs 2018.6
- the same state is defined to lambda=0 by modifying the topology (use heavy.top with test_lambda0.mdp in the tar.gz)

closed_issues.title: MiMiC likely doesn't work with virtual sites
closed_issues.description:
While investigating #3866, @ptmerz observed that MiMiC computes forces before projecting positions of constructing particles to virtual particles. So probably the forces of the first step are garbage and forces of future steps are based on old positions. 

Mark emailed Emiliano Ippoliti to check:
> We suspect that the implementation with virtual sites has never worked, because the forces were computed before the positions of the real particles were used to compute those of the virtual ones. (Virtual sites are points in space where forces are felt, e.g. water lone pairs, but those forces are projected back onto the constructing atoms before the positions are updated.) Does that seem consistent with past usage of MiMiC? Should we remove the unused (and apparently untested) virtual site support?

Emiliano replied:
> I think so. Indeed, MiMiC is not using virtual sites right now. Technically, MiMiC has the infrastructure to handle them but they are not used at the moment by any group who is currently working with the interface. Therefore, if you remove them from GROMACS it should be not a problem for MiMiC users, and the new users will not start thinking at those :-) (at least until somebody will decide to introduce them back into GROMACS).

Probably a form of the change of !1107 would be enough to fix the bug in `release-2021`, but clearly there is no test coverage and little interest in the capability from its user community. Disabling vsites with MiMiC is a comparable amount of work, so I suggest we apply the fix and hope it serves the purpose.

closed_issues.title: Cosine acceleration is only implemented in leap-frog, but allowed to run in other integrators
closed_issues.description:
When using `cos-acceleration` != 0, two things (should) happen:
1. An acceleration is added during particle propagation
2. Viscosity-related quantities are computed and reported

Part 1 is only implemented for `integrator = md`. `mdrun` and `grompp` do, however, happily accept non-zero cos acceleration with other integrators, and report the (likely wrong) viscosity quantities.

This has probably been allowed since a very long time - I haven't done all the digging, but I couldn't find any sign of this ever having been different.

closed_issues.title: Problem (Bug?) in RDF calculation for Group-Based RDFs in 2021
closed_issues.description:
There appears to be a problem with calculation of RDFs between center of masses between globular protein molecules. When calculating (using whole_mol_com selections) the C.O.M. RDF between the globular proteins (radius of gyration around 2-2.5 nm), code version 2021.1 produces spurious peaks in the RDF below 2 nm, whereas version 2020.1 (standard ubuntu 20.4) does not produce these spurious peaks. Visual trajectory inspection proves that the protein molecules do NOT denature, thus, no spurious peaks should occur. 

Command Line for the RDF calculation:
```
gmx rdf -pbc -rmpbc -f ../../protein_mod50.xtc -s topol.tpr -n index.ndx \
  -selrpos whole_mol_com -seltype whole_mol_com -norm rdf -o rdf.xvg \
  -b 6000 -e 8000 -rmax 16 -bin 0.1
```

Further info:
Similar (but less pronounced) spurious problems occur when using the res_com selection scheme. 

Additional info: this seems not to be a problem of the method to generate the topol.tpr/index.ndx files, since these were created both by the 2020 and the 2021 gromacs version, with identical bad results when running gmx rdf from the 2021 code suite. I also noted that, when calculating the RDF for short 2ns segments of the long trajectory that sometimes these spurious peaks occur, sometimes not, which might be an indication that this is an initialization problem?

I append a comparison of the RDFs from two different time intervals of the trajectory for demonstration. For better visibility I shifted the difference between 2021 and 2020 down by 0.1 units and the 2021 version up by 0.1 units. The orange 2020 curve is physically reasonable. 

Thanks for looking into this.

Eckhard

closed_issues.title: Decide on explicit vs. implicit synchronization in SYCL
closed_issues.description:
In SYCL, it is possible to avoid explicitly synchronizing computations and data copying by relying on the data-dependency graph and hoping the runtime is smart enough.

It does work ok for NBNXM, but there are the following concerns, [raised](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/877#note_498577695) by @pszilard:

- Divergence between CUDA/OpenCL/HIP and SYCL in code organization and task scheduling, potentially causing hard-to-catch bugs.
- Efficiency of the scheduling by the SYCL runtime.

Benchmarking and thorough analysis in light of the proposed GPU code merger is necessary.

Related: #3847, #3311 (#3020, #3323)

closed_issues.title: Add -maxtau option to gmx msd
closed_issues.description:
The current gmx msd algorithm is roughly

for frame:
1. calculate msd against all stored frames
2. if a restart point, store frame
    
    

The problems with this are
- unlimited frame storage in RAM. Every stored frame will be compared against every new frame, so must be saved.
- unlimited increases in the number of frames to compare against per new frame
- Potential calculation of tau values for which you'll never get good sampling. Take the example of the COM of a protein - the final tau (last frame - first frame) will ALWAYS be calculated, even though it's pretty much useless. You need hundreds of data points to get anything approximating a reasonable estimate of the msd at a given tau. Users can restrict the D-coefficient calculation to use well-sampled taus (though they often don't), but the data is always collected.

I propose a -maxtau flag, where frames will only be compared if tau <= maxtau. This allows users to cut down on computation they will never use, and more importantly, allows us to start discarding old frames once there are no more tau values in the range to compare against, so we can reach a steady state of RAM usage and per-new-frame computation.

closed_issues.title: Clarify gmx msd -mw and -mol options
closed_issues.description:
gmx msd is unclear in documentation exactly how -mw (mass-weighting) and -mol (per molecule diffusion coefficients) work. At minimum we need better documentation, but I'd like to reconsider the default behavior, which is in some cases non-intuitive, or could even be interpreted as buggy. 

| -mw (default = yes) | -mol | result
| ------ | ------ | ------ | 
| no | no | Masses are not used  | 
| yes | no | Contributions to the msd per group are mass-weighted |
| no | yes | -mw is ignored, -o gives MW mol-COM based averages, -mol gives MW per-mol diffusion coefficient | 
| yes | yes | Sames as with -nomw| 

Some points here:
- It's counterintuitive to me that without -mol, we default to mass-weighted MSDs. That is, even though particles are not necessarily related, their contribution to the average MSD for a given tau is mass-weighted. I don't think there's a physical reason for that
- The -nomw option is silently ignored with -mol. There may not be a ton of reasons one might want non-mass weighted centers to calculate COM for, but right now we're giving the illusion of option.
- In the docs, it's unclear that with -mol, the -o output is mol-COM based

closed_issues.title: Clarify meaning of virtual site velocities
closed_issues.description:
Below, we decided to calculate the velocities (when required) directly. This changed the to do list for this issue:

- [x] Derive velocity expressions and update the documentation
- [x] Implement new velocity calculation, to be performed only if trajectory writing is about to happen
- [x] Remove previous workarounds needed to keep positions stable during update
- [x] Move virtual site calculation to top of the loop right before force calculation, avoiding a) problems with pressure scaling, b) reducing the likelihood of interference with other algorithms between the moment they are calculated and the moment they enter the dynamic properties (forces), and c) remove the need for any initialization before the loop.
- [x] Introduce tests (see below)
- [x] Check compatibility with GPU integration
- [ ] Check possible bug in MiMiC

I'm leaving the original description below for reference

---

Virtual sites are massless "particles" whose positions are fully determined by a function of other (non-virtual or virtual) atoms. They may be involved in interactions, but forces acting on them are redistributed to particles having mass. Their positions are updated after non-virtual particles were updated and constrained. Their velocities are not used in their propagation, but are calculated from their displacement. This suggests that 
* virtual site positions should only be changed by the virtual site algorithm,
* virtual site velocities are zero at the first step, and calculated from the displacement of the positions after that, and should only be changed by the virtual site algorithm.

Calculation of the velocity from the position displacement is done as `v = (newX - oldX) / dt`. This results in half-step velocities as expected in leap-frog. Velocity verlet integrator reports atom velocities at full steps, which can't be calculated for the virtual sites until after the next position update. This would be an argument not to report the virtual site velocities. Current md-vv is setting the velocities to zero shortly before trajectory writing, but it's unclear whether this is by design or by accident. Reporting zero velocities can be confusing to users, however - the virtual site positions might seem frozen.
- [ ] **Action item 1.1: Decide if virtual site velocities should be reported at all - almost all issues below could easily be solved by simply zero-ing the virtual velocities right before trajectory output... What is the use case for virtual site velocities?**
- [ ] **Action item 1.2: Decide if md-vv virtual site velocities should be half-step velocities or explicitly zero-ed.**
- [ ] **Action item 1.2a: Adapt implementation to decision of 1.2.**
- [ ] **Action item 1.3: Implement test checking that virtual site velocities conform to expectation.**

Calculating the velocity from the displacement requires that the **virtual positions are not updated outside of the virtual site algorithm** (e.g. during the propagation of regular atoms). To avoid that virtual site positions get updated, algorithms can either check each atom for its particle type and skip propagation (done in md-vv, sd, bd, which also zero the velocities - probably not necessary) or zero the virtual site velocities before update (done by the simple and simple SIMD versions of leap-frog, such that the update [now with zero velocities and zero forces] can be vectorized). The general leap-frog propagation does neither of the two, resulting in wrong virtual site velocities. 
- [ ] **Action item 2: Fix the general leap-frog update to skip virtual sites.**

The virtual site positions and velocities are recalculated after the regular propagation, but they are changed again in `update_pcouple_after_coordinates` when using Berendsen (positions only), C-Rescale (positions and velocities) and Parrinello-Rahman (positions only). Scaling the virtual site positions as the normal particle positions can lead to **small errors in the virtual site positions**, as not all virtual sites are calculated as linear combinations of other particles.
- [ ] **Action item 3: Move virtual site calculation after pressure coupling (make sure positions are final before updating virtual sites).**

Even after moving the virtual site calculation after the pressure coupling scales the coordinates, having the pressure coupling scaling the virtual site positions will cause the virtual site velocities not to be exactly `v = (newX - oldX) / dt`.
- [ ] **Action item 4: Exclude virtual site positions from pressure coupling position scaling.**

The virtual site velocities are scaled during COM motion removal. Since the velocities represent the previous propagation, and virtual sites don't have a mass, they should probably not be affected by COM motion removal.
- [ ] **Action item 5: Exclude virtual site velocities from COM motion removal.**

The virtual site velocities are also rescaled during temperature coupling for md-vv. For non-Trotter schemes, this does not matter because it happens right before coordinate propagation (which zeroes the velocities), but has some potential for future bugs. For Trotter, this might influence the velocities if we decide to report them (see action item 1).
- [ ] **Action item 6.1: Exclude virtual site velocities from md-vv Trotter temperature coupling rescaling, unless they are defined to be zero (Action item 1.2).**
- [ ] **Action item 6.2: Decide if we need to exclude virtual site velocities from temperature coupling rescaling in other cases.**

Subtask of #3849.

closed_issues.title: GenerateRandomSeed returns the same value with time-adjacent calls on Ryzen
closed_issues.description:
The makeRandomSeed() function uses std::random_device where possible, but for Ryzen 3k CPUs without a specific microcode patch (see [here](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2019/10/how-a-months-old-amd-microcode-bug-destroyed-my-weekend/)), it falls back to std::mt19937_64.

The problem is with the seeding of that rng, which is done with the <time.h> time() function. That  only returns seconds since epoch - so any two calls to makerandomseed() that fall within the same second yield the same result. This causes unit test failures on this specific machine setup.

At least when GPU direct communication is used and update is also offloaded the DLB region timers will in most cases collect meaningless data (unless the CPU force computation is on the critical path) and may try to balance on this. closed_issues.title: Make inputrec const everywhere, clarify simulation parameter updates
closed_issues.description:
The inputrec is mostly used to represent the input received from the user. In a few cases, it is also used by other functionalities to change simulation parameters:
* Simulated annealing and simulated tempering might change the target temperature (do_md)
* ~~The COM motion removal frequency is adapted to other parameters in setup (do_md)~~ → !955
* Change calculation frequencies (do_rerun, do_mimic)
* Change rlist (do_tpi)
* Change nsteps (do_nm, do_steep)

This is dangerous, as some functionalities are copying inputrec values to local variables, or using it to compute local variables (e.g.: thermostats calculating their masses based on reference temperature), and might not be aware that changes happened that could require them to update their local copies / variables.

The inputrec should be constant at the simulator level. Simulation parameters which are supposed to be updated need to be implemented in a different way including a mechanism to inform other modules that a change has happened.

closed_issues.title: gmx wham reports confusing things
closed_issues.description:
```
GROMACS:      gmx wham, version 2020.4

Command line:
  gmx wham -it topol.dat -ix pullx.dat

Found 24 tpr and 24 pull position files in topol.dat and pullx.dat, respectively
Reading 24 tpr and pullf files
```

This should probably be pullx files. Then the output continues:

```
Automatic determination of boundaries...
Reading file analysis/run-00/topol.tpr, VERSION 2020.4 (single precision)

File analysis/run-00/topol.tpr, 1 coordinates, with these options:
	Geometry distance   k = 5000      position = 0.05      dimensions [Y Y Y] (3 dimensions). Used: Yes
	Pull group coordinates of 0 groups expected in pullx files.
	Reference value of the coordinate not expected in pullx files.
	Use option -v to see this output for all input tpr files
```

It reports that it expects pull-group coordinates and not reference values in the pullx files. These look like

```
@    title "Pull COM"
@    xaxis  label "Time (ps)"
@    yaxis  label "Position (nm)"
@TYPE xy
0.0000  0.31683
0.1000  0.314568
0.2000  0.312896
0.3000  0.304701
...
```

That agrees. But then `gmx wham` continues

```
Reading pull position file analysis/run-00/pullx.xvg, expecting 2 columns:
	Columns for pull coordinate 1
		reaction coordinate:             1
		center-of-mass of groups:        0
		reference position column:       No
	Found 50001 times in analysis/run-00/pullx.xvg
```

which is confusing. Two columns are expected and found in the ``pullx.xvg`` file, one of which is the time. The report looks like it identifies the second column (numbered 1) as the reaction coordinate for the first pull group, and the first column (numbered 0) as the center of mass. In fact the first column is the time. ``gmx wham`` did not identify a column for the reference position, which is good. But it should report "No" for center-of-mass.

closed_issues.title: Proposal: use git submodules for dependencies in `python_packaging`
closed_issues.description:
`pybind11` and `googletest` are support packages that are typically embedded with the sources for a dependent package. We did not have the option of using git submodules on Gerrit, but on GitLab, we do. The python packages under `python_packaging` use these external projects unaltered. It doesn't make sense to bloat the repository with them or to clutter the review process with more than just a commit hash id.

If we allowed each dependent library to reference a specific commit of a git submodule, we would have more flexibility when testing and updating dependencies, while reducing the size of the repository and git noise. Note that this would likely require that the dependent sub-projects be built as CMake `ExternalProject` rather than directly in the main build environment to avoid dependency target collisions.

The sub-projects under `python_packaging` should probably be git submodules, themselves, instead of being embedded directly, but that is a subject for a separate issue.

It is reasonable to exclude these dependencies from source distributions, since the dependencies are clearly documented. (Installation of these packages from the GROMACS source distribution is not expected, but dependency resolution can be improved as needed.)

*update:* The proposed solution to #4092 includes removing the bundled pybind11 files and relying entirely on an installed Python package.

closed_issues.title: Python package version handling
closed_issues.description:
Some refinement is warranted for the `gmxapi.version` module and the management of the package's semantic versioning.

A "to do" in `gmxapi/version.py` is being updated to track this issue.

# Note

Versioning of the Python package and the `libgmxapi` C++ library is intentionally loosely coupled, pending further discussion of the ultimate disposition of each. The Python package should not strongly depend on specific GROMACS releases, but
* library versions should be incremented at releases in accordance with contribution policies, and
* we currently think of "gmxapi version" as abstractly indicative of the functional level of the pre-1.0 public GROMACS API, whether accessed through C++ or Python.

## Update: 2022 release preparation

CMake-level versioning has been removed for the gmxapi Python package to reduce confusion with respect to the versions associated with the `gmxapi` C++ library target.

Recent updates to the Python package installation infrastructure have consolidated the source of Python package version information to the `python_packaging/src/gmxapi/version.py` file. This file is the source of the package metadata from which release names are derived, such as on https://pypi.org/project/gmxapi/

# See also

* https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/python_packaging/README.md
* hard coded details in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/python_packaging/src/setup.py
* hard coded details in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/python_packaging/src/gmxapi/version.py
