closed_issues.title: Resolve "to do"s in gitlab.rst
closed_issues.description:
There is some lack of clarity regarding the maintenance and usage of the CI infrastructure. We should document the motivation and intention of the GitLab CI Pipeline stuff before memories get too stale.

This will also help efforts to clarify or improve the configuration and to allow more developers to contribute to maintenance.

# Notes

Per !725 we expect to use the new `workflow` semantics to run one pipeline for every commit, plus one pipeline after merging to a release branch, plus one pipeline for each schedule or web trigger.

The `when: always` rules seem to have been erroneously chosen. `when: on_success` appears to be the logic that was intended, generally.

The GitLab documentation is not clear what to expect when multiple jobs are chained in a `needs: []` DAG and an upstream job does not run because of a `rules: when:` parameter, but presumably the behavior is sensible, rather than creating "blocked" jobs.

# Further suggestions

One way to improve clarity would be to change to a naming scheme that conveys the intention of the job so that the rules can be maintained independently of the jobs.

* `screen`: light-weight jobs that can run on any CI Runner for basic commit validation.
* `dev`: more extensive testing that requires gromacs project resources.
* `mr-full-coverage`: a superset of `screen` and `dev` to validate merge requests.
* `ci-post-merge`: jobs that _only_ run for trunk branch pushes.
* `nightly-only`: jobs that _only_ run nightly.

I don't see any reason to exclude `schedule` and `web` triggers from any of these rule sets.

Some rule sets warrant special cases for release version, for jobs that should not be run after a certain release.

If we need fancier logic, I highly recommend we rewrite most of the command scripts from YAML to shell scripts. This would allow jobs to be more easily emulated from the command line and would make all of the testing easier to maintain. We could define fewer jobs that run under more circumstances, and put the more sophisticated logic in the shell script.

I expect that the job logic based on custom environment variables can be handled by shell scripts, but there may be jobs that should depend exclusively on a variable, such as to generate a source distribution or repackage the regression tests. Thoughts?

# Tracking

The `testing` label may not adequately link these issues, and `infrastructure` is too overloaded. A GitLab "milestone" may be appropriate to coordinate tasks related to a year-end push to tidy up the CI infrastructure configuration and documentation.

closed_issues.title: Clarify update of freeze groups, virtual sites, and shell particles
closed_issues.description:
I have been trying to understand the algorithms updating frozen / partially frozen atoms, virtual sites, and shell particles. These are handled differently in different integrator schemes, which (in the best case) is confusing and prone to the introduction of errors, and likely already yields slight differences between the integrator schemes.

This issue has several goals:
- [ ] Establish and document the protocol the update of these particles should follow
- [ ] Verify whether the current implementation is correct
- [ ] Understand whether there is potential for simplification or unification across the different integration algorithms.

The three types of particles have characteristics that require special treatment during updates:

* **Frozen particles** are immobile in some or all dimensions. Their position should stay invariant, their velocity should be zero. The inverse mass and inverse mass per dimension of completely frozen atoms is set to zero (infinitely heavy). The inverse mass per dimension of partially-frozen atoms is set to zero, inverse mass of the atom is 1/(mass of atom type). Frozen particles experience forces as any other particle, i.e. forces on them are expected to be non-zero.
* **Virtual site** positions are recomputed from the position of other particles (after their propagation). Their velocity is recalculated from the difference of their position between steps. Forces on virtual sites are redistributed to their constructing particles. The forces are expected to be zero at the end of do_force. The inverse mass of virtual sites is set to zero.
* **Shell particles** represent polarization. Their position is determined by minimization of the potential energy every step (during force calculation). *I am not familiar with the shell code. Looking over it, I think to see that (but I'd be happy if someone could confirm or correct me!):*
    * *Forces are non-zero*
    * *Inverse masses are zero*
    * *Velocities are never used, but printed to trajectory (or is there a check somewhere to exclude them?)*
    * *Positions are updated in do_force, printed to trajectory (?)*

Treatment in current `do_md`:

1. Before start of the main loop if new runs (input not read from checkpoint), the velocities of frozen dimensions, virtual sites and shell particles are set to 0.
1. During removal of COM motion, some velocity might be reintroduced (except for frozen particles / dimensions which are explicitly exempt)
1. *Beginning of simulation loop*
1. Force calculation
    * If shell & vsite, vsite positions & velocities are updated.
    * If shell particles, shell particle positions are updated.
1. If md-vv, do half-step velocity update
    * md-vv update sets velocities of freeze dimensions, virtual sites and shell particles explicitly to zero.
1. If md-vv, call compute_globals, might include COM motion removal adding some velocity to zero-ed non-frozen velocities.
1. Write trajectory & checkpoint
    * For frozen atoms / dimensions, we expect the velocity to be zero
    * For v-sites, we expect the velocity to be equal to the velocity calculated at the last step (zero if first step)
1. Update positions (full step) and velocities (half-step for md-vv, full step for other algorithms)
    * md-vv, bd and sd explicitly check particle type, set velocities of freeze dimensions, virtual sites and shell particles to zero.
    * md-vv, bd and sd explicitly check particle type, set the positions of freeze dimensions, virtual sites and shell particles to their previous values (`xp[i][d] = x[i][d]`).
    * md has three update paths:
        * Simple SIMD
             * No Nose-Hoover, no Parrinello-Rahman, no acceleration, single temperature scaling value (one T-group or non-T-coupling step), no partially frozen atoms (SIMD version uses invMass instead of invMassPerDim to reduce cache pressure).
             * v-site velocities get set to zero before update
             * Does not check particle type - all atoms treated equally
        * Simple
             * No Nose-Hoover, no off-diagonal Parrinello-Rahman, no acceleration
             * v-site velocities get set to zero before update
             * Does not check particle type - all atoms treated equally
        * General
             * Only used if Nose-Hoover, off-diagonal Parrinello-Rahman, or acceleration groups are used
             * Does not zero v-site velocities
             * Does not check particle type - all atoms treated equally
    * As md does leap-frog integration, the basic operations for the simple and general code paths is (`i`: atom, `d`: dimension)
      ```
      v[i][d] += dt*f[i][d]*invMassPerDim[i][d]
      x[i][d] += dt*v[i][d]
      ```
      while SIMD does not differentiate by dimension
      ```
      v[i] += dt*f[i]*invMass[i]
      x[i] += dt*v[i]
      ```
        * Frozen atoms will not change velocity thanks to the inverse mass / inverse mass per dimension being zero and SIMD being disallowed for partially frozen atoms. Non-zero velocities are unlikely to be introduced anywhere, as COM motion removal is explicitly excluding frozen dimensions → positions should not change.
        * Virtual sites will not change velocity since their forces and inverse masses are zero. In the simple and simple SIMD implementation, v-site velocities are set to zero before the update. In the general implementation, the v-site velocities are not zero-ed, and will propagate the positions.
        * The shell particle velocities are not zero-ed in either leap-frog implementation. The inverse masses are zero (?), so the velocities will not change, but velocity introduced via COM motion removal might slightly move the particles.
1. Constraining: This might be a problem when using lincs or shake (which uses invMass) and partially frozen atoms. The constraining might displace the atoms along the frozen dimensions. Fully frozen atoms don't suffer that problem due to the zero inverse mass.
1. Finish update: If we have partially frozen atoms and constraints, we avoid copying back the updated positions (`xp`) to the position vector in the state object. In all other cases, we copy back all positions. *What about the velocities? Velocities are updated in lincs / shake as well, wouldn't we expect to have non-zero velocities in the frozen dimensions of partially frozen, constrained atoms?*
1. Virtual site recalculation: This calculates the virtual sites from the new positions, and the velocities from the displacement between the old and the new virtual site position. This only works if the positions were not changed during the update. *If we moved the virtual sites in the general leap-frog implementation, the velocities might be off.*
1. Compute globals / remove COM motion, might subtract COM motion from vsite / shell velocities.

I see the following problems in the current implementation:
* ~~If we use the general implementation (Nose-Hoover / off-diagonal Parrinello-Rahman, acceleration), the virtual site velocities are not zeroed (and they are not expected to be zero except in the first step!). This will not result in wrong virtual site positions (since they are recalculated from non-virtual atoms), but in wrong v-site velocities (since the algorithm expects unchanged positions since the last call).~~ → #3866, !979
* ~~md-vv will always print zero / almost zero velocities for the v-sites (due to the velocity half-step before trajectory printing), while the other algorithms will print the v-site velocities calculated at the last step. Md-vv should probably not zero the v-site velocities in the first half step.~~ → #3866, !979
* ~~Virtual sites and shell particles get changed by COM motion removal - this is likely to be a very small contribution in healthy simulations, but is it correct? If it is correct, md-vv needs to be investigated exactly, as it is zero-ing the velocities and removing COM at different places compared to the other algorithms. If it is not correct, the COM removal should expand its particle check to include v-sites and shell particles.~~ → #3866, !979, !980
* ~~Partially-frozen atoms might have non-zero velocities due to constraining, unless I've missed something.~~ → No, the frozen-dimension velocities are zero-ed in the constraining implementation. The frozen-dimension positions, as mentioned above, are not copied back, so this is all as expected. However, the initial constraining might move partially frozen atom *positions*.
* ~~Shell particle velocities will accumulate the COM motion removal velocity changes, but be unused otherwise.~~ → !980

I think that otherwise, the frozen / partially frozen atoms and shell particles implementation looks ok. Since the leap-frog update does not care about shell particles, it seems that it wouldn't be necessary to check for it in md-vv / sd / bd either, somewhat unifying the code paths.

closed_issues.title: trx frame reading from modular simulator checkpoints might be off
closed_issues.description:
The trx frame reading functionality in src/gromacs/fileio/checkpoint.cpp is populating a trx frame from the global t_state checkpoint data. The global t_state is still present in modular simulator, but is only up-to-date when using domain decomposition. 

Getting rid of the global t_state in the checkpoint format is not currently possible due to setup work in mdrunner depending on it. Note that the global t_state doesn't matter for modular simulator restarts. Also, the runner level setup work is not affected by a slightly outdated t_state object. 

The trx frame reading is, however, used by other gromacs tools to extract the configuration of the checkpoint file, and could lead to inaccuracies. If the read checkpoint is written by modular simulator, the modular simulator needs to populate the trx frame.

Affected versions: master and the 2021 betas only (modular checkpointing was introduced in summer 2020).

closed_issues.title: index mistakes in the output file of gmx hbond -hbn
closed_issues.description:
I find mistakes in the output file of gmx hbond -hbn when I run a simulation where I want to know the hydrogen bonds between 2 kinds of moleculars, H2O and glycerol.

The command I use to analyze the hydrogen bonds is:

_echo 0 1 | gmx hbond -f frame10.gro -s md_1.tpr -n traj0.ndx -a 20 -r 0.31 -hbn wg0.ndx_

Here is part of the index content of [ hbonds_water_glycerol ] in wg0.ndx:

-   44533  44534  25652
-   44533  **44534**  29978

By comparing the indexes and the ones in the frame10.gro file, it is easy to know that the order of the indexes above corresponds the order of donor-Hydrogen atom-acceptor. Firstly, although it may occurs that the same donor-Hydrogen atom forms 2 different hydrogen bonds with 2 acceptors (sometimes 3 in the file) due to the geometric criterion, I find too many of them. Secondly by calculating the angles of Hydrogen atom-donor-acceptor which demand <20°, I find the second line above should be: 44533  **44535**  29978(see the figure attached).

I use gromacs2018.4 to run the md and analyze the H-bonds, and similar issues can be found using gromacs5.0.7. The relevant files and the figure showing the angles I calculate manually are attached.

closed_issues.title: Format long function signatures with one argument per line
closed_issues.description:
Long function signatures are hard to read at any time, but generate a lot of noise when changed in merge requests. This makes code review more challenging, but also makes development harder.

It is more difficult to compare the function signature to the function call or to compare calls at different sites.

Collaborative development, even *efforts to remediate long call signatures through refactoring*, are more challenging because of needless merge conflicts.

My understanding is that we tried to normalize on a one-argument-per-line policy when switching to clang-format, but may have missed an option.

Proposal: set `BinPackArguments: false`

closed_issues.title: Kinetic energy and temperatures slightly off for md-vv Trotter NPT
closed_issues.description:
When using Nose-Hoover with md-vv (Trotter decomposition, legacy code path), the call sequence of the first half step looks something like
1. calculate forces at time t
1. propagate velocities v(t-dt/2) → v(t) & constrain
1. compute globals - calculate kinetic energy at time t
1. propagate Nose-Hoover chain degrees of freedom using Ekin at time t
1. scale velocities and Ekin according to Nose-Hoover chain
1. print x/v/f, store Ekin / T for output later in the step

This is followed by the second half step and the energy output.

Step 5. was guarded by `if (inputrecNvtTrotter(ir) && ir->eI == eiVV)`, which is only true when doing NVT (no pressure coupling), not when doing NPT. This is the same problem as in #3796, Bug 1 - the meaning of the function changed, but this wasn't fixed in all places.

This means that KE and Temperature were very slightly off since GROMACS 4.6. The difference is unlikely to have been significant for any application except for rigorous algorithm validation.

closed_issues.title: Nose-Hoover conserved energy is incorrect for non-integer ndof
closed_issues.description:
When using Nose-Hoover thermostat, the number of degrees of freedom in temperature groups are casted to integer when calculating the conserved energy. In the original implementation, the number of degrees of freedom was used as `real`, but the variable type was changed to `int` during refactoring in f2854f89.

Somewhat related to #3796.

closed_issues.title: gmx density scales output according to last frame/crashes with certain combination of switches for unknow reason
closed_issues.description:
GROMACS version: 2020.1 among others
GROMACS modification: No

When calculating the density profile across the box axis for lipid bilayer simulations, I noticed that gmx density scales the output to the dimension of the last frame. This poses a problem eg. when one wants to Fourier transform the electron density from NPT simulation to compare with scattering experiments. Something like an average box dimension or max box dimension would make more sense for the axis scaling, and is also what I would expect based on the documentation. I created two 2-frame trajectories with the frames (numbers 2 and 31 from another trajectory, attached) in opposite orderings to demonstrate:

gmx density -f frames31_2.trr -s …/prod.tpr -ei electrons.dat -dens electron -o electronDENSITYsys31_2.xvg -xvg none -sl 100

[antila@hot nocentered]$ tail -n 3 electronDENSITYsys31_2.xvg
6.47416 327.088
6.54056 310.069
6.60696 368.365

gmx density -f frames2_31.trr -s …/prod.tpr -ei electrons.dat -dens electron -o electronDENSITYsys2_31.xvg -xvg none -sl 100

[antila@hot nocentered]$ tail -n 3 electronDENSITYsys2_31.xvg
6.95413 327.088
7.02545 310.069
7.09678 368.365

While going down this rabbit hole I also noticed that the 2020.1 gromacs (and some others) crash on random frames of the trajectory depending on the set of switches and number of bins (even vs uneven). This perhaps signals some general issue with the binning when an atom is at a bin boundary etc?

Here is a case where I get a crash:

echo 0 | gmx density -f frame2.gro -s ../prod.tpr -ei electrons.dat -dens electron -o electronDENSITYsys.xvg -xvg none -sl 101

Frame31 (attached) runs perfectly. Changing the bin number to 100, turning on -center also prevents the crash.

closed_issues.title: NB-LIB should add compiler flags only after checking them
closed_issues.description:
While testing the portability of GROMACS 2021, in `api/nblib/samples/tests/CMakeLists.txt` I find

```
set_source_files_properties(samples.cpp PROPERTIES COMPILE_FLAGS "-Wno-header-hygiene")
```

GROMACS must compile cleanly on all supported compilers, and this compiler option is not supported e.g. by icpc 19.2. NB-LIB should check whether compiler options are recognized by the compiler before conditionally using them, as GROMACS does. It is preferable to do this by trying a compilation, as GROMACS does, rather than trying to list compilers and/or versions.

closed_issues.title: Functionality to deprecate before GROMACS 2021 is released
closed_issues.description:
We prefer to deprecate something before we remove it, so that users have time to adapt, plan, and perhaps discuss with the developers.

Note that deprecate does not mean "remove immediately." We're announcing deprecation so that the developers have the option to remove it without unduly surprising the users, and users may have an opportunity to discuss the deprecation before removal happens. It has often been the case that deprecated functionality is not removed for some years after, though this is not a general promise.

Suggested functionality to deprecate
- legacy SIMD architectures (Power 7 ie impl_arch_vmx (see discussion at https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/870), impl_arch_neon (not impl_arch_neon_asimd), impl_x86_mic)
- MIC support (KNC is no longer used in HPC; KNL will remain working even when MIC is removed)
- mdrun-only build #3808 
- OpenCL (but we leave pulling it out until we've got something running on both Intel and AMD devices that seems good compared to OpenCL)
- hwloc 1.x
- legacy API (not just headers, see Eric's comment below)
- .pdo file reading in `gmx wham`

closed_issues.title: libz linked statically with GMX_BUILD_MDRUN_ONLY=ON
closed_issues.description:
Under Linux, the default linking behavior of libz has changed between 2021-beta1 and -beta2.

beta1 and earlier versions: `-DGMX_EXTERNAL_ZLIB=ON` and `-DGMX_EXTERNAL_ZLIB=ON -DGMX_BUILD_MDRUN_ONLY=ON` both link to the shared library libz.so.

beta2: `-DGMX_EXTERNAL_ZLIB=ON` links to the shared library, but `-DGMX_EXTERNAL_ZLIB=ON -DGMX_BUILD_MDRUN_ONLY=ON` links statically to libz.a.

This can be worked around with an additional manual setting of `GMX_PREFER_STATIC_LIBS=OFF`, but it's a bit of a change in behavior, and the older behavior (shared linking to system libraries when possible) remains documented as the default in `INSTALL` under "Static linking".

closed_issues.title: Trotter decomposition NPT conserved energy is incorrect
closed_issues.description:
The MTTK (NPT Trotter decomposition) conserved energy is incorrect. My current understanding is that they were initially implemented correctly, but bugs have crept in with subsequent changes. Both bugs only affect the conserved energy and do not influence the dynamics.

**Bug 1: MTTK lacks system NHC integral**

MTTK uses separate Nose-Hoover chains to couple the different temperature groups (system chains), plus one to couple the barostat. The integral of the system chains is only calculated in the Trotter NVT case, but not in the NPT case. The system chains integral is only calculated if `inputrecNvtTrotter(ir)`. This function used to be a macro called `IR_NVT_TROTTER(ir)`. The bug was introduced in c7a82654f2eb8992067079c3196f59d69e3f95f6 , when the macros `IR_NPT_TROTTER(ir)` and `IR_NVT_TROTTER(ir)` in `legacyheaders/types/inputrec.h` were changed from meaning "has Trotter pressure coupling" and "has Trotter temperature coupling", respectively, to "is Trotter NPT" and "is Trotter NVT". In other words, `IR_NVT_TROTTER(ir)` was true in the NPT case before the change, but not anymore after.

Versions affected: 4.6 and later

**Bug 2: MTTK NHC integral formula**

The contribution to the conserved energy from the momenta of Nose-Hoover chain degrees of freedom is $`\sum_{k}\frac{p^{2}_{\eta k}}{2 Q_{k}} = \sum_{k}\frac{1}{2}Q_{k}v^{2}_{\eta k}`$ (see, e.g., eq. (5.4) in Tuckerman et al 2006, http://dx.doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/39/19/S18). In GROMACS, the single thermostat contributions are written as `0.5*gmx::square(ivxi[j])/iQinv[j]`. In f2854f89deb479835c02855e107bbe03b16e98b9, this was refactored to `0.5*gmx::square(state->nhpres_vxi[i*nh + j]/iQinv)` for the barostat chain only, erroneously squaring the masses.

Versions affected: 2018 and later

closed_issues.title: MdrunIOTests segfault
closed_issues.description:
MdrunIOTests tend to SegFault occasionally. The issue was especially common for me on `intel-gpu01` and Puhti. Even no-GPU no-SIMD builds are affected.

**Why the bug happens**

In Modular Simulator, we wish to have two copies of `ComputeGlobalsElement<ComputeGlobalsAlgorithm::VelocityVerlet>`. To avoid making two separate objects, a `static thread_local` singleton was introduced. Then:

1. The first test in MdrunIOtest creates a new VV integrator Element, stores the pointer to it in a static variable, and returns std::unique_ptr to it.
1. Test ends, all the objects, including our Element, are destroyed. But the static value lives.
1. One of the next tests creates another element **at the same memory location**.
1. When getElementPointerImpl of VV integrator Element is created again, it finds out that the pointer stored in its static variable is already known to the builder, and, none the wiser, happily returns it.
1. We try to call a virtual function on the object of the wrong type.
1. Boom!

**Expected damage**

Unlikely to affect end-users, except for failing `make check`, because the bug is triggered by repeatedly constructing `ModularSimulatorAlgorithm`. Besides `MdrunIOTests`, it can also be the reason for `MdrunNonIntegratorTests` crashes -- while the integrator is not used there, it is constructed, and the crash happens inside `ModularSimulatorAlgorithmBuilder::build`, when attaching topology to topology holders.

closed_issues.title: manage CI containers better
closed_issues.description:
DockerHub limits pulls to 100/hour for non-authenticated users, or 200/hour for authenticated users. We are experiencing behavior consistent with being limited (`ERROR: Job failed (system failure): prepare environment: image pull failed: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Error response from daemon: toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. You may increase the limit by authenticating and upgrading: https://www.docker.com/increase-rate-limit. Check https://docs.gitlab.com/runner/shells/index.html#shell-profile-loading for more information`). This is not surprising given that our CI workflows pull dozens of images per pipeline. Caching in the k8s runner reduces bandwidth, but doesn't help with limiting because DockerHub counts checks of the manifest, not downloads of blobs. (See https://www.docker.com/blog/scaling-docker-to-serve-millions-more-developers-network-egress/)

Tasks
- [ ] Authenticate e.g. as gromacs during CI jobs before pulling (if we are not doing it already)
- [ ] Apply to DockerHub for special consideration as an open source project (see above link, and https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd11DjfgeaKSRdqp6Br85MzQQuM4igt-xmn6rmzA2StFGLndQ/viewform). If we get more access, we'll surely need to authenticate, so we should do that first.

closed_issues.title: [Feature Requests][gmxapi][Python] Access to the simulation loop through Python gmxapi
closed_issues.description: There is access to the simulation loop in Python's gmxapi ? So, you can modify it, e.g. get access to the calculated forces, make some statistics and pass it an external function, and repeat.

closed_issues.title: Help clients find MPI-enabled GROMACS
closed_issues.description:
Client CMake scripts have to take unconventional steps to find MPI-enabled GROMACS.

Currently, MPI-enabled GROMACS is found by defining `GROMACS_SUFFIX` before performing `find_package()`.

Modern CMake allows us to search for "components" or provide other constraints on the features of a package we search for, so we have several options to update the semantics of `find_package(GROMACS...)`.

There does not appear to be any fall-back logic to allow `find_package(GROMACS)` to simply return any GROMACS installation found.

closed_issues.title: Sensibly serve CMake clients of MPI-aware Gromacs::gmxapi
closed_issues.description:
Follow-up from "Tell gmxapi to look for MPI, when appropriate."

@eirrgang started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/775#note_438834720): 

> The choice of `PUBLIC` was probably inappropriate.
      I don't think we want to require the MPI dependencies for all code.
      We should follow up on how best to address this.

We need to do one or more of the following.

- [X] Make this `target_link_libraries` `PRIVATE`.
- [ ] Provide more CMake support to help clients build.
- [ ] Provide optional mechanisms for getting MPI compatibility info.

closed_issues.title: MTS with SD integrator gives wrong temperature
closed_issues.description: Using multiple time stepping with the sd integrator results in too high temperature (in some systems). This might have to do with the different velocity update scheme. A quick-fix would be to disable this combination (for 2021), but since FE calculations (for which the sd integrator is recommended) is a common use-case it should preferably not be postponed too long.

closed_issues.title: Converge on gmxapi Context as the only way to manage running a simulation
closed_issues.description:
There are currently three ways to manage running a simulation within the current source:

* by invoking a `gmxapi::Workflow` on a `gmxapi::Context`
* by calling `gmx mdrun`
* by using `gmx::test::SimulationRunner` in the mdrun integration tests

There's noteworthy duplication between the first and both of the subsequent two. Having to consider all three use cases complicates #3688 because responsibility for initializing MPI libraries is handled in three places. Likewise #3768 needs similar changes in three places.

In the long term, we should use only one way to run a simulation. Simplest and most generalizable is to re-use the gmxapi implementation for the other two. That prepares for re-using some of the infrastructure currently used for testing to provide capabilities to the user also via the API.

Tasks have been identified to achieve this:

- [ ] Discuss with nblib any efforts to re-use or further de-duplicate
- [ ] Make `gmx::test::SimulationRunner` use a `gmxapi::Context` to run mdrun
- [ ] Identify an approach that lets `gmx::test::SimulationRunner` call grompp
- [ ] Make `gmx::test::SimulationRunner` use that approach to call grompp
- [ ] Understand whether the apparent need to broadcast `gmx` command-line arguments before invoking `gmx_mdrun` can be resolved within the approach of `gmxapi::Context`
- [ ] Have `gmx` infrastructure implement `gmx mdrun` by creating a `gmxapi::Context` and transforming the command-line arguments to a `gmxapi::Workflow`
- [ ] Move sole responsibility for MPI library initialization to `gmxapi::Context` (see also #3688)
- [ ] Eliminate any superseded infrastructure, e.g. `gmx::init()/finalize()`

closed_issues.description:

#4  0x00000000004816b3 in gmx::test::(anonymous namespace)::SimdMathTest_cbrt_Test::TestBody (this=0x5857b0) at [[...]]/src/gromacs/simd/tests/simd_math.cpp:652

The problem happens when [`frexp`](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/b6460d51b09e58108c8e8859f8db137dfa496407/src/gromacs/simd/impl_x86_avx_512/impl_x86_avx_512_simd_float.h#L297) is called from within `cbrt` with an argument containing `0`. `_mm512_getexp_ps` returns `-inf`, and `_mm512_cvtps_epi32` raises SIGFPE when trying to convert it to integer.

This is generally fine, because much later this value is ignored. But the FPE is raised, and the test is failed.

Not sure about the best way to solve this problem. Shall we add masked `frexp`?

Tagging @erik.lindahl as the author of the original code.

closed_issues.title: Manage lifetime of hardware detection better
closed_issues.description:
Currently `mdrunner()` detects hardware once, managing the lifetime with a file static pointer associated with a mutex so that other thread-MPI ranks skip the detection and just use the result. That also works fine for real MPI because nothing else in mdrun tries to detect hardware. That approach is a legacy of designing only for a command-line tool, many moons ago. It's serendipitously efficient for test binaries that perhaps want to loop over the GPUs and then call mdrun many times because the file static pointer remains valid until the binary exits; the multiple calls to the detection routine each time mdrun runs will do very little work.

However

* the destructor of that file static pointer called at process exit does bad things to current beta09/10 oneAPI, and
* API-driven simulations would also like to direct the use of a particular communicator, so that hardware detection should work within that, and then be able to be retained for future re-use for successive simulation sessions.

That means we want better lifetime management for the hardware detection result.

Andrey's attempt to fix the SYCL issue at !781 created further issues to resolve. I'd already started !739 to address the API case, so perhaps it is better to extracting the core of !739 to resolve the SYCL issue for release-2021, while preparing to have better control for API-driven simulations.

That will likely
* make MdrunnerBuilder a bit more ugly, but perhaps minimally if done by an `addHardwareDetectionResult` method that simply takes a const pointer for now, and can be improved later to take a deep copy (Edit: was done that way)
* pessimize quite a few test binaries that will now call hardware detection each time they invoke mdrun, unless we can find a way to pass such a handle up through both the call stacks from the `gmx` entry point *and* the test-binary setup code. (Edit: a way was found to pass the handle from test-binary setup through `gmx_mdrun` #3774 will resolve the issue properly)

closed_issues.title: Get rid of `gmx_release_hardware_handles` in release-2021
closed_issues.description:
In !781, a helper function `gmx_release_hardware_handles` is introduced to manually destroy `g_hardwareInfo` singleton.

This is needed for a combination of the following two reasons:

- This global object is destroyed at the end of process's lifetime, after returning from `main`.
- Destructors of `cl::sycl::device` segfault when called after the end of `main`, as of OneAPI 2021.1-beta10

Both limiting the lifetime of `gmx_hw_info_t` objects (as done in !730 and proposed for inclusion in the current `master` (to become release 2022), or fixing the Intel runtime should completely remove the need for this function.

This issue is the reminder to do just that.

closed_issues.title: StatePropagatorDataGpu cycles double-counted in several instances
closed_issues.description:
We are double-counting in some places due to nesting of `StatePropagatorDataGpu` counters in other cycle counters.

E.g. most of the `stateGpu->copy/wait` calls in md.cpp (see https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/gromacs/mdrun/md.cpp#L1264) are within the `ewcUPDATE` counter (see https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/gromacs/mdrun/md.cpp#L1208).

This is the reason why already in the 2020 release the cycle counter table can have the last entries missing (when the amount of time double-counted is relatively large), so ideally it would be good to fix in 2020 too.

closed_issues.title: Follow-up from "Clear constraints RMSD values upon domains reset"
closed_issues.description:
Constraints RMSD is not computed when using GPU update, which may lead to floating point exception. Current fix zeroes the values on each DD step to ensure that zero is returned for constraints RMSD values. Proper solution is needed.

The intended behaviour was to not report the RMSD values with GPU update. However, the CPU Constraints object is initialized unconditionally, which made some conditions false-positive and led to this bug.


The following discussion from !754 should be addressed:

- [ ] @acmnpv started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/754#note_434095471):  (+4 comments)

    > can this be handled differently instead of having to remember to zero out those elements by hand?

closed_issues.title: Incorrect initial histogram size in AWH
closed_issues.description:
The formula used for setting the initial histogram size in AWH uses a Gaussian geometry factor, taken from Metadynamics, and sums inverse crossing times. The Gaussian geometry factor is actually not relevant for AWH, so should be removed. For multiple dimensions we should sum the crossing times, not the inverse times.

For 1D this changes the initial histogram size by about a factor of 3, which doesn't affect the convergence much. For multiple dimensions with different covering times it might be affected more.

We don't want to change this behavior in a bug fix release, but we should fix this for the 2021 release.

closed_issues.title: COM pulling gives incorrect results with DD with weighting or with >32 DD ranks
closed_issues.description: The pull code uses local atom sets when using DD and global atom weights or when using more than 32 DD PP-ranks. closed_issues.title: Add function for Hadamard (element-wise) product of RVec
closed_issues.description:
The following discussion from !698 should be addressed:

- [ ] @rolandschulz started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_431388257):  (+9 comments)

    > ```suggestion:-0+2
    >                 vp -= prVelocityScalingMatrixDiagonal * v;
    > 
    > ```

Relevant comments (see [here for the full discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_431388257)):

- [ ] @mark.j.abraham [commented](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_432050895)

    > Using a c++ operator for a Hadamard product would be prone to misunderstandings

- [ ]  @rolandschulz [commented](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_432190354)

    > I would argue that
    > - if a scalar isn't implicitly convertible from a vector (the case for `RVec`) than this isn't prone to misunderstanding because the return type makes is clear
    > - these operations are so commonly used that it's not something hard to remember.
    > 
    > But I suppose we don't want to change this now. But even if we don't have the operator we should have a function. It is weird that we have `elementWiseMin` and `elementWiseMax` but not `elementWiseMul`. Potentially better than adding extra function would be to have a single:
    > ```cpp
    > template<typename VectorType, typename Op>
    > static inline VectorType elementWise(const VectorType& a, const VectorType& b, Op f)
    > {
    >     return { f(a[0], b[0]), f(a[1], b[1]), f(a[2], b[2]) };
    > }
    > ```
    > 
    > Than this line would be:
    > ```cpp
    > vp -= elementWise(prVelocityScalingMatrixDiagonal, v, std::multiplies());
    > ```

- [ ]   @artemzhmurov [commented](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_432741680)

    > I would vote for leaving it as is: It is only two extra lines of code and it is very clear what this code is doing.

- [ ]   @rolandschulz [commented](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/698#note_433051362)

    > I agree it is very clear what the code is doing. But the function is already very complex and with ~50 lines above what most consider ideal (e.g. https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Write_Short_Functions). I also agree that only removing 2 lines improves this very little but given that this could help in other places it is still a net plus for me. We often have too large functions. We need to get better at having more helper functions and/or break it into smaller parts if we want to improve that.

Related issues:

- #3312 Data type for coordinates, xyzq data, LJ parameters data to use for GPU buffers.
- #3611 vector (Rvec) - scalar multiplication - type restrictions
- #1017 C++ Vector/Matrix classes

closed_issues.title: Major difference between thread-MPI and OpenMPI versions of GROMACS-2020-RAMD
closed_issues.description:
We investigate a protein-drug complex trying to determine the average time for its dissociation. For this, we used GROMACS-2020.3-RAMD modification of GROMACS-2020.3 code that applies a random force to the ligand in a receptor-ligand complex. It aborts the run when the ligand detaches from the receptor. We have done several runs with the same magnitude of the force (ramd-force = 400) to collect good statistics. Each run was started from identical initial configuration with identical parameters except "ld-seed" and "ramd-seed" which had individual values. The quantity of interest was the run duration (that is the time needed for the complex dissociation).

We found that builds with thread-MPI and OpenMPI produce strikingly different results even if runned on the same computer. They are presented on the graph below. Each point is the run number (X) and its duration (Y). An Excel spreadsheet with the values, run input files, log and edr files are available here:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KjDtJ_RBvtOnluGWnJ1TUKXuN077pDvf/view?usp=sharing
The same situation is observed with force 250 and on other computers running GROMACS-2020.1-RAMD. We can provide more simulation files upon request.
Albeit we used the modified GROMACS version, the modifications in it are rather limited. Hence we suspect the problem may lie in the corresponding vanilla version.

The build options were:

Thread MPI build:
cmake .. -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$SOFT/gromacs-2020-ramd -DGMX_THREAD_MPI=ON -DFFTWF_INCLUDE_DIR=$SOFT/include -DFFTWF_LIBRARY=$SOFT/lib/libfftw3f.so -DGMX_OPENMP=ON -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++

OpenMPI (version 3.1.6) build:
cmake .. -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$SOFT/gromacs-2020-ramd-openmpi -DGMX_MPI=ON -DFFTWF_INCLUDE_DIR=$SOFT/include -DFFTWF_LIBRARY=$SOFT/lib/libfftw3f.so -DGMX_OPENMP=OFF -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=mpicc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=mpicxx -DGMX_SIMD=AVX_256

The version of GCC is 5.4.0, the version of FFTW is 3.3.3-sse2.

![times2](/uploads/64b32eede58a3db27d077c914cdffcc9/times2.png)

Specific issues to consider

* compilers might re-arrange to use FMA, which we should make explicit with `std::fma`
* computing angles with atan2 might be better for very small angles - but do we even care? only for FEP runs?
* angle and bond interactions involve differences from reference values that also can be very small - sometimes catastrophic cancellation might occur, so are there alternative forms we might evaluate or should we do the subtraction in double in some cases?
* PBC removal is different in SIMD and not - suggest we always use the approach of the SIMD and GPU module
* currently no tests on the GPU bondeds

closed_issues.title: CMake may find an unintended Python version.
closed_issues.description:
By default, `FindPython3` will find the most recent version of Python in all search locations. This means that the `Python3_ROOT_DIR` hint does not work on recent versions of CMake if `FindPython3` is able to find more recent versions than the hinted installation.

CMake 3.15 introduces the `Python3_FIND_STRATEGY` hint. When set to `LOCATION`, FindPython uses the *first* compatible Python installation (and `Python3_ROOT_DIR` is checked first.)

CMake 3.13 and 3.14 users can not direct FindPython to use a specific Python installation if CMake is able to find a more recent version, so standard path manipulations are the only mitigation.

closed_issues.title: Set required versions for GROMACS 2022
closed_issues.description:
For GROMACS 2022, specify minimum support versions of dependencies, tools, and interacting software. Document and confirm test coverage.

Remember that they start being relevant to users when we release in 2022.There is a trade-off between what new things we can do (because we support a smaller range of things) vs what things we might require some users to do (because GROMACS no longer builds out of the box for them). Your workload as a GROMACS developer goes up for each extra version we support, even if that only shows up in what you have to do to keep CI happy, or how hard it is for you to get access to others’ feedback because they are thinking about something that is mysteriously broken in some CI combination. Also, versions that may or may not be the bases for forks that support hardware that GROMACS users might have that isn’t already shipping in early 2022 really shouldn’t factor highly.

## CMake
We have previously generally adopted the minimum version of the latest Ubuntu LTS 20.04, which is cmake 3.16.3. We decided to adopt that as the minimum. Perhaps some find modules from more recent CMake versions could be back ported if there was enough need for someone to do the work.

## Compilers
Minimum supported versions are currently implied by the requirement for C++17 support

### gcc
We require 7, no need to change

### clang
No need to change

## msvc
We require 19.15 (ie Visual Studio 2017), no need to change.

### icc
Remove support, Intel's direction seems to be focussed on icpx. Any benefits from better codegen from icc have to be weighed against the problems and workarounds we've introduced to our codebase to keep it happy.

### icpx
See below for SYCL

### xlc
Not supported because not conformant

### pgi
Ignore it, it's basically been rebranded as the Nvidia hpc c++ compiler.

### cray
Has no release with C++17 support

## CUDA

Currently we require 9.0 (for C++14 compatibility.) For approx CUDA release dates, see https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit-archive

* CUDA 10.0 (released Sep 2018) is the first to support graphs.
* CUDA 11.0 (released May 2020) is the first with C++17 support. (Currently gmx host-side code is restricted to C++14, which has caused minor inconveniences and inconsistencies.) It no longer supports the SM 3.0 (ie.) earlier members of the Kepler generation, but the server-grade K20/40/80 hardware still work, albeit their SM versions are deprecated.
* clang officially supports up to cuda 10.1 (though in practice gmx code probably works anyway)

Generally we have supported two major versions at the time of release, so choosing 11.0 as minimum would likely mean we also support 12.0 when GROMACS 2020 is released.

Decision: Move forward to CUDA 11.0 as minimum requirement for the improved C++17 compatibility permitting some simplification of common GPU code sometimes compiled with CUDA.

## SYCL

We'll require SYCL2020 and suggest latest available compilers. We'll defer until later in the year any question of minimum required versions for dpcpp/icpx, hipSYCL, etc. These are all changing rapidly so a decision now would be premature.

## OpenCL
As OpenCL support is deprecated, the version requirement will not change

## MPI

2\.0 is suggested at #3591 (actually 2.0 is already implicitly required by the use of `MPI_THREAD_FUNNELED`)

## Python interpreter

Python 3.7 is [now final](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0537/#schedule-security-binary-release).
Python 3.6 will receive security fixes only until [December of 2021](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0494/#id28).

The gmxapi package would benefit from an update to the required version immediately (#3716). The overall project infrastructure does not have particularly compelling need to update other than, perhaps to reduce CI image size or tested software permutations.

Decision: 3.7 is the minimum required version, but we'll aim to test others

## Documentation

### Doxygen

Some enthusiasm for updating to e.g. Ubuntu LTS version 18.17. But it would need some volunteers to hack together to fix all the new warnings. That might be easier if we'd already dropped the use of the Doxygen XML output for include sorting and module dependency checking.

### Sphinx

No new features are needed. @acmnpv pointed out that the CMake version check is intended only as a minimum version, not a required version. @eirrgang will propose an update to the version check to try to address some spurious errors.

### GoogleTest

v1.10.0 is out (and latest) and finally now requires a conformant C++11 compiler. That probably simplifies life for the compiler that compiles GROMACS. Mark will update.

## Source code checking and other infrastructure

clang-format (currently 7) and clang-tidy (currently 9) may warrant coordinated clang infrastructure versioning as clangd becomes more useful and widespread. Updating to at least version 11 would help reduce future mismatch between e.g. IDE versions of clangd and our CI infra. The same `.clang-format` file can produce different results with different version of the tool.

closed_issues.title: GPU force buffer ops, reduction and comms on virial steps
closed_issues.description:
- Currently, Force buffer ops, force reduction and halo exchange fall back to CPU on virial steps. PME-PP comms are still active, but go from PME GPU to PP CPU.
- Virial steps are irregular, so there is insignificant overall performance benefit to having GPU force buffer ops, reduction and comms on virial steps.
- But code quality improvements related to reduced complexity of conditionals in do_force()/do_md() could be possible, due to more uniformity across steps.

	
- GPU force Buffer ops on virial steps are relatively straightforward, but don't offer much improvement on their own
     - see patch at https://gerrit.gromacs.org/c/gromacs/+/15960


- GPU force reduction on virial steps is much more complex
     - On non-virial steps, there is only one active force buffer and this is reduced with both the NB and PME forces.
     - On virial steps, there exist 2 separate force buffers forceOut.forceWithShiftForces().force() and forceOut.forceWithVirial().force_. The former is reduced with the NB force, and the latter with the PME force.
     - We currently have no concept of a second force buffer in the Stata Propagator or the GPU force reduction, and no concept of these distinct reductions.
     - It seems that the additional complexity associated with introducing this would outweigh any reduced complexity in conditionals from having the GPU codepaths active on virial steps.
		

- GPU force halo exchange on virial steps is relatively straightforward, but not clear there is any benefit to this without GPU force reduction.

		
- My feeling is that the simplest solution is to keep force buffer ops, reductions and halo exchange on CPU for virial steps, as we have at the moment.

closed_issues.description:
The implementation of transformation pull coordinates (pulling/pull.cpp) uses a hard coded epsilon for numerical derivatives. Since an optimal choice of epsilon probably depends on the variables as well as the mathematical expression, this value should be configurable by the user.

closed_issues.title: Revisit use of MDAtoms in modular simulator
closed_issues.description:
The use of the MDAtoms provided by the runner / LegacySimulatorData in modular simulator is bug-prone.

In the current implementation, it is written to by the TopologyHolder (non-DD cases, at build time only) or DomDecHelper (after every DD distribution). These set the masses to their lambda=0 value (within mdAlgorithmsSetupAtomData). FreeEnergyPerturbationData is setting the masses within MDAtoms to their actual, lambda-dependent value. This requires that FreeEnergyPerturbationData reacts to domain decomposition to reset the masses to their actual value, even if lambda is constant over the course of the simulation.

This is currently solved by having DomDecHelper prompting FreeEnergyPerturbationData for an update. This should be revisited to find a more elegant approach.

Note that in the legacy simulator, the problem is avoided by calling the function updating mdAtoms every step. A possible solution could involve fixing mdAlgorithmsSetupAtomData to be aware of the mass lambda state, avoiding the need for a follow-up call to fix the wrong masses introduced by mdAlgorithmsSetupAtomData.

    > This is still a bad idea, creating a circular dependency between thread MPI, and GROMACS to suit a downstream project who might stop using it any time.
    > 
    > There's several alternatives, dependending where one wants to consider having the configuration point, and how much run time overhead might be acceptable.

I eventually adopted the solution that creates the above-mentioned coupling, but we should remove it and simultaneously resolve other excessive uses of the GROMACS `config.h` (e.g. to set `TMPI_WAIT_FOR_NO_ONE`). tMPI has the notion of `tmpi_config.h` so we should use it. closed_issues.title: OpenCL kernel caching triggers assert in mdrun-tests
closed_issues.description:
While trying to enable the OpenCL kernel caching, I ran into the following assert on current master HEAD

`Source file: src/gromacs/nbnxm/opencl/nbnxm_ocl.cpp (line 386)
Function:    Nbnxm::select_nbnxn_kernel(NbnxmGpu*, int, int, bool, bool)::<lambda()>

Assertion failed:
Condition: cl_error == 0
clCreateKernel failed: CL_INVALID_KERNEL_NAME
`

Note (Szilard):
The (main) reason is that, unlike in CUDA where we generate all combinations of LJ/electrostatics at compile-time (see src/gromacs/nbnxm/cuda/nbnxm_cuda_kernels.cuh), in OpenCL we only obtain the kernel flavors required by the run. To be able to reuse binary caches across runs (e.g. tests) that require different kernel flavors we'd need a "non-FASTGEN" top-level generator that does essentially what the CUDA counterpart.

closed_issues.title: Replace GMX_ASSERT with assert in the gromacs public API
closed_issues.description: A regular assert is the correct tool in the public API, where currently GMX_ASSERT is used. The macro GMX_ASSERT has the same compilation dependence on `NDEBUG` as `assert` from `<cassert>`, so there is no difference there. Additionally, `assert` only depends on headers that any C++ implementation must have defined, while GMX_ASSERT depends on `current_functoion.h` to get information about where the asserted-upon call occurred. Such information is generally now provided by compilers. The main roadblock for this issue is that many files have transient dependencies on files also included in `gmxassert.h`, but it is good to unwind these anyway.

closed_issues.title: Update 2022 CMake infrastructure for MPI.
closed_issues.description:
`gmxManageMPI.cmake` can be reworked to make better use of updates to the built-in `FindMPI.cmake`.

Importantly, we can improve support for MPI-enabled client builds.

We should rely more heavily on the inputs and outputs of https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.13/module/FindMPI.html and derive FindMPI input variables that we can provide to client packages through our CMake import machinery.

# Further considerations

A key issue is that `CMAKE_<lang>_COMPILER` is set by the time a language is enabled by the `project()` command. After that, it is too late to adjust the main compiler in response to imported targets. We can only generate messages.

The current provided tool (`function (gromacs_check_compiler LANG)` in `gromacs-config.cmake`) does not provide or link to sufficient information to resolve the issue it reports, and does not check the full MPI tool chain.

We previously tried to improve the help provided to client packages by providing a "toolchain" file that client packages could use to get the right compilers set, but
* the toolchain file does not carry sufficient information to ensure a compatible MPI compiler wrapper, and
* using a toolchain file forces "cross-compilation".

Cross-compilation help can be useful if GROMACS itself is being cross-compiled, but is not the primary use case we were attempting to address, and forcing the CMake cross-compilation path is not really what we want.

One possibility may be to specify `NONE` for the client project language, then using [enable_language](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.13/command/enable_language.html) _after_ importing the GROMACS target and setting `CMAKE_<lang>_COMPILER` with hints from GROMACS.

It may be appropriate to decouple the search for MPI from the value of `GMX_MPI`. There are various reasons that tMPI GROMACS builds may be run in MPI environments or linked from MPI-enabled client code. If we can detect MPI, it is useful to run a few additional tests for MPI-enabled client code on tMPI GROMACS builds.

# Update (14 September 2021)

`gmxManageMPI` now centralizes a single call to `find_package(MPI COMPONENTS ...)` with additional checks for the requirements of individual software components. Some of the legacy handling has been remediated, but there are still some global compiler/linker details that get passed around instead of just linking individual targets to `MPI::CXX`, etc. (See also #3288).

Before closing the current issue, we should review what remains to be done to limit the scope of MPI dependencies while using modern CMake facilities for transitive requirements to make sure that the right code gets built the right way. (The remaining "to do" items will likely become a separate follow-up issue.)

closed_issues.title: multi-sim hardware assignment broken

closed_issues.title: Update header inclusion order policy and enforcement
closed_issues.description:
Our includesorter script is a maintenance burden, and does not correctly apply our documented header order policy.

We should cut our infrastructure overhead by switching to a popular third-party tool like clang-format for include order maintenance and reconcile our policy to something that can be enforced with such a tool.

It should be possible to implement something like our current file-inclusion blocks with IncludeBlocks and IncludeCategory regexes. See https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormatStyleOptions.html

closed_issues.title: Enforce change of behavior of ReadCheckpointDataHolder between checkpoint reading and state restoring
closed_issues.description:
- @eirrgang started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/440#note_406673832):  (+2 comments)

    > It took me a while to understand the significance of the `const` here relative to the various usages, especially when passing ownership via unique_ptr.
    > 
    > Let me see if I've got it:
    > 
    > I think what happens is that
    > * data providers have non-const access to put data into ReadCheckpointDataHolder, whereas it is appropriate for consumers to use const access to read the data. However, copy semantics are not specified, so it is unclear whether a const ReadCheckpointDataHolder can/should be converted to a non-const copy.
    > * You want to establish at the interface that the constructor is receiving an immutable object, but taking ownership, and neither const-ref nor rvalue semantics, so you are using unique_ptr to convey this, rather than to reduce exposure of the ReadCheckpointDataHolder type. However, this is a private interface, and such details are only part of the relationship between the ModularSimulator builder. R-value semantics seem appropriate.
    > 
    > Please clarify with explicit copy semantics and/or documentation of the behavioral protocol / call sequence.
    > 
    > Does the consumer need to consider the `const ReadCheckpointDataHolder` mutable? Or do we guarantee that it is fully populated before being acquired by ModularSimulator? Can this policy be expressed more strongly in the future? The client (ModularSimulator) could hold either an explicitly immutable (logically const) type, rather than a const-qualified version, or a std::future or other conventional data provider pattern. The provider could operate on a CheckpointDataBuilder, issue a future, etc.
    > 
    > In the mean time, can we add clarity through the variable names? Here, maybe `checkpointDataSource_`. At the provider, maybe `checkpointDataTarget` or `publishedCheckpointData`.

- Comment by @ptmerz:
    > You got this right. However, thinking about this a bit more, this was rather *observing* what was happening than *enforcing* a specific behavior. I think that there are too many moving pieces yet to really enforce such a policy. In combination with actually passing the unique_ptr into the consuming object (the `CheckpointHelperBuilder`), I have removed the `const`-ness. I think this can be revisited when input reading and simulator builder have evolved a bit more and we have a better feeling for what restrictions should be imposed.

See also comment in simulatorbuilder.h, SimulatorBuilder::add(std::unique_ptr<ReadCheckpointDataHolder> modularSimulatorCheckpointData).

I have attached tpr file which has such a problem, it has been built with Gromacs 2020.2, the system is quiet big, but usually it crashes within 100-200 steps.

closed_issues.title: Refine SimulationInput
closed_issues.description:
This umbrella issue describes work planned under the https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues?label_name%5B%5D=simulation-input label in the GROMACS 2022 development cycle.

GROMACS 2021 introduces `gmx::SimulationInput` as an abstract way to reference data sources for initializing the simulator state. Some utility functions have been proposed, but not yet implemented, because more work is needed both on implementation and on design aspects of how SimulationInput will be used.

- [ ] Implement the utility functions described in #3374.
- [ ] Replace `gmxapi::System` usage with SimulationInput and remove `gmxapi::System` (#4467)
- [ ] Refine the specification of SimulationInput constituent data. (What should be added to/removed from SimulationInput? Does it encapsulate a well-defined set of data, or is it a Facade for a big composition of data sources?)
- [ ] Modularize ownership of the `-s` and `-cpi` `gmx::internal::OptionSectionImpl::optionMap_` entries.
- [ ] Decouple SimulationInput from details of file-based input sources. (Suggest reading files once and capturing deserialization streams.)
- [ ] Manage distributed state. Maintain and improve data locality optimizations.
- [ ] Refine creation method for SimulationInput objects.
- [ ] Refine the path for creating SimulationInput from simulation output (e.g. Simulator object or Simulator client scope objects). #3439 
- [ ] Apply SimulationInput directly to consumers (or appropriate management facilities for constituent data), instead of storing intermediate data structures at `apply...` call sites.
- [ ] Use SimulationInput for utilities (and analysis tools) that currently rely on TPR and/or CPT files.

closed_issues.title: Improving Energy Minimization accuracy with stepsize changes.
closed_issues.description:
While looking through the code concerning energy minimization, I discovered a part of the code which I thought could bear improving in order to increase the accuracy of the energy minimums as well as the force distribution. In particular, I believe the portion of the code in question is responsible for setting the initial step size in nm for the energy minimization process. The code is on line 2904 and reads as 

```
ustep = inputrec->em_stepsize;
stepsize = 0;
```
I decided to change the stepsize variable here to see if it had a difference in the energy minimization process. 

My first finding was that the integer that gave me the biggest improvement in energy minimum and force reduction was 4. Any value above or below 4 would result in worse results and in some cases no notable improvement. 

Then, I tested this modified variable on several different molecules and proteins of various sizes, shapes, and functions to see whether or not this change actually consistently improved the energy minimization process. 

I have included the spreadsheet in which I tabulated my results below, but in short, I recorded a significant 0.5% decrease in the final energy minimum, close to a 6% decrease in maximum force, and a 8.6% decrease in the norm of force. Thus, I propose changing this variable to 3 in the source code in order to get better energy minimums and better force distribution. [GROMACS_Results.xlsx](/uploads/f67f91e17bf481a46ce76135348b5c20/GROMACS_Results.xlsx)

closed_issues.title: Finish MDModule Notifier pattern.
closed_issues.description:
The following discussion from !348 should be addressed:

- [ ] @eirrgang started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/348#note_398980856):  (+3 comments)

    > We want to unsubscribe before the call-back becomes invalid.

The collaboration by which the call-back remains safe is not well documented or enforced, but currently involves at least four objects.

Usually, design patterns like this exist to confine the collaboration to two objects. A Publisher-Subscriber pattern like this one uses the Notifier intermediary to limit the collaboration to two objects even when there are multiple senders and multiple consumers. In the absence of some other reference counting, the common behavioral protocol is that a `subscribe()` must be followed by an `unsubscribe()` so that the program state is verifiable and the notifier knows that the call-back is still safe. If the Notifier cannot wait for expected `unsubscribe()`s, it should log an error if it has not received all of the expected `unsubscribe()`s when it shuts down so that it is clear either where developer assumptions have been violated or to help identify the scope of other errors (asserts or exceptions would be inappropriate). The Notifier guarantees that there is a way to `unsubscribe()` (i.e. without seg-faulting).

closed_issues.title: thread-MPI + CUDA with GPU direct communication & update fails with memory error in LINCS
closed_issues.description:
A colleague encountered a test case using gromacs 2020.3 with thread-MPI + CUDA.  The case runs OK when updates are on the CPU, but the job fails after varying numbers of steps when updates are on the GPU.  When a job fails, the error text is

```
Program:     gmx mdrun, version 2020.3
Source file: src/gromacs/gpu_utils/devicebuffer.cuh (line 134)
Function:    copyToDeviceBuffer(ValueType**, const ValueType*, size_t, size_t, CommandStream, GpuApiCallBehavior, CommandEvent*)::<lambda()> [with ValueType = int]
MPI rank:    1 (out of 6)

Assertion failed:
Condition: stat == cudaSuccess
Synchronous H2D copy failed
```

The code runs OK for several thousand steps (variable in number), then aborts with the message above.  If I set env variable CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1, the code runs a lot longer ... typically several hundred thousand steps, or up to a million steps or more, but eventually will fail with the same signature.  No errors are reported when updates are left on the CPU using either thread-MPI or a multi-node build using IBM Spectrum MPI.  The target system is Summit at Oak Ridge National Labs, where the nodes have six NVIDIA V100 GPUs connected via NVLINK.  The marked sensitivity to CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING suggests some kind of race condition.  If I put in alternative error checking for the same source line, the CUDA runtime reports

Error invalid argument at `gromacs-2020.3/src/gromacs/gpu_utils/devicebuffer.cuh` line 134

A core file is generated, and gdb reports the call stack

```
1  0x00007fff7f16f4e0 in gmx::internal::printFatalErrorHeader(_IO_FILE*, char const*, char const*, char const*, int) ()
2  0x00007fff7f17f6d0 in gmx::internal::assertHandler(char const*, char const*, char const*, char const*, int) ()
3  0x00007fff7f13ea60 in void freeDeviceBuffer<int2*>(int2**)::{lambda()#1}::operator()() const [clone .isra.30] ()
4  0x00007fff7fbb89b4 in gmx::LincsCuda::set(t_idef const&, t_mdatoms const&) () 
5  0x00007fff7fbbf4dc in gmx::UpdateConstrainCuda::Impl::set(float*, float*, float*, t_idef const&, t_mdatoms const&, int) ()
6  0x00007fff7fbbf8fc in gmx::UpdateConstrainCuda::set(float*, float*, float*, t_idef const&, t_mdatoms const&, int) ()
7  0x00007fff7f9c31a0 in gmx::LegacySimulator::do_md() () 
8  0x00007fff7f9c0720 in gmx::LegacySimulator::run() () 
9  0x00007fff7f9fa1b4 in gmx::Mdrunner::mdrunner() () 
10 0x00007fff7f9fcb14 in gmx::mdrunner_start_fn(void const*) () 
11 0x00007fff7fc3b020 in tMPI_Thread_starter () 
12 0x00007fff7fc2a730 in tMPI_Thread_starter(void*) ()
```

This issue is not blocking the research project because we can suffer a minor performance hit and run the simulation with updates on the CPU.  However, a robust implementation with updates on GPU is desirable because there is a performance advantage.  A copy of the test case is currently on the Summit system and can be shared.

closed_issues.title: Allow MPI communicator to be provided by client.
closed_issues.description:
This task is essentially to finish GMX11 from #2585: i.e. allow client software to use MPI at a high level whether or not libgromacs is built for MPI parallelism.

The client is then able to provide the library with a sub-communicator, restricting a given SimulationContext to a subset of the run time MPI ranks. For example: allow a trajectory ensemble to be managed by client code, in which 8 simulations each run on 4 nodes in a 32-node HPC job.

The MPI communicator is already provided to Mdrunner via the SimulationContext. We will extend the MpiContextManager RAII helper to provide scoped access to an appropriate communicator.

However, there are implicitly two versions of SimulationContext, depending on whether gmxmpi.h references an MPI implementation or tMPI. (In the latter case, the communications have not been initialized at the time that SimulationContext has been initialized, but we defer reevaluation of these semantics to followup issues.)
Importantly, the creator of the SimulationContext may be exposed both to tMPI GROMACS internals and an MPI implementation in the client environment.

To reconcile this, we reaffirm that tMPI is an internal detail, and provide some translation layering to insulate client-provided `MPI_Comm` from translation units that might have tMPI symbols.

Also ref #2395 and #3307

(Discussed for a while, but reaffirmed for the 2021 release roadmap at planning meeting in August 2020 as a deliverable for 2021 release.)

# Tasks

1. !474 Describe the design and provide the public headers.
2. !605 Move the MpiContextManager instance from "Session" to "Context" scope.
3. !606 Give MpiContextManager the additional responsibility of providing the communicator for the SimulationContext.
4. !606 Allow MPI-enabled clients to provide a communicator to MPI-enabled GROMACS.
5. !607 Allow the new interface to support MPI-enabled clients for both tMPI and MPI GROMACS as abstractly as possible.

# Follow-up

#3650 
#3688 

# Deferred

Future work can further decouple the multisim code from the libgromacs internals, since Mdrunner can be sensibly simplified by separating concerns regarding concurrently executing simulations.

closed_issues.description:
(gmx, version 2020.3 compiled on MAC, no modifications of source)

The nature of this issue is related to [2954](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/295)

I am curious if there is any development on these issues.
It would be very useful,  to retain the "original residue numbering" and additionally "Chain naming", to be compatible with any downstream analysis that needs specifying residue and chain numbers.

-----------

I was working with getting interaction energies between specific residue groups in a protein complex. However, with the residue renumbering by gromacs, it is very difficult and laborious to accurately make index and select the required residue groups.

Specifically I found that the following two issues are making manual or programatic changing of residue numbers or chain names difficult.

ISSUE-1:
==========

when I ran genion on solvated structure, there was a gap introduced in residue numbering. 

See the jump from residue number 433 to 435 after running genion. 
The structure after solvation (solvated.pdb) has GLU-433 followed by SER-434, but after 
running genion (ionized.pdb) GLU-433 is followed by SER-435! (see figure: solvated_structure.png vs after_genion.png )

I am thinking this maby be a bug.

ISSUE-2:
==========

Another issue is with Chain names. Chain names get changes during genion.
Residue G39 which had chain name as "A" is changed to "B"
(see solvated_structure_2.png vs after_genion_2.png or the files solvated.pdb vs ionized.pdb)



---------------------------


These are my sequence of commands to reproduce these issues: 

1. gmx pdb2gmx -ignh -f protein.pdb -ff charmm27 -water tip3p -o conf.pdb -p topol.top -nochargegrp
                  # I renamed this first topology output as "initial_topol.top" for easy reference

2. gmx editconf -f complex.pdb -o boxed.pdb -bt dodecahedron -d 1.0

3. gmx solvate -cp boxed.pdb -cs spc216.gro -p topol.top -o solvated.pdb

4. gmx make_ndx -f solvated.pdb -o index.ndx

5. gmx grompp -f ions.mdp -o ions.tpr -p topol.top -c solvated.pdb

6. gmx genion -s ions.tpr -o ionized.pdb -p topol.top -pname NA -nname CL -neutral

We could either say
1. CUDA 11.0 is not supported in release-2020 (easy to implement a nice error message, not very helpful to users), or
2. CUDA 11.0 is supported from 2020.4 onwards (straightforward to implement, and consistent with what we usually do for CUDA major versions released in the year after GROMACS, since their usable lifetimes overlap strongly)

If 2, then we could say

3. that compute_30 is not supported in GROMACS 2020.x at all (easy to implement, not very helpful to users), or
4. that compute_30 is only supported in GROMACS 2020.x with earlier versions of CUDA (fairly easy to implement, most helpful to users).

Thoughts? @acmnpv @artemzhmurov @pszilard

closed_issues.title: Replicate exchange gives 0 probability despite sharing the same hamiltonian
closed_issues.description:
I have two systems, One is decharging the chloride ion

```
[ atoms ]
; id    at type         res nr  residu name     at name  cg nr  charge
1       Cl		1	CL		CL	 1	 -1.000000     35.45000          Cl   0.00000     35.45000
```

The other is the reverse, which is charging the chloride ion.

```
[ atoms ]
; id    at type         res nr  residu name     at name  cg nr  charge
1       Cl		1	CL		CL	 1	 0.000000     35.45000          Cl   -1.00000     35.45000
```

The lambda state 0 of decharging the chloride ion (charge = -1) should have the same hamiltonian as the lambda state 1 of charging the chloride ion (charge = -1).

Thus, the replicate exchange between the lambda state 0 of decharging the chloride ion and the lambda state 1 of charging the chloride ion should happen with 100% probability.

However, the computed probability is 0%.

The steps to reproduce the problem [Archive.zip](/uploads/fc9b65528b3d0b75583fa95b00f4dc36/Archive.zip)

```
gmx grompp -f 1/prod.10.mdp -c prod.gro -o 1/prod.tpr -p 1/topol.top -maxwarn 2
gmx grompp -f 2/prod.0.mdp -c prod.gro -o 2/prod.tpr -p 2/topol.top -maxwarn 2
mpirun -np 2 mdrun_mpi -deffnm prod -multidir 1 2 -replex 1000 -v
```

From #3618,
@mark.j.abraham suggests
> CMake binaries are very small, we can have many of them in our images. CUDA isn't so it can be separate. closed_issues.title: Streamline merge request pipelines
closed_issues.description:
We run at least <s>4</s> 3 CI pipelines for the same repository state for every commit and usually several more. I propose we remove 1 <s>or 2</s> of those, and trigger entire pipelines *only* for a `push` or `merge_request_event` (never both).

**Note 1:**
The merge train pipeline duplicates the final merge request pipeline, wasting resources and slowing down the merge process without adding utility.

**Note 2:**
Pipelines triggered by merge requests do not include all of the tests that we consider essential because we divide some jobs between pipelines that we expect to run concurrently.

# Background
GitLab CI is architected with the expectation that we run one pipeline per commit, and only the pipeline triggered by the merge request event is considered for "require pipeline success" merge request checks. 

GitLab assumes that customers will not be using both "Merge Trains and pipelines for merged results" and "Pipelines must succeed" options at the same time because they are redundant: the purpose of the merge train is to enforce a required successful pipeline before merge.

Merge trains do more harm than good in our fast-forward-only workflow. They do not perform the automatic rebase that is required to maintain multiple pending merges and they merely duplicate the final pipeline of a MR that is ready to be fast-forward squash-merged.

# Proposal

Make sure that exactly zero or one pipeline runs for each ref update. Alternatively, make sure the important pipeline is the merge request pipeline: https://gitlab.com/help/user/project/merge_requests/merge_when_pipeline_succeeds.md#limitations
See also https://gitlab.com/help/ci/yaml/README.md#differences-between-rules-and-onlyexcept

**Suggestion:** Use the logic suggested in https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/lib/gitlab/ci/templates/Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml to **disable branch push pipelines in the gromacs project namespace**. Make sure that blocking test jobs are included in the pipelines triggered for merge requests.

# Additional notes and consequences

## It becomes possible to push a branch that does not trigger any pipelines.

Pipelines will no longer be automatically triggered for pushes to https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs branches if those branches are not tied to active merge requests. Pipelines can be manually triggered for any such branch through the https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/pipelines web interface or by pushing to a fork instead of the main repository.

Note that when GitLab 13.3 is released in late August, it is possible to [Create pipelines in the parent project for merge requests from a forked project](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/merge_request_pipelines/index.html#run-pipelines-in-the-parent-project-for-merge-requests-from-a-forked-project)

## More jobs will execute in multiple pipelines...

... but fewer pipelines will run. The intention of Proposal 1 is to avoid running pipelines that don't actually block merge requests, while making sure that the pipelines that can block merge requests are complete.

## Job rules can be simplified

We currently evaluate the pipeline trigger source for `push` and `merge_request_event` types. It is more relevant to apply logic regarding whether the job should run on free resources or whether it requires special GROMACS project resources. We can move the `push` versus `merge_request_event` logic to the `workflow` level (based additionally on source and target branch per conventional [`workflow:rules`](https://gitlab.com/help/ci/yaml/README.md#workflowrules-templates), and on whether `$CI_PROJECT_NAMESPACE != "gromacs"`)

## See also

Ref https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/3472

[Preventing duplicate pipelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/yaml/README.html#prevent-duplicate-pipelines)
and [related issue](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/201845)


# Progress

A related proposal was adopted 30 July 2020

> **Disable "Merge Trains and pipelines for merged results".**
> 
> The option is redundant with "Pipelines must succeed" and does not provide additional utility to us, because we already require fast-forward-only merges.
> 
> ## Alternate
> 
> If proposal 2 is rejected for some reason, we need to make sure that the pipeline that is executed actually provides a useful check. Make sure that "Merge When Pipeline Succeeds" references the correct pipeline. See also https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/12267#note_205295612 and https://gitlab.com/help/ci/merge_request_pipelines/pipelines_for_merged_results/merge_trains/index.md#unable-to-add-to-merge-train-with-message-the-pipeline-for-this-merge-request-failed

# Deferred

A pipeline runs for the `push` event on the master branch after a merge request is merged. If the `merge_request_event` pipelines had complete coverage, this extra pipeline should not reveal anything new. However, there is some logic in the job scripts that operate on the the git history of `HEAD`, which may have changed if the merge request was squashed during final submission. If we can or should adjust or eliminate the pipeline triggered for `push` events on `master`, let's tackle that in a separate issue.
