closed_issues.title: Incorrect handling of “Distance between pull groups” with PBC
closed_issues.description:
While doing some AWH scans of the ligand complexes with proteins and DNA, I sometimes get the errors at some unpredictable points in the simulation
~~~
Fatal error:
Distance between pull groups 3 and 10 (5.204208 nm) is larger than 0.49 times the box size (5.203962).
~~~

In previous cases I was able to work around it by including an additional restraining potential that supposedly prevented the ligand from going too far. However, with the recent system (DNA 28-mer + organic ligand in water box) I was not so lucky.

**Moreover, I cannot understand why the error occurs when it does. I also wonder what the correct options should be and/or if the logic in pull code might actually be incorrect.**

So, the box is actually quite large (10.6 nm including 1 nm margin on all sides) and the flat-bottom restraint is set at 5 nm. However, the system never reaches that distance. In one run, it started at 1.9 nm and crashed soon after 3.35 nm. I guess that, due to some random drift of molecules, the pull code **suddenly** finds another periodic image of one or both molecules more “attractive”, leading to this discontinuity.

I tried playing with `pull-pbc-ref-prev-step-com`, `pull-groupN-pbcatom`, and COM motion removal options (even tried setting the ligand `pbcatom` to another molecule’s reference) but to no avail. Increasing the box size obviously would not help either, as the desired distance is not reached anyway (but the simulation would take longer to crash)))).

However, while trying larger box (12.6 nm), I have luckily stumbled upon a seed combination that reproduces this crash quickly (see attachment [pulldist.7z](/uploads/8d564718e7d23dd3f90d486c99719783/pulldist.7z)). Unfortunately, VMD crashes on the incomplete trajectory.
~~~
           Step           Time
            841        1.68200

Program:     gmx mdrun, version 2020.2
Source file: src/gromacs/pulling/pull.cpp (line 497)

Fatal error:
Distance between pull groups 3 and 10 (6.173351 nm) is larger than 0.49 times the box size (6.172868).
~~~

The starting value for this distance (t=0) is **1.951** and the last recorded `pullx.xvg` state (t=1.5420) is **1.93284**, so obviously it could not possibly have reached **6.17** at t=1.682 in normal way.

closed_issues.title: Refine CMake options and handling for installed targets
closed_issues.description:
We should reconsider the semantics and processing of
* `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS`
* `GMX_BUILD_MDRUN_ONLY`
* `GMXAPI`
* `GMX_INSTALL_LEGACY_API`

The choices for SHARED or STATIC library targets are unnecessarily intertwined with the build-system-internal linking and enabled-feature choices.

# Suggestion

Allow the user to choose whether installed libraries are STATIC or SHARED, but statically link internal dependencies.

# Assumption

Assumes there is no compelling reason to dynamically link the `gmx` or `mdrun` binaries in terms of the current `libgromacs.so`.

If action is ever taken on https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/issues/951 or a similar issue, additional build system infrastructure will be required (e.g. new library targets) with or without the changes proposed here. Action on #951 should be simplified, though, if the installed targets are already decoupled per this proposal.

# Proposal

* Separate `libgromacs` build tree target into the `Gromacs::libgromacs` installed target and a build-tree-only `core` STATIC library target (with PIC enabled by default, where possible)
* Make `Gromacs::libgromacs` definition and installation conditional on `GMX_INSTALL_LEGACY_API`
* Reduce mutually exclusive install options. Deprecate `GMX_BUILD_MDRUN_ONLY` in favor of two options:
    * `GMX_CLI_TOOLS` (the `gmx` command line program) enabled by default
    * `GMX_STANDALONE_MDRUN` (bare `mdrun` program) disabled by default
* Link all installed targets against `core` instead of `libgromacs`
* Let installed library targets (Gromacs::gmxapi, nblib...) respect `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS`

# Potential issues

* Do we need to support dynamically linked `gmx` CLI tool in terms of *the current libgromacs* architecture?
* Are there systems of interest that support shared libraries but do not support PIC-enabled static libraries?

closed_issues.title: Setting -nmol in gmx energy does not change all mol-based terms
closed_issues.description:
Setting `-nmol` when using `gmx energy` scales some terms, but not all quantities with units of kJ/mol. I did a simple test with `-nmol 1` and setting the actual number of molecules and looked at what quantities changed.

The terms that are correctly scaled: 
- Bond
- Angle
- Fourier Dih.
- LJ (SR)
- Disper. corr.
- Coulomb (SR)
- Coul. recip.
- LJ recip.
- Potential
- Kinetic En.
- Total Energy

Terms I would expect to be scaled (but aren't):
- pV
- Enthalpy
- Vir-** (all 9 terms)

If using `--fluct_props`, all quantities with units of `*/mol` are correctly scaled. *However*, this raises a disagreement in Enthalpy values, since one output can have the un-scaled Enthalpy in the initial table of quantities, but then the scaled Enthalpy in the fluctuation properties table.

Fluctuation properties that are correctly scaled:
- Volume
- Enthalpy
- Coefficient of Thermal Expansion Alpha_P
- Isothermal Compressibility Kappa
- Adiabatic bulk modulus
- Heat capacity at constant pressure Cp
- Cp-Cv

My testing was in GROMACS 2019.6, but looking through the source code in src/gromacs/gmxana/gmx_energy.cpp, it looks like it might still exist on `master`.

Erik Lindahl:
We do. The one challenge is actually for lower-end Xeon systems with only a single AVX-512 unit, where at least GROMACS will do better by using the dual AVX2 units (less throttling and higher algorithm efficiency). There we could consider adding the option.

Erik Lindahl:
The slightly different instruction flavors available is no problem, but I would argue the surprising lack of CPUID support to check if we have 1 or 2 AVX-512 units is by far the biggest problem.

Erik Lindahl:
Any host that has 2 AVX-512 units will perform *great* with AVX-512, even if there's a bit of frequency throttling - but if it only has a single unit there's a performance regression compared to AVX2.

Erik Lindahl:
... and I've noticed that even the assembly-level heuristic timing code we and Intel use occasionally fails to detect 1 vs 2 AVX-512 units when running in containers...

Erik Lindahl:
That means I don't know of any fool-proof detection apart from checking the CPU brand string. For Xeons that should be fine, but for HEDT parts there is no official specification  (promise?) of the number of AVX-512 units available.

closed_issues.title: Make Selection objects clonable
closed_issues.description:
For parallel trajectory analysis, the selections for a single frame need to be fixed so that subsequent frames can be processed in parallel. There are two ways to do this:

1. Have each analysis thread hold it's own copy of the SelectionCollection object, which is the entry point to evaluate selections for a frame. For each frame, the SelectionCollection for the thread assigned to that frame performs the evaluation.
2. Have the SelectionCollection dump a local copy of its selections for a frame before moving on to evaluate the next frame, and passing those selections to the relevant analysis thread.

While option 1 is slightly more elegant, adding copying functionality SelectionCollection is difficult, and working multiple collection objects into the existing analysis framework and initializing them is also complicated. Implementing option 2 is much simpler. It does add a bit of serial work copying selections, but shouldn't add much overhead.

closed_issues.title: Add C++ wrapper for t_trxframe
closed_issues.description:
A memory-managing wrapper for t_trxframe would be useful for parallel trajectory analysis, where multiple frame objects will need to be held in memory. Constructors that initialize underlying memory either from a topology or read_first_frame would be helpful. 

A TrajectoryFrame class exists alongside t_trxframe, but this class is more of a view into an existing frame. I suggest as part of this we rename that class, and allow easy construction of a frame view from a frame object.

closed_issues.title: Require MPI 2.0
closed_issues.description:
Currently there's no minimum version required. MPI 2.0 was standardized in 1997, so probably all relevant vendors have got with the times.

Edit: We've also been using `MPI_Init_thread` for many years, which was only added to MPI in 2.0, so all we're doing is formalizing the requirement we've had for years.

Adopting MPI 2.0 formally lets us simplify the code in the following ways:
* MPI_IN_PLACE can be assumed, so we don't have CMake detection to dispatch preprocessing and runtime logic to work around that, nor manage the temporary buffers that are required for each type that might be involved in such MPI traffic, nor remember to check that it compiles and works (or have a CI config that tests it).
* Possibility to require MPI file I/O (e.g. for API clients?)
* Possibility for MPI one-sided operations e.g. MPI_Put and MPI_Get (though we know there's currently implementation issues that probably mean they don't actually help in our DD halo exchange)

Known compatibility levels
* MPICH2-1.1 was released June 2009 (https://www.mpich.org/2009/06/02/mpich2-1-1-released-jun-2nd-2009/) and it claimed MPI 2.1 support (https://github.com/pmodels/mpich/blob/master/CHANGES#L945)
* OpenMPI 1.3 was released January 2009 (https://github.com/open-mpi/ompi/blob/master/NEWS#L3737) and it claimed 2.1 support https://github.com/open-mpi/ompi/blob/master/NEWS#L3754)
* MVAPICH has been based on MPICH for a long time (currently MVAPICH2 2.3.4 is a fork of MPICH2 3.2.1, see http://mvapich.cse.ohio-state.edu/static/media/mvapich/mvapich2-2.3.4-quickstart.html)
* vendor libraries tend to be forks of MPICH (including IBM, Cray, Intel, Microsoft; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MPICH). Fugaku supports both MPICH and OpenMPI (https://www.fujitsu.com/global/Images/supercomputer-fugaku.pdf) so that should be fine. (Historically the K computer had a fork of OpenMPI.)

We should document that in the install guide and release notes, but it should matter to approximately nobody.

closed_issues.title: Usage of C++17 features in headers
closed_issues.description: `std::is_pointer_v` and `std::is_pod_v` are C++-17 features that are now used in our headers, hence I think we need to inject `-std=c++17` (or equivalent) in the CMake exported target.

closed_issues.title: Decrease threads/ranks automatically to match ability of domain to be decomposed
closed_issues.description:
I was running GROMACS via folding@home when I encountered an error much like this one https://github.com/FoldingAtHome/fah-issues/issues/1307. In short: the F@H supervisor tells GROMACS to process a simulation with X threads/ranks, GROMACS decides the simulation cannot be split between that many and returns with an error. F@H supervisor tries the exact same thing 30 seconds later, again and again.

There is a relatively easy fix: the user just needs to lower the "Folding Power" (aka, threads.) However this requires the user noticing the problem and figuring out how to fix it, which is not certain given how F@H may run for hours/days without supervision and users may be less technically-savvy.

So, could mdrun be made to automatically decrease the requested number of ranks/threads to the highest allowable value, either by default or by a flag?

closed_issues.title: Remove unsigned number arithmetic overall
closed_issues.description:
Implementing C++ core guideline ES.106
https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#es106-dont-try-to-avoid-negative-values-by-using-unsigned

In the context of gromacs, this means avoiding index calculations with std::size_t types like

```
std::size_t endIndex = static_cast<std::size_t>(range.second / spacing + 2);
```

As the clearness of intent expressed by size_t is outweighted by potential bugs due to overflow. 


See also discussion at #2010 and https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/361#note_373950889

closed_issues.title: Replace two-sided communication in GPU PP Halo exchange code path with one-sided communication
closed_issues.description: Currently, PME-PP and PP halo exchange use cudamemcpyasync for direct data copy for thread MPI implementation. This requires passing around CUDA events between ranks to make sure GPU streams execute operations in correct order. Currently, these events are passed using two-sided communication with MPI_SendRecv which causes unnecessary synchronization  This can be replaced with one-sided communication - either using MPI_Put or just use a shared pointer as all thread-MPI ranks are part of the same process.

closed_issues.title: Check that lambda values will always be valid at grompp time
closed_issues.description:
When using dynamic lambda values it is up to the user to set values such that lambda does not leave the range [0,1] and there is no check in place to warn when going from,e.g., inital-lambda = 1 towards a positive direction or overshooting 0 when choosing a negative step size.

The soft-core potential on the other hand makes some assumptions about lambda and will silently crash if too far from lambda [0,1].

However, consider that lambda outside [0,1] might be reasonable and was used in some constant pH prototypes to achieve an ensemble average of lambda = 1 or = 0 by slightly over-shooting.

closed_issues.title: gmxapi pytest may oversubscribe GitLab Runner resources
closed_issues.description:
When a lot of GitLab-CI jobs are running, the MPI jobs get slow, and the gmxapi MPI tests slow down suspiciously dramatically.

I suspect they are oversubscribing resources by inappropriately relying on automatically-detecting the number of threads to use.

It looks like the regression tests, at least, use multiple command line arguments to specify all of the parallelism details. If this is the appropriate way to proceed, a task list would be as follows.

- [x] Add a command line argument for the pytest suite to receive parallelism-related user input.
- [x] Either (a) pass `mdrun` command line arguments to `gmxapi.mdrun`, or (b) expose a configuration hook / UI module for mdrun parallelism specification at a higher level.

Obviously, the latter seems like a more substantial change, but I include it here because there has been a lot of discussion in the last half-year about such things, and features may have been developed that I am not aware of yet. Even if not, it is worth documenting the use case.

Request: Please share, if you have information about the expected results of the automatic threading configuration of mdrun in the Kubernetes CI environment and options to influence it.

An extension of this issue may emerge when we use gmxapi to invoke MPI-enabled libgromacs, but I believe libgromacs still assumes external process management of MPI tasks. While I don't expect ambiguity in the numbers of ranks to be used, automatic allocation of threads will proceed differently: libgromacs will try to allocate OpenMP threads versus tMPI threads.

See also #3563

closed_issues.title: Refine SimulatorBuilder framework
closed_issues.description:
This issue coordinates completion of the SimulatorBuilder implementation.

Templating and argument forwarding (currently used to instantiate Simulators) blocks further encapsulation of Simulator implementations.

Completion will allow extra layers (the MdRunner and MdRunnerBuilder) to be reconsidered and ultimately removed in favor of more explicitly modular Simulator composition.

The monolithic `build()` signature means that the class adds no utility and remains hard to use or maintain.

We do not need to wait for all of the required data to be captured by mature modules to make progress here. Instead, we can make a reasonable attempt to break up groups of data conceptually and to allow future refinement to occur under more limited scope.

We adopt a convention that `add()` parameters are strongly typed to support encapsulation and refactoring. We cannot assert the correct ownership of underlying data at this time, but we *do* assert that the argument passed to `add` is an object or interface/handle that is transferred to the builder, unless an exception is justified and well-documented. Where possible, we use rvalue semantics in `add()` signatures to allow arguments to be constructed in place or acquired earlier in the calling block.

The type of the parameter should become maintained as part of the code responsible for managing the data represented, and we defer data validity, UI, and lifetime management to compartmentalized development outside of the simulatorbuilder.h scope, as possible.

The resolution to this issue consists of a chain of commits to be reviewed and applied together. The commits are applied in an unbroken sequence to simplify review/submission and to help identify the related changes when examining the repository history. The changes are separated into separate commits to allow for easier change regression (if necessary) and to improve readability for future developers. Every commit must pass review and testing, but the final chain will be rebased and merged without squashing.

Design and layout were established in late April, 2020 through a collaboration of 8 developers who have committed to resolving follow-up changes as needed. The primary form of feedback appropriate at this stage of review is requests for additional documentation. Additional commits to the tip of the MR branch should be made only very judiciously, and after separate testing, to reduce developer/reviewer cost and CI Runner load.

closed_issues.title: Separate ISimulator interface and data
closed_issues.description:
Decouple Simulator interfaces, implementations, and builders.

* Reduce ISimulator to a pure virtual interface class.
* Encapsulate data members in a LegacySimulatorData class.

LegacySimulatorData can be inherited as a mix-in for LegacySimulator to minimize maintenance of the old code, but ModularSimulator will have an explicit member object. We presume (but do not require) that LegacySimulatorData will be decomposed over time, or that at least the ModularSimulator may reduce dependence incrementally.

This change interacts well with other efforts underway to update ModularSimulator infrastructure, and neither needs to be serialized with respect to the other. This change will be easier to apply _after_ refining the SimulatorBuilder framework.

closed_issues.title: restraintpotential.h has ambiguous specification
closed_issues.description:
`gmx::IRestraintPotential` and `gmx::PotentialPointData` need to be defined in the public libgromacs interface, but they have ambiguous definitions.

The classes are expressed such that they may produce indistinguishable and incompatible definitions depending on client precompiler macros. Member variables and member function signatures depend on the definition of `real`, which is a configuration parameter of a GROMACS installation, not a part of a specified API.

One reasonable remediation strategy could be to move this dependence to a class template parameter.

Alternatives could involve use of `std::variant` or simply multiple symbols, distinguished either by name or an ABI namespace. Adjustments would need to be made to the extension protocol to make sure that it is easy to overload the right virtual functions and that non-overloaded virtual functions don't result in confusingly quiet no-ops.

Note that this is a specific case of the issue described at #3560

closed_issues.title: Consider adding the Bernetti-Bussi stochastic barostat
closed_issues.description:
Bussi and co-workers developed a stochastic version of the Berendsen barostat, much in spirit of his v-rescale variant of the Berendsen thermostat.  An arXiv preprint is here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09250. 

There are a couple of variants, and we need to think carefully about which ones make the most sense to incorporate.  I would suggest that the basic Euler variant is not sufficient, since it is not reversible, but it's not clear which of the others would be easiest to include without performance cost (or if there is another variant with a different trotter decomposition that he missed)

He has incorporated this in a fork of the GROMACS code, https://github.com/bussilab/crescale-gromacs, which although it might not be the desired way to code it up, would provide a useful reference implementation and removed any ambiguity about what is being done.

I will keep looking at the formalism - Pascal should probably at some point evaluate what would need to be done to put it into the modular simulator framework (better to add it in just one place)

closed_issues.title: How to express floating point precision in public API
closed_issues.description:
As we move towards a new public API specification, one of the legacy ambiguities that we need to figure out how to express better is the implicit duality of some symbols (or behaviors) based on the definition of `real`.

GROMACS has a type alias (`real`) that is determined to be `float` or `double` through the CMake configuration. Currently, the library is built with a single instance of code that relies on the choice of `real`. The binaries are (usually) distinguished by name (with a suffix `_d` for "double-precision") and the information is available to client packages through CMake infrastructure.

However, there may not be a sufficiently clear policy regarding the effect of this typedef on the installed headers and how client packages should consistently find the correct symbols.

I think we can agree that the installed headers should not include a typedef of `real` in a global namespace that could allow the API specification to change between installations, but it also seems a bit awkward for the installed headers to require a client to provide a compile-time definition that can change the meaning of a header.

A reasonable alternative is to change the way the public API expresses interfaces. Symbols that may be implemented for either `float` or `double` can use a template parameter, such as `Scalar`, `GmxReal`, or `RealT`, to clarify declarations that are affected by the client context. Incompatible library and client builds would result in the same sort of linking error as with a typedef when only one of two possible call signatures is available. For classes, a type trait could provide additional or alternative confirmation of the configuration of the library.

We should also consider explicit symbol naming to distinguish definitions that might otherwise be ambiguous, such as by encoding the ABI spec in the symbol's namespace.

We could also make the potential linking error more obvious by including both declarations in the public interface explicitly. For user convenience, they could be wrapped in a pre-compiler ternary conditional that clarifies the dependence on client environment. This could be preferable if any supported compilers may produce incompatible C++ ABI symbol names for templates.

Finally, we might consider that there are few cases for which the public API needs to account for a build-dependent object type, and require explicit precision in the public API. In cases where there is an actual performance issue to be addressed, we should use self-describing data structures or protocols (such as Eigen's or Numpy's data descriptors, for example), to make the precision into a (const, potentially constexpr) instance detail rather than a type detail.

* [x] Can we use custom-defined transitive usage requirements to enforce consistent precision settings in CMake targets?
      *Yes. See https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.13/manual/cmake-buildsystem.7.html#compatible-interface-properties*
* [ ] What lessons can we take from our favorite math libraries and how they have handled this?

closed_issues.title: Improve cycle counters for GPU backend
closed_issues.description:
Multiple cycle counters issues in GPU backend:
1. With new GPU Halo exchange path, “Comm. coord" and “Wait + Comm. F" is not measured. 
2. Most of the cycle counters measured for GPU backend are not correct due to asynchronous nature of GPU execution. These timings mostly measure kernel launch time or some other async CUDA API overhead (cudamemcpyasync), actual execution is not measured.
3. Replace “Send X to PME" counter with “Receive X from PP". Basically cycle counter will be part of PME thread/process instead of PP thread/process. As the sends from PP are asynchronous, it makes sense to count these cycles in PME which actually waits for co-ordinates receive.

Point 2 can be fixed using CUDA events. Basically record CUDA events before and after various GPU tasks. Synchronize stream after every step or every few steps, readback timing information and dump that data.

Edit:

closed_issues.title: Bugs in gmx hbond
Expand gmxapi.cli output availability
closed_issues.description:
`gmxapi.commandline_operation` was written with the assumption that all interesting I/O happens through files represented as command line arguments, but this is clearly not the case.

The behavior of the `erroroutput` port is a bit strange because it mixes stdout and stderr, and it is guaranteed to be empty unless the wrapped command had a non-zero exit code.

# Background

One reason for this design choice was to mitigate potential dead-locks in i/o stream buffering that have since been (supposedly) mitigated in the Python `subprocess` module.

A deeper issue is that the uniqueness and completeness of a standard-output stream or a standard-error stream are not well-defined, and there is not a clear and universal answer for how to identify these products of commands. The behavior of `erroroutput` does not resolve this question, though, so I suppose an alternative behavior can't drive objections on the same grounds if it improves utility.

# Proposal

* Deprecate *erroroutput*
* Add *stdout* and *stderr*, which map as expected to the process *STDOUT* and *STDERR*.

The logic within `gmxapi.commandline.cli` should be expanded to account for which outputs actually have subscriptions, but that is a separate issue that depends first on updates to the data flow model, and can be deferred for the context of this issue.

# Reference

https://github.com/kassonlab/gmxapi/issues/262

See also #3394

closed_issues.title: Update supported doxygen version
closed_issues.description:
In order to move away from doxygen 1.8.5 to a more modern version, a number of changes to the doxygen documentation are needed. Following is a list of issues and fixes where I can find them. Note this is only for check-source and doxygen-full make targets, so other errors might appear with other targets. To get a fuller picture, we would likely want to create a container and pipeline for the candidate doxygen version.

**Structure of the list**
* warning
  * possible fix

* warning: unbalanced grouping commands
  * This can sometimes be traced to there actually being an extra, unused, grouping command, usually `//! \}`
* NOTE: You are using Doxygen version 1.8.*. The documentation is designed for 1.8.5. Other versions may or may not work, but very likely produce extra warnings.
  * change: docs/CMakeLists.txt:59:set(EXPECTED_DOXYGEN_VERSION 1.8.5)
* warning: Tag 'MSCGEN_PATH' at line 36 of file 'Doxyfile-common' has become obsolete.
  * remove line 36 in doxygenfile-commone.in
* warning: unbalanced grouping commands
  * This can sometimes be traced to there actually being an extra, unused, grouping command, usually `//! \}`
* warning: Reached end of file while still inside a (nested) comment. Nesting level 1 (probable line reference: [linenumber])
  * usually caused by a math symbol that makes doxygen unhappy, can be fixed by adding extra "\"
* warning: end of file while inside a group
  * fixed by adding `//! \}  end of name-group ...`
* warning: no matching class member found for ... Possible candidates:
  * seems to be an issue arising from having doxygen for multiple constructors, e.g. with different signatures
* warning: included file name template.cpp is ambiguousPossible candidates:
  * giving the fully qualified path solves this error but may not be the solution we want
* warning: @copydetails or @copydoc target 'func()' not found
  * this can in some cases be solved by changing `\copydoc` to `\overload`, namely cases where the function signatures differ
  * in other cases this seems to be caused mostly by virtual functions that for some reason do not pass docs to their children
* todo:[linenumber]: warning: unexpected token TK_COMMAND_BS as the argument of _internalref
  * undetermined, might be a problem with formatting of todos but I could not find a solution
* warning: argument 'arg' of command @param is not found in the argument list of FUNC()
  * set `ENABLE_PREPROCESSING   = YES` in appropriate doxygen.in file
* doxygenxml.py fails
  * need to rework `merge_definition()` in that script


**doxygen-full**

* src/gromacs/mdlib/energyoutput.cpp:92: warning: Member boxs_nm (variable) of file energyoutput.cpp is not documented. (in doxygen-full)
  * add `EXCLUDES = src/gromacs/mdlib/energyoutput.cpp` to appropriate cmake file 
  * add doxygen
  * replace `\{ ... \}` with `\cond label ... \endcond label`

closed_issues.title: Loss of precision in Parrinello-Rahman pressure coupling at high pressure
closed_issues.description:
It seems there is an issue with Parrinello-Rahman pressure coupling when coupling to high pressure. The box velocity may become so small that the update to the box is less than the floating point precision. This leads to a density that changes in discrete steps (see figure dens.xvg). In double precision the fluctuations are continuous and the box follows the same "trajectory".

In addition to this there maybe be an issue with the coupling in that it makes the box grow indefinitely (but this may be a force field issue as well).

The example is a CGenFF model for carbon dioxide.[co2.zip](/uploads/18313fad540aca66873bda7ed5b4ffef/co2.zip)

Examples are src/gromacs/nbnxm/benchmark/bench_setup.cpp:232 and src/gromacs/mdlib/tests/constrtestdata.cpp:105

This makes any refactoring of the actual MDAtoms class for proper access patterns and data handling pointless, because I need to keep the access anyway for those places.

Those access patterns need to be changed, so that the actual class can be properly refactored.

closed_issues.description:
Scripts such as `admin/clang-tidy.sh` process the text output of wrapped tools, but miss error conditions when the tools exit abnormally. Errors from wrapped tools should either be propagated or handled, rather than silently ignored.

One option can be to check the exit status (`$?`) after invoking a tool, but this is not possible for pipelines of commands.

Another option is to `set -e` early in the bash script.

Ref #3528

closed_issues.title: All clang-tidy linting steps broken by missing python
closed_issues.description:
In the docker image used to run the clang-tidy script, no base python is defined or symlinked in /usr/bin/

This leads to scripts expecting this to exist to fail, in most cases silently.

One example is the admin/clang-tidy.sh script that tries to run run-clang-tidy-9.py, but fails because it can't find the python version.

I don't know when this got broken but it must have been rather recently, because the scripts worked fine before.

Symlinking /usr/bin/python3 to /usr/bin/python fixes the issue when testing in a fresh docker image.

This needs to be fixes ASAP because we are missing coverage in our basic push commits.

closed_issues.title: Allow untagged jobs to run on both public and private Runners.
closed_issues.description:
We would like to primarily use the GROMACS project Kubernetes GitLab Runner resources for pipelines triggered within the project, but to allow some jobs to run in other project spaces (such as on forks without the k8s-scilifelab tag). However, the current `gitlab-ci` config does not find Runners for jobs with `job:tags: []` when we turn off the Shared Runners in the GitLab Project configuration.

We theorize that this is because GitLab CI is looking for a Runner with an explicitly empty *tags* array, rather than removing the tag requirement.

A merge request should switch from the global default *tag* specification to no global default *tag* specification, and let jobs explicitly add the `k8s-scilifelab` tag, rather than explicitly adding `[]`. Then we can quickly confirm whether this resolves the issue by toggling https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/runners/toggle_shared_runners and triggering a pipeline.

closed_issues.title: AWH domain change issues
closed_issues.description:
Hello,

When using AWH, sometimes it is desirable to change the coordinate domain definition in the course of a simulation without wasting the efforts and resources spent on preceding computations. For example, upon inspection of the already generated PMF map, one could recognize that the interesting regions extend beyond the initial coordinate limits. Conversely, in order to minimize the calculation time, one might also want to discard some regions that proved uninteresting. Changes in the force constants and thus grid spacing, aiming to refine the plot, are also conceivable. 

I think all these use cases are reasonable. In fact, one can easily get the impression that the `"awh1-user-data"` functionality is intended exactly for importing and reusing the previous simulation results. However, when trying to use it, I encountered a couple of problems.

1) When trying to restart the simulation using the MDP file with changed AWH coordinate limits, **mdrun** causes CUDA assertion failure if a checkpoint file is provided using `-cpi` option. This happens regardless of whether `continuation=yes` and/or `awh1-user-data=yes` are specified. Reproducible with the latest CUDA libraries and driver.
```
Program:     gmx mdrun, version 2020.2
Source file: src/gromacs/gpu_utils/devicebuffer.cuh (line 84)
Function:    freeDeviceBuffer(DeviceBuffer*)::<lambda()> [with DeviceBuffer = float*]

Assertion failed:
Condition: cudaFree(*buffer) == cudaSuccess
cudaFree failed
```

2) Even if we decide to start a new simulation, the user data file (`awhinit.xvg`) fails to load due to "missing values". Taking into account that the PMF and bias data are already smoothed using Gaussian convolutions, one would intuitively expect the AWH code to rediscretize the values on a new grid (with changed limits and/or spacing), initializing the uncovered regions to default values. In the current form, I am not sure what meaningful use is there for the `awhinit.xvg` (exact restarts are served by checkpoints while grid changes are impossible and modifications of the system or general parameters obviously are undesirable).
```
step5_241.xvg does not contain data for all coordinate values. Make sure your
input data covers the whole sampling domain and is correctly formatted.
```
Could you please take a look into these issues.

Here is the archive that might help in reproducing and debugging: https://www.dropbox.com/s/zs83zz6fe0o939o/awherrors.7z?dl=0

Best regards,
Eugene

closed_issues.title: Checkpointing tests are not adequate
closed_issues.description:
https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/blob/master/src/programs/mdrun/tests/exactcontinuation.cpp is supposed to catch problems with checkpoints. It runs a simulation of 16 steps, and then compares the results to a (hopefully) identical simulation consisting of two segments of 8 steps each. Testing is done by comparing potential energies over the trajectories.

Test simulations include a relatively broad selection of test systems under NVE (with and without FEP), NVT, NPT, NPH using most available integrators and temperature / pressure control schemes.

Unfortunately, a quick test shows that the tests are not sensitive enough. While it catches cases in which the positions or velocities were not saved, it won't notice things like the box, thermostat / barostat state or energy history not being stored or read. This means that this test is currently not suited to give us confidence that a change to the checkpointing architecture as planned in #3517 would be correct.

We should spend more effort in trying to make these test fail (e.g. by excluding certain values from checkpoint files), and improve the tests if expected failures don't lead to tests actually failing.

closed_issues.title: Modularized checkpointing format
closed_issues.description:
This issue should serve as a place to discuss a checkpointing format that allows for a modularized approach, i.e. allows objects to store and retrieve data without having a central data structure or infrastructure that has knowledge about all objects and their stored data. As this has repeatedly been discussed in different subgroups in the past, this issue is rather a _design proposal_ than a completely fresh design discussion. Nevertheless, the goal is to have a design that finds broad agreement from all developers involved in efforts touched by the decision. It will likely be beneficial to implement this approach for checkpointing of all code paths.

## Current implementation
**Legacy checkpointing approach:** All data to be checkpointed needs to be stored in one of the following data structures:
* `t_state`, which also holds pointers to
  - `history_t` (history for restraints)
  - `df_history_t` (history for free energy)
  - `ekinstate`
  - `AwhHistory`
* `ObservableHistory`, consisting of 
  - `energyhistory_t`
  - `PullHistory`
  - `edsamhistory_t`
  - `swaphistory_t`
* Checkpoint further saves details about the output files being used

One possibility to add data to the checkpoint is to expand one of the objects that is currently being checkpointed, and edit the respective `do_cpt_XXX` function in `checkpoint.cpp` which interacts with the XDR library. The alternative would be to write an entirely new data structure, changing the function signature of all checkpoint-related functions, and write a corresponding low-level routing interacting with the XDR library.

**The MdModule approach:** To allow for modules to write checkpoints, the legacy checkpoint was extended by a KVTree. When writing to checkpoint, this tree gets filled (via callbacks) by the single modules, and then serialized. When reading, the KVTree gets deserialized, and then distributed to the modules which can read back the data previously stored.

**The modular simulator approach in 2020:** To allow for checkpointing before a truly modularized checkpoint infrastructure existed, modular simulator as implemented in GROMACS 2020 passed a t_state object to the checkpoint clients, which they could fill with their data. This is obviously not a permanent solution.

## Proposed new design

The MdModule checks off almost all requirements to a modularized checkpointing format. The proposed design is therefore an evolved form of this approach. Notably, two improvements include
* Hide the implementation details of the data structure holding the data (currently, a KV-Tree) from the clients. This allows to change the implementation details of reading / writing checkpoints without touching client code.
* Offer a unified way to read and write to data, allowing clients write one (templated) function to read to and write from checkpoint. This allows to eliminate code duplication and the danger of having read and write functions getting out of sync.

Branch https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commits/ptmerz-checkpointdata is a working prototype of a modularized checkpointing for modular simulator. It does not currently change the way that the legacy simulator is checkpointing. Some data structures involved in the legacy checkpoint did, however, get an implementation of the new approach. This is needed for ModularSimulator checkpointing, but also gives a glimpse of how implementing this for legacy data structures would look like.

The most important design part is the `CheckpointData` class (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/c48747105bb38bf5366d1de44b90d73033ae91aa). It exposes methods to read and write scalar values, ArrayRefs, and tensors. It also allows to create a "sub-object" of type `CheckpointData` which allows to have more complex members implement their own checkpointing routines. All methods are templated on the chosen operation, `CheckpointDataOperation::Read` or `CheckpointDataOperation::Write`, allowing clients to use the same code to read and write to checkpoint. Type traits and constness are used to catch as many errors as possible at compile time. `CheckpointData` uses a KV-tree to store the data internally. This is however never exposed to the client. Having this abstraction layer gives freedom to change the internal implementation in the future.

All `CheckpointData` objects are owned by a `ReadCheckpointDataHolder` or `WriteCheckpointDataHolder`. These holder classes own the internal KV-tree, and offer `deserialize(ISerializer*)` and `serialize(ISerializer*)` functions, respectively, which allow to read from / write to file. This separation clearly defines ownership and separates the interface aimed at file IO from the interface aimed at objects reading/writing checkpoints.

The templating and type traits might make the `CheckpointData` class look somewhat complicated, but its use is straightforward. https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/93f4166f7dd81992be580c5ed97bd70e15cea7f2 implements checkpointing of some legacy data structures (energyhistory_t, delta_h_history_t, ekinstate_t) using CheckpointData.

The approach has been used to implement checkpointing for modular simulator entirely in terms of this new approach (tip of https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commits/ptmerz-checkpointdata). Aside from the development discussed above, this was achieved by passing a `ReadCheckpointDataHolder` or `WriteCheckpointDataHolder` object legacy checkpoint read and write operations (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/09f63989c90de8fcda729556c3e511b9870d249b). Finally, the elements were rewritten to exclusively read and write checkpoint data from the new `CheckpointData` format (https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/077f104b9e9e916837f4cd298083ec7041ee743b).

### Notes about the new design

**Distinction of data between clients:** The proposed design envisions that separate clients have independent sub-`CheckpointData` objects identified by a unique key. This key would be the only thing that needs to be unique between clients, i.e. clients are free to use any key _within_ their sub-`CheckpointData` without danger to overwrite data used by other clients.

**Versioning:** The proposed design relies on clients keeping their own versioning system within their sub-`CheckpointData` object. The top level checkpointing facility has no way to know when the internals change, so only fundamental changes to the checkpointing architecture could still be tracked by a top-level checkpoint version. The versioning system was implemented for the legacy data structures in https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/commit/e28d03e31246871a0607dafb13e61ce80fc6913f.

**Key existence:** The currently uploaded design does not allow to check whether a key is present in `CheckpointData`. This could be introduced if needed - however, if clients write self-consistent read and write code, this should never be needed. It seems that checking for key existence would rather be a lazy way to circumvent versioning?

**Callback method:** The modular simulator and MdModules don't use the exact same way of communicating with clients. The two methods could easily be unified if needed. The only _fundamental_ difference is that modular simulator clients need to identify with a unique key to receive their dedicated sub-data, while MdModules all read from and write to the same KV-tree. MdModules could be adapted to that by either requiring a unique key from the modules, or by using the same `CheckpointData` for all modules and using a single unique key (something like "MdModules") to register that object with the global checkpoint.

**Performance:** One of the major differences between the new approach and the legacy checkpointing is that data gets _copied_ into `CheckpointData`, while the legacy approach only took a pointer to the data and serialized it. This slightly reduces performance. Some thoughts on that:
* By default, checkpointing happens at the start of the simulation (only if reading from checkpoint), every 15 minutes during simulation runs, and at the end of the simulation run. This makes it a low priority target for optimization. Consequently, I haven't put too much thoughts in the optimization, but I'm sure there's some way to improve things here and there if we consider it necessary.
* The copying will only have measurable effect when large data gets checkpointed - likely only for saving the positions / velocities of the entire state, so that should be the first target for optimization if needed.
* Copying data could have advantages moving forward - we could continue the simulation as soon as the data is written to the `CheckpointData` object, and don't necessarily need to wait for writing to the physical medium to happen.
* If, however, we wanted to use the same approach for other operations such as saving/restoring states for MC type algorithms or swapping of states between running simulations in multi-sim type settings, performance would become more of an issue.

**ISerializer vs KV-tree:** The new approach uses a KV tree internally. The KV tree is well suited to represent the design philosophy of the approach: An element offers a functionality which allows clients to write/read any data they want. This data remains opaque to the checkpointing element. Elements can read or write in any order, and in the future, maybe even simultaneously. Data written by any element should be protected from access from other elements to avoid bugs. The downside of the KV tree is that all data gets copied before getting written to file (see above).

Replacing a KV tree by a single ISerializer object which gets passed to clients would require elements to read and write sequentially in a prescribed order. With the help of InMemorySerializer, a KV-Tree could likely be emulated (with sub-objects that serialize to memory, and then a parent object that serializes this memory to file), but I don't see a clear advantage.

## (Un)Related issues
* This discussion is probably unrelated to #3229, which discusses the location of checkpointing within the simulation loop rather than its format.
* This issue is related to #3422, which requires a format to have modularized checkpoint reading and writing within modular simulator.
* This issue is related to #2059, which explores the types of data stored in t_state.
* This issue is related to #3518, since we could switch the implementation of checkpointing with much more confidence if our tests were better.

closed_issues.title: SIMD kernels are no more built by default
closed_issues.description:
My understanding is that SIMD kernels should be built by default, and this option allows developers to `cmake -DGMX_USE_SIMD_KERNELS=OFF` in order to save some compilation time.

If this is correct, there is then an issue since SIMD kernels are **not** built by default anymore.

@mark.j.abraham  `git bisect` points to gromacs/gromacs@f5be681aeb9db9b9350e174a746f6c1da8606ad7

A workaround is to `cmake -DGMX_USE_SIMD_KERNELS=ON`.

FWIW, adding debug statement in the cmake files show that `GMX_USE_SIMD_KERNELS` is empty when used in `src/gromacs/nbnxm/kernels_simd_4xm/CMakeLists.txt`, and is then set to `ON` in `src/gromacs/CMakeLists.txt`

I am afraid my understanding of `cmake` is too limited to suggest a fix.

here is the patch I used to debug this

closed_issues.title: Implement "meta" pull-coordinates
closed_issues.description:
We would like to extend the library of pull coordinates with some of the most used ones. So we should implement:
1) A non-linear transformation of an existing pull coordinate using some sigmoidal function. Todo: decide which functional forms, likely a subset of what Plumed supports. Todo: decide on a name
2) A linear combination of existing pull coordinates. Parameters N pull groups and N coefficients.
These "meta" coordinates can be mostly treated as normal pull coordinates. But the, obviously, take pull coordinates as input instead of normal coordinates and output forces that should be passed to other pull groups. The implementation should loop sequentially over pull coordinates to compute the coordinates and sequentially backwards to distribute the forces. That way everything will work when these new meta coordinates only take pull coordinates with lower index then their own index (this requirement should be checked).

For using these meta pull coordinates the user should normally set the force constant of the underlying pull coordinates to zero. That way only the meta pull coordinate acts and the user can still get observables for the underlying pull coordinates. This should be added to the documentation.

Oliver Fleetwood volunteered to implement this, but as of now it is unclear if he will have sufficient time to finish this before the 2021 deadline.

closed_issues.title: Certain tests occasionally time out.
closed_issues.description:
The following discussion from !98 should be addressed:

- [ ] @eirrgang started a [discussion](https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/98#note_332856156):  (+5 comments)

    > It seems like we might need to increase the time-out for some of the tests for the TSAN job to pass consistently.

Some tests take close to the standard time-out of 30 seconds and occasionally time out when the CI resources are busy or with more expensive TSAN binaries. The solution can include some combination of adjusting time-outs and splitting up the tests.

* GmxPreprocessTests
* Pdb2gmx1Test
* Pdb2gmx2Test
* Pdb2gmx3Test
* ToolUnitTests
* TrajectoryAnalysisUnitTests

INTEGRATION_TEST and SLOW_TEST are commonly used with the gmx_ CMake macros, but are not appropriate as hammers for passing slow tests because they have additional effects, such as to disable memory leak checking.

Most simply, `set_tests_properties(${NAME} PROPERTIES TIMEOUT ${_timeout})` could be applied at the definitions of the tests.

MdrunNonIntegratorTests already has a long time-out through additional macro logic. If its time out is not enough, timeout set through the helper function can be increased.

closed_issues.title: Suggested Build Settings Changes for MSVC 2019
closed_issues.description:
Summary: I suggest the following configuration changes for the next Windows release,
1. Build with the latest toolset (VS 2019 latest update)
3. Enable /Oi on all projects
4. Enable /Ob3 on all projects
5. Enable /Zc:throwingNew on all projects
7. Statically link the CRT (this is more a quality of life issue than performance)
8. Build all configurations, all favors with /Zi

Full explanation: 
Hey! I'm Terry on the MSVC compiler team. I was trying to help out Folding@Home on Windows, and they directed me to you guys, and I have been building/playing with the 2020.1 release the past couple days.

So, explanation:
1. Obviously, I'd want you to build with the latest toolset. If you hit any code quality or correctness bugs, I can easily hotfix a drop of the compiler to you if you use something relatively recent. If you need a license let me know.
2. <del>This enables "link time codegen", our highest optimization level.</del> This didn't give expected benefits
3. Intrinsic expansion is typically many times faster than intrinsic function calls, for some reason this is disabled. I suspect you care more about perf than codesize. Inline intrinsics actually can be smaller as well - sometimes disappearing entirely - when constants are involved.
4. Ob3 is a new inlining option, you won't find a CMAKE option for it: you'll need to explicitly specify it under "other options" somehow. This option increases the internal thresholds of the inliner to be closer to what other compilers use (MSVC has historically been not as aggressive as our peers). This will increase inlining.
5. Zc:throwingNew is an option to explicitly tell the compiler that operator new doesn't throw. For historical reasons, MSVC has always had secret null checks after every call to new. Looking at your project, you don't assume a null returning new, so this is just pure codesize and runtime waste.
6. <del>PGO training offers the best opportunity for optimizations for any binary. But, this requires a training set. Also, we need to do this for the final binary (like the FAH core, is it a dll or exe?) - it doesn't make sense to train a lib file like libgromacs.</del> This depends on /GL being enabled
7. As we discussed in another issue; I believe this is the intention.
8. Another quality of life issue, the only reason not to build with Zi is build throughput, but the debug information is generally indispensable both for fixing bugs before a release and debugging user issues later after a release - and worth the extra build time.

Ultimately the delivery mechanism of gromacs to fah is unclear to me. Do you give them a lib they link in the client? A dll that the client loads? What project produces that binary for them?

closed_issues.title: Request to add a .mdp option that sets a (possibly stochastic) maximum EM step size
Request to add actual value of gen-seed to .tpr file so that gmx dump can find it
closed_issues.description:
The purpose would be to allow one to reproduce a failed run as closely as possible while changing some parts of the .mdp file. For instance, I sometimes build a system with an infrequent coordinate output, then find errors and want to re-run while saving coordinates very frequently. I do realize that some errors are stochasticly related to parallelization, but I have a system for which repeated parallel runs from the same .tpr file error out, but if I re-run grompp then it is fine, so I’d like to be able to keep the same velocities while changing trajectory output frequency.

When I set ld-seed=-1, the actual ld-seed is saved in the .tpr file, as viewed by gmx dump:
 
inputrec:
   ld-seed                        = 1097225599

But gmx dump provides no information about gen-seed. Also, when I use a .mdp file with gen-seed=-1, the mdout.mdp file reports gen-seed=-1 (similar to the ld-seed behavior, though the actual number there is recoverable from gmx dump).

I realize that this information is printed to stdout from the grompp command, and that has solved this particular need for me in this case since I saved that output, but I still think that this is something that others might find useful in the future so I thought I'd suggest it as a feature request.

Thank you,
Chris.

closed_issues.title: GmxapiMpiTests should not automatically choose its number of threads
closed_issues.description:
Reference mailing list discussion at https://mailman-1.sys.kth.se/pipermail/gromacs.org_gmx-developers/2020-April/010797.html

We use `gmx_register_gtest_test()` to configure the CTest GmxapiMpiTests test in terms of the gmxapi-mpi-test executable target. This CMake function takes arguments MPI_RANKS and OPENMP_THREADS to determine the run time resources of the test.

OPENMP_THREADS simply sets the -ntomp command line option, but gmxapi-mpi-test is not an `mdrun` based executable, so the `gmx::Mdrunner` in gmxapi-mpi-test takes the default action of trying to grab all available threading resources, which can cause a fatal error when the automatically determined number of threads is greater than GROMACS thinks is practical.

Until further API development evolves, we use `src/api/cpp/tests/testingconfiguration.h` to package run time arguments that mimic a command line, so the simplest quick fix is to add an `-ntomp` option to the argument list constructed in that header.

closed_issues.title: Pipelines are not failing as early as they should.
closed_issues.description:
Normal behavior of a GitLab pipeline is that a stage fails if any job in it fails, and subsequent stages are not executed.

The *needs* job parameter can override this behavior to cause jobs to be executed on a job dependency graph (DAG). We use *needs* extensively, but not between the first and second stages (*pre-build* and *configure-build*). It is unclear from the GitLab documentation whether the presence of any jobs with *needs* is supposed to change the behavior of the entire pipeline.

In our current configuration, a failing first stage is not preventing execution of succeeding stages.
I thought that maybe the explicit *dependencies: []* could be the culprit, but removing this parameter from the jobs in *configure-build* does not resolve the issue. See https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/pipelines/135165318

If we plan to always run as many jobs as possible, then the *simple-build* job does not serve a purpose and can be removed.

If there is something in our CI or Runner configuration that is overriding default behavior, we should consider changing that. For instance, is there configurable logic on whether a stage success requires *all* vs. *any* jobs to pass?

If the presence of *any* `needs` specifications in the pipeline causes the entire pipeline to ignore stage dependencies, then we should make all jobs ultimately depend on all of the *pre-build* jobs through (a chain of) `needs` parameters, or reconsider our use of `needs`.

If none of the above seem to be the case, then we should open a support ticket with GitLab to figure out how to get the behavior we intend.

closed_issues.title: Improve merge request policies and procedures
closed_issues.description:
Since migrating to GitLab, GROMACS developers have been discovering a few wrinkles.

1. CI pipeline logic (when to run jobs and when not to) needs refinement.
2. <s>Changes are getting merged with insufficient or inaccurate commit messages.</s>
3. The review process/discussion for a commit is not easily recovered, once merged.
4. Contributions are not efficiently reviewed.

Implementation details include configuration of GitLab, GitLab CI, and GitLab Runner, but also definition of responsibilities for contributors and reviewers of merge requests.

Some discussion may be necessary to codify priorities and agree on policies so that we can implement procedures to improve our throughput and development transparency.

For more on challenges associated with certain development workflows in GitLab environments, see https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/issues/11934 and https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/26996
Also reference https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/merge_request_pipelines/pipelines_for_merged_results/merge_trains/ 

## Commit messages
<s>
The squash-and-merge strategy is [supposed to](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/merge_requests/squash_and_merge.html#overview) allow editing of the squash commit message, but the GROMACS `master` branch history indicates we have had trouble getting this to work right when squash-and-merge is [combined with fast-forward merge](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/merge_requests/squash_and_merge.html#squash-and-fast-forward-merge).
</s>
<s>
https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-foss/-/issues/48324 indicates the feature was recently added, and I don't see any open or closed issues that the feature is not working as expected. May be related to https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/18142 or https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/26748
</s>

Since disabling the merge train, the MR option to edit the squash commit message seems to work as intended.
# Criteria for completion

This issue can remain open as long as it is useful to coordinate conversation, but could be closed once the outcome of community discussion on the above items is recorded, if resulting action items is recorded elsewhere.

closed_issues.title: wrong dhdl with lj-pme
closed_issues.description:
In solvation free energy simulations with **gmx 2020.1** the vdW component of dG and DHDL is **~2X overestimated** at the lambda region in which vdw-lambdas are changing. Additional testing has shown that this issue is related to "**vdw-type = PME**".


I have compared (for lambda-state=4) <dVvdw/dl> results of **gmx2020** with vdw-type: **PME** and **CutOff**, with the result of old **gmx5.1** with vdw-type = PME. All was run on CPU for 5 nanosecs with **PME electrostatics**. It turned out that **gmx2020** with **vdw-type=CutOff** reproduces (within the accuracy) the <dVvdw/dl> result of **gmx5.1** with **vdw-type = PME**, which is expected. In the uniform environment both vdw-types should give accurate solvation FE. The result of **gmx2020** with **vdw-type=PME**, however, is around 2X exaggerated, which seems to be a bug.

Here are the numbers:

| gmx-ver/vdw-type | <dVcoul/dl> | <dVvdw/dl> |
| ------ | ------ | ------ |
| 2020/PME | -6.39450e-01  |   9.72647e+01   |
| 2020/CutOff | -3.99985e-01  |  4.39876e+01  |
| 5.1/PME | -3.08675e-01  |  4.36738e+01 | 

Note, the problem is related to **DHDL only**, all potential energy components (including vdW) in all runs are consistent. Test files are in the attached archive [test_solvation.tar.gz](/uploads/33ce1ca6b088cf05c029445c0ca99afa/test_solvation.tar.gz). Compare log in lambda.04 folder.

closed_issues.title: Restrict write access to global topology at simulator level
closed_issues.description:
The global topology is owned by the Mdrunner object, which passes a (non-owning, write-access) pointer to the simulator object. Although some functions request a write-access pointer, with the exception of do_mimic() (and its rerun in do_rerun()), none of the LegacySimulator's simulation run functions **actually needs** write access to the global topology. No modular simulator modules need write access, either.

I would suggest two improvements:
1. Check all functions called by the ISimulator objects which request a write-access pointer to the global topology, and make const wherever possible. This is expected to leave only the initial setup in do_mimic() (and do_rerun() if rerunning a MiMiC trajectory) to require write access.
2. Discuss how we can restrict write access to the topology at runner level, especially in view of the needs of MiMiC and other upcoming QMMM implementations.

closed_issues.title: Gromacs 2020.x misses public headers to read tpr files. Any workaround?
Restarted simulations with expanded ensemble (and trotter decomposition)
closed_issues.description:
When restarting from checkpoint, expanded ensemble will silently be ignored.

In 88c7ed2de9e66d3ad80598e0534a165205371fe7, `startingFromCheckpoint` was replaced by `startingBehavior != StartingBehavior::NewSimulation`. The difference between the two variants is that `startingFromCheckpoint` was set to false at the end of the first step, while `startingBehavior` stays unchanged throughout the simulation. As a consequence, a line like `(step > 0) && (!startingFromCheckpoint)` used to be true for every step after step zero, except for the first step of a restart. `(step > 0) && (startingBehavior == StartingBehavior::NewSimulation)`, on the other hand, will never be true in simulations restarted from checkpoint. Expanded ensemble is now guarded by a boolean set as
```
            bDoExpanded  = (do_per_step(step, ir->expandedvals->nstexpanded)
                            && (ir->bExpanded) && (step > 0) &&
                            (startingBehavior == StartingBehavior::NewSimulation));
```
which will never be true in restarted simulations.

This bug affects the master and release-2020 branches.

Due to the same change, we are also resetting the force and shake virials to a backup-ed state every step. This does, however, not have any major implications, as the backup is also done every step, and the virials are not used between their backup and reset.

Note that the same problem caused a bugfix in 6529c2da4073fd5930928d17f7dad323de4c2cfd, but failed to detect the full magnitude of the problem.

closed_issues.title: Add CUDA support in thread MPI
closed_issues.description:
Currently, for PP Halo exchange and PP-PME communication, we have two communication paths between GPUs-
1. CUDA direct implementation for Thread MPI which passes buffer addresses, events across different ranks and then does explicit cudamemcpy for data transfer. This code-path was implemented last year and is enabled using GMX_GPU_PME_PP_COMMS and GMX_GPU_DD_COMMS env variables.
2. Implementation for Real MPI using CUDA-aware MPI for which merge request is generated: https://gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs/-/merge_requests/37

The code base for both is encapsulated in same classes but, it is largely different. And, it is an unnecessary development and maintenance overhead. Also, for future tasks such as PME decomposition, we will have to write separate implementation for thread-MPI and real-MPI.

I propose that we add support for CUDA buffers in thread MPI. MPI is not stream aware but, it seems we don't see any performance difference in CUDA-aware MPI and CUDA-direct approaches.
Following are the results I got for different test-cases on 4-GPUs in a single node with thread-MPI and real-MPI-

|               | tMPI (ns/day) | rMPI (ns/day) |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| stmv          | 41.72         | 39.56         |
| Cellulose     | 114.83        | 117.2         |
| adhd          | 376.08        | 382.87        |

For large system, we see minor drop with rMPI but, we see a gain with smaller systems. Moreover, rMPI implementation uses CUDA-IPC for communication which will have some overhead. An implementation in threadMPI will have no such overhead.

Given no perf cost and reduction in code-complexity, it would be good to have CUDA support in thread-MPI implementation.

closed_issues.title: support CI with Intel products
closed_issues.description:
HPCCM supports building a container with intel stuff (see intel*py at https://github.com/NVIDIA/hpc-container-maker/tree/master/hpccm/building_blocks). I can prepare that for icc 19.1 for master branch. Maybe we'll backport icc support to release-2020.

The main stumbling block is the license file. We have several permanent license files from Intel to use for GROMACS CI, some of which were in use in Jenkins, and they're stored in a hidden place on Jenkins (iirc, but I forwarded Roland's original license file emails to Paul anyway). If we have an existing mechanism for storing a secret file and mounting it into a running container, then I'm happy to use that e.g. some way to tell k8s that here's some secret files that should be mounted at /some/path for certain containers.

Otherwise, I suggest we use https://secrethub.io/ which integrates well with gitlab runner - see https://secrethub.io/docs/guides/gitlabci/ and https://secrethub.io/docs/guides/key-files/

I suggest we target icc+mkl in a container built with hpccm for now, on Ubuntu if I can and Centos if I have to. Later we might add impi and/or Intel OpenCL. Later still, DPC++.

closed_issues.title: Refine CI job selection logic and runner requirements
closed_issues.description:
Currently, all jobs require the `k8s-scilifelab` runner tag. Most jobs shouldn't need it, but it prevents any jobs from being able to run in external GitLab CI environments.

Also, there does not seem to be a tag to distinguish jobs that need GPUs from those that don't. I don't know if there is another more appropriate mechanism, but I assume we have a limited number of GPUs in the Kubernetes cluster, and we don't seem to be restricting the number of runners that may simultaneously use one. I wonder if this is why so many CUDA jobs are timing out in the pipelines.

We should use an environment variable provided through the Runner to allow *job:only:variables* or *job:rules:if* to activate only on the GROMACS CI infrastructure.

Also, we should consider reducing the number of jobs executed for pushes that both update a branch and update a merge request: https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/yaml/#exclude-jobs-with-rules-from-certain-pipelines

closed_issues.title: request to speed up grompp
closed_issues.description:
Hello,

(this is a feature request to speed up grompp dramatically).

I am trying to figure out why grompp is so slow when given a long lists of
bonded interactions. For example, my base system takes 7 seconds to run
grompp and 37 seconds to do 100 steps of EM. However, when I add ~250,000
distance restraints grompp takes 3 minutes, and when I add ~600,000
distance restraints grompp takes 18 minutes. In both cases, the mdrun
command is almost as fast as it was without any distance restraints (~42
seconds in each case). I made a bit of progress by converting the distance
restraints to type-6 bonds, in which case the addition of ~250,000 or
~600,000 type-6 bonds results in grompp finishing in 1.5 minutes and 6
minutes, respectively.

These numbers indicate to me that there is some type of non-linear slowdown
when adding bonded interactions (like possibly a check for duplication of
bonded terms as each one is read in, or memory reallocation).

I would appreciate it if anybody knows which routine I should look at to
see if I can get rid of this grompp lag. I am currently working with
gromacs 5.1.2. Newer versions should be OK, but since ideally I want to use
energy group exclusions, gromacs-2020 and it's verlet-scheme-only code is
probably not an option for me. However, I did verify that I get the same
type of non-linear slowdown when adding many bonded terms to gromacs-2020.

* This was recently posted to the gmx users list: https://mailman-1.sys.kth.se/pipermail/gromacs.org_gmx-users/2020-March/128882.html

Thank you,
Chris.

closed_issues.title: apply maintainability updates across all GPU kernels - Redmine #3446
closed_issues.description:
Before the CUDA and OpenCL GPU device code greatly diverges, in order to
improve maintainability, we need to refactor/introduce in the OpenCL
kernels the simplest (form of the) changes made in the CUDA PME kernels:

\- <s>add threadsPerAtom=16 constant</s>

\- move spline calculation to separate clh file

\- introduce the c\_recalculateSplines paths in spread/gather  
- introduce c\_useAtomDataPrefetch code-paths

The items above are the low-effort maintenance needs to avoid major code
divergence. Implementing threadsPerAtom=4 can be considered separately
as in contrast with the above that’s mostly code-path (re)organization,
it is a new feature to be implemented.

about 20% higher for the 2020 version.  
Apparently, it affects the energy calculation steps where the GPU bonded
computational did get significantly slower (as a side-effect of
optimizations that mainly targeted the force-only kernels).

All logfiles of the benchmarks can be found with the following link:  
https://faubox.rrze.uni-erlangen.de/getlink/fiUpELsXokQr3a7vyeDSKdY3/benchmarks\_2019-2020\_all  
Additionally, with this link there are setup files (.tpr/.gro/.top/.mdp
in \`C60xh.7z\`) and scripts, starting the benchmarks (\`runfiles.7z\`).

Some background info on the benchmarks:

\- System contains about 2.1 million atoms.

\- Hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6134 („Skylake“)
`3.2 GHz = 16 cores + SMT; 4x NVIDIA Tesla V100
  (similar results with less significant performance drop (~15%) on a different machine: 2 or 4 nodes with each [2x Intel Xeon 2660v2 („Ivy Bridge“) `
2.2GHz = 20 cores + SMT; 2x NVIDIA Kepler K20\])  
- Several options for -ntmpi, -ntomp, -bonded, -pme are used to find the
optimal set. However the performance drop seems to be persistent for all
such options.

Please let me know, if you need further information.

Cheers,

closed_issues.title: Optimize successive simulation segments - Redmine #3439
closed_issues.description:
Filesystem I/O and various initialization code impose a lot of overhead
in transitioning from one simulation job to the next. Traditionally,
dynamic simulation parameters or bundles of sequential simulation
segments (replica exchange) have required deep integration into the
simulator code. There is a lot of middle ground that could be addressed
to improve the maintainability of logic that is traditionally invasive
and improve the performance of logic implemented outside of the GROMACS
core.

In general, this issue is filed to coordinate discussion of the
reusability of resources within a GROMACS process and the evolution of
lighter-weight transitions between simulation segments.

Two major paths of optimization
-------------------------------

1. **Reduce I/O requirements for resource ownershi** Resources that are
currently expensive to acquire, or that are potentially reusable, need
to have a representation that is decoupled from expensive operations. As
interfaces are converted to be agnostic to filesystem (or other
expensive) sources, we can provide less expensive mechanisms for
resource acquisition or transfer, as appropriate.  
2. **Increase resource reusability.** For various resources that are
historically assumed to be used only once in a GROMACS program, we can
work towards being able to (a) use a resource an arbitrary number of
times in a process, and (b) prototype a new single-use resource on a
previous instance to reduce initialization costs. We need to
compartmentalize resource acquisition and clean-up, identify invariants,
encapsulate the (re)establishment of valid state, and formalize
dependency relationships.

Near term optimization targets
------------------------------

I think the biggest overhead in simulation (re)launch is probably  
(a) the initial file I/O and (presumably to a much lesser degree)  
(b) the coordinate data scatter. Comments? What else?

This seems like a two-step optimization, then, requiring (a) conversion
to initialization from an abstraction that may be memory-backed instead
of file-backed, and (b) allowing the external representation of
TPR/input data to (internally) rely on the data locality management
framework.

Proposed road map
-----------------

1. Decouple gmx::Mdrunner initialization from filesystem I/O (ref
\#3374)  
2. Allow gmx::Mdrunner output to be manipulated/converted into input
(trivial example: extend `nsteps`) for a new runner (complete
reinitialization, but no extra filesystem I/O) through Builder
interaction and/or Prototype pattern.  
3. Begin identifying and handling components that do not always need to
be reinitialized in terms of various inputs/parameters. Avoid
unnecessary reinitialization in special Builder cases.  
4. Expand subscription/signaling for initialization dependencies so that
components can be converted to take charge of their own
(re)initialization logic.

Concepts / Questions
--------------------

General philosophical question: to avoid miscommunication, do we prefer
to think in terms of modifying and reusing a gmx::Mdrunner or separating
out the reusable bits for lightweight creation of new Mdrunners? My
inclination is to use unique and tightly scoped implementation objects
at each level, and to think in terms of optimizing their acquisition,
but this is an important conceptual detail that needs to be clear in
discussion. It seems reasonable to me that the MdModules container might
be longer lived, but previous discussions concluded that long-lived
state should live in outer code scopes, with something like the
SimulationContext (or a conceptual parent XContext) being the only thing
expected to persist for the entire program life time.

Essentially, there are roughly three ways we could think of simulation
segments in terms of evolving the current code base. (1) The work
represented by a gmx::Mdrunner instance, (2) The work represented by a
Simulator instance, or (3) the scope of an API “run” call or call-back
interval. The technical impact of the decision is minimal, but the
architectural impact is significant.

closed_issues.title: Implement additional temperature and pressure control algorithms for modular simulator - Redmine #3423
closed_issues.description:
Currently, the modular simulator implements

-   v-rescale
-   Parrinello-Rahman (both md and md-vv)

Legacy simulator implements

-   Berendsen T-coupling
-   Nose-Hoover (md and md-vv), Nose-Hoover chains (md-vv only)
-   v-rescale
-   Berendsen P-coupling
-   Parrinello-Rahman (md only)
-   MTTK (md-vv, Parrinello-Rahman equivalent with Nose-Hoover, no
    constraints)
-   Andersen (md-vv without constraints only), Andersen-massive (md-vv only)

To be able to call modular simulator feature-complete, we need to either
implement all algorithms in the second list into modular simulator, or
officially deprecate them.

closed_issues.title: Implement modular checkpointing for modular simulator - Redmine #3422
closed_issues.description:
In GROMACS 2020, checkpointing modularization is approximated by passing
around a t\_state object for writing, and restoring using the global
state created by the runner. Moving forward, the checkpointing module
should not need any knowledge about the details of the checkpointed
data.

A possible design to achieve this is to simplify the checkpointing
object to serialize and deserialize a key-value tree. In checkpoint
reading, this tree can then be passed to the constructor / builder of
the modules to restore a previous state. In checkpoint writing, the
checkpointing object passes the tree to its clients, allowing them to
write arbitrary data needed to restore themselves to their current
state.
